ANSWERS. Summer wind, let the hawthorns rest, Leave the blossom to deck the bough. *Nay, I scatter them east and west— Who lasows where they are drifting now ?" Gentle sea, let the white sails stay; Life is brief, and to part is pain. "Nay, I carry them far,away— £ Who knows when they may come again?" Father Time, let the dreamer be; Spare the visions that charm my sleep. "Nay, I laugh at thy dreams and thee; Thou shalt lose them, and wake to weep." Wind, and billow, and ruthless Time, All your triumph shall soon be past! I am bound for a fairer clime, Where lost treasures are found at last. Blooms of summer, and loves of old, Hopes that faded and seemed to die, Things more precious than gems or gold God has stored in His house on high. .--Susclay Magazine. SARAH DOIIDNEY.

The pedant sets himself to teach us what he knows rather than what we want to learn. The anonymous calumniator changes his name which no one knows for that of coward which every one be- stows upon him. "If my employer does not retract what he said to me this morning I shall leave his house." ." Why, what did he say ?" "He told me I could look for another place." It is all very well for our Mentors to tell us to walk so quietly through the world as not to awaken envy or hatred; but, alas ! what are we to do if they never sleep? Husband (jokingly)—" Oh, I'm the mainstay of the family." Wife—S' Yes, and the jibboom, and the—and the—." Small boy (from experience)—" And the spanker, too, mamma.' In the gardens of a certain nobleman's country house there happened to be fixed up at different spots painted boards, with this request—" Please do not pick the towers without leave." Some wag/got a paint brush and added an s to the last word. A Texas cattle man married a refined yoting lady be- longing to the best society of Dallas. A friend meeting him shortly after his marriage congratulated him on his happy fortune. "It's all right, but I had to make sac- rifices," replied the newly--made husband, shaking his . head. " What sacrifices?' "I had to give up going to bed with my boots and spurs on when I came home tired." TAKING THE CHANGE OUT OF is itold Of a popular solicitor that lie recently called upon :another brother of the profession and asked his opinion upon a certain point of law. The lawyer to whom the question was addressed drew himself up and said, "I generally get paid for what I know." The questioner drew half- _ a-crown from his pocket, handed it to the other, and coolly remarked, "Tell me all you know, and give me the change !" Two Irishmen one sultry night, immediately after their arrival in India, took refuge underneath the bed- clothes from a skirmishing party of mosquitoes. At last one of them, gasping from heat, ventured to peep beyond the bulwarks, and by chance espied a firefly which had strayed into the room. Arousing his companion with a punch, he said, "Fergus, Fergus, it's no use. Ye might as well come out. Here's one of the craythurs searchin' for us with a lantern!" JAPANESE COTNS.—The mind of the Japanese prolataire has been much troubled in recent years with regard to the coinage of his country; not that he ever has much of the currency in question, but the Japanese proletaire has no pockets, and he finds it awkward to carry in his hands such coins as he contrives to possess. In ancient times his rulers were more considerate. They punched square holes in the centre of the coins, through which he passed a string, and was thus able to carry about his available capital del tound his neck or to his waistband, which in those days was his sole garment. The coins were not large in amount; it took a thousand of them to make a few shillings, while a cart was required to convey a sovereign's worth. But with civilisation came an im- proved coinage. larger in value, and with to holes, and the pocketless proletaire naturally grumbled that dviii- sation treated him hardly in this respect Paper cur- . rency for small amounts partially satisfied him for a , time, but at last his cries have been heard, and the Japanese Government have promised to issue a new coin specially for his behoof. Its value is rather less than one-fifth pf a halfpenny sterling, and it is to possess the indiepeneable hole, by which he can string it as a child strings beads, and he is probably content.—P ill Malt Gazette. • A LITTLE MAIDEN'S REPLY.—A French teacher was in the, habit of relating to his pupils, as they stood in a semi-circle round him, stories' of illustrions men, and their opinions about them and their actions, rewarding those who. answered well with tickets •of merit. One, day he told them an anecdote of Marshal Turenne. "On a fine, summer day," said he, "while the Marshal was leaning out of his window, only his back towards the room, his valet approached with a very soft step, and gave him a sudden and violent blow with his hand. The pain occasioned the Marshal to cry out; and, turn- ing instantly round, he saw his valet on his knees im- ploring his forgiveness, saying that he thought it was George, his fellow-servant' The question was then put to each of the scholars, "What would you have done to the servant had you been in the Marshal's place?" A haughty lad, who stood first, said, "I would have run him through with my sword." The reply shocked even his comrades, and the master declared he must forfeit the tickets he already had. After putting the question to others, with varying answers, he came at length to a little English girl, who was a visitor, about eight years old. "Now, dear, tell us what you would have done, supposing you had been Marshal Turenne ?" She replied, quite sedately, "I should have said, 'Suppose it had been George, why strike so hard ?' " The simple words drew smiles from the whole school, and all voted that she should have the prize, which such a reply richly de- served. ' THE ORIGIN or rex RIISSIANS.—Those interested in folk lore may perhaps be glad to read', the following legend as to the origin of the Russians found;by Colonel Prjevalsky to be current among the Mongol inhabitants of Zaidan, and published in the Russki Invalide :—" In former times there lived in a cave, far away from all people, a good hermit lama, On priest, who passed his life in praying. A pair of nomads, consisting of an aged mother and her daughter, happened to go that way, and the daughter while tending cattle came upon the cave of the holy lama, who wag at that time ill. The com- passionate maiden offered him some siour:milk, but he did not like to taste it. At last he gave way to her en- treaties, and took the sour milk every day until he got well. Eventually, out of gratitude for:the cure, the lama married the maiden. As soon as the Czar of that country heard of this, he sent his troops to kill the priest who had so flagrantly broken his vows and committed the sin of marriage. When the troops approached the lama gathered a bunch of reeds and stuck them in the ground round his tent, and then by force of prayer caused them to be all turned into soldiers, who defeated the troops of the Czar. The latter sent a second and a third army, but both were beaten, as the lama continued t) pray and turn into more fighting men the reeds broken off by his first created defenders, so that the holy lama soon had a great number of troops. After the defeat of his third army. the Czar left the lama alone in peace, but the latter did not wish to live any longer on the earth. The lama left his wife to,rule the people created fromthe reeds, and from those arose the Rus- sians. They have white bodies, and their hair is often fair, because the stems of the reeds were of a yellowish colour, and the tops somewhat darker."—Times. latmoirrat ANlMALS.—Biitschli. Weismann, and Goette have for some time past maintained, on fairly tenable grounds, that the monocellular Protozoa, i.e., the mar- vellously numerous animals that consist merely of a wide-awake, sensitive, and locomotive stomach-bag, are immortal. These creatures increase and multiply by the very simple device of subellviding. They produce no Children, but split up into unlimited generations of sisters or brethren. One of these animated bags divides itself impartially from mouth downwards, through the middle, but instead of each half flapping open as would a dead bag if thus divided, the severed edges of each section unite, and two bags of equal pattern are pro- duced. I have witnessed the whole proceeding at a sitting within one of those small worlds contained on a strip of glass under a microscope. They remain side by side for a few seconds after completing the fissure, then make a mutual salaam, and each' goes on his way re- joicing, presently to repeat the multiplication. Neither is older nor Younger than ,the other, and thus we have merely a growth forming an endless series, an ever- multiplying brotherhood, every member of which is as old as tho species itself, a survival of its primary Adam. The individuality or personal identity of these creatures must be rather mixed. It has been discussed by Mobius, who maintains that the question of their immortality depends upon the determination of "who's who?" that if the aged individual on the completion of its " fissipar- ous generation" loses its matronly individuality and be- %lnes a duplicated creature with rejuvenated impulsive- ness and susceptibility, while these were gradually fading in the matron, then we must describe these youthful hslves as twin daughters of a dead mother. On the other hand, it is contended that "there are only two alternatives, death and deathlessness. If death occurs let the dead body, the mass of organised matter which has ceased to perform any vital function, be produced." Extrication from this dilemma demands too great a strain of intellect for me to attempt it. I therefore leave .ray readers to decide.—Gentleman's Magazine. .STABLISHRD EAnLY 50 YEARS. To hide a fault with a lie is to replace a blot l*a hole. I Let us respect gray hairs; but, above all, our own.— Petit-Sean. Love pitches its tent in our heart; but friendship builds there. The experience time brings is not worth the illamions it takes away. Livery has saved more than one master from being taken for his valet. Depend upon it, the people who declare they are of no party are not of ours. 1 We forget the origin of a parvenu if he remembers it; we remember it if he forgets it. The defects of an honest man are more readily dis- covered than the vices of a rascal. _ .

As under a hot iron creases disappear, so does the weight of adversity press out of a man ids pride and vanity. Where the intellectual level is low, charlatans rise to distinction. They are like those rocks on the sea-shore which only look high at low water. Public speakers who fret and fume about nothing seem to me like the ships one sees in bad:engravings, with all their sails puffed out while the sea is as smooth as a millpond.—Petit-Senn. TIME PAYMENT.—" You charged me fifty sequins," said a Venetian nobleman, "for a bust that only cost ten days' labour." "You forget," replied the artist, "that I have been thirty years learning to make that bust in ten days." "Hallo !" said a policeman the other night to Brown. "What are you sitting out here in the cold for? Why don't you go into the house ? Have you lost thePley "No," responded Brown; " I—hic—haven't lost the key. I've—hic—lost the key-hole. "Here," said the farmer, as he exhibited a broken jar to a manufacturer, "I packed this jar full of butter, and the jar split from top to bottom. Perhaps you can ex- plain this phenomenon ?" "Oh, yes, I can," was the ready reply, "the butter was stronger than the jar." One day last summer,.as two English students were on their way for a day's fishing on the Earn, they passed through a field where a young rustic beauty, "whose ruddy cheeks made blush the rose," was thinning tur- nips. One said to the other, "Let me give you a laugh at the expense of this lqvely nymph. Ho, there, my beauteous lily, born to blush unseen, come here and I will kiss you, said the would-be wit. She looked up with a sweet smile and a merry twinkle in her eyes, and said, "Na, na, I ne'er was sae fond o' veal as to kiss a cauf."

An epicurean Bishop was neatly taken in by a smart boy at Banbury. Being desirous of testing the famous cakes, he beckoned to the lad to come to the window of the railway carriage, and asked the price of the cakes. "Threepence each, sir," replied the boy. Giving him sixpence, the Bishop desired him to bring one, and added as he was running off, "Buy one for yourself with the other threepence.' Presently the boy returned, munch- ing his "Banbury" and, handing threepence in coppers to the Bishop, announced in the most ingenuous manner, "There was only one left, sir." BRIDGE Acizoss Two CENTURIES.—A remarkable in- stance of a bridge extending across a considerable por- tion of two centuries has been communicated to me by a gentleman of official position resident in Dublin. A near relative of his a hale old gentleman now living, sneaks of having had, when a young man, an intimate friend in Scotland, at that time a vigorous centenarian and in full possession of his faculties, who had fought in 1745 in the battle of "Preston Pans," in which General Gardner was defeated. These two lives, therefore, con. nect the present with that memorable period fatal to the fortunes of Prince Charles Edward and the House of Stuart; and probably, as the Scotchman must have been, assumably, twenty years old when going into ac- tion at Preston Pans, the two lives would connect the present time with the period of George the First, Sir Christopher Wren, Sir Isaac Newton, and the great Duke of Marlborough.—Gentlemait's Magazine. A Mum FRAUD ON BRIDES.—One of the "sights" of Washington is the vault of the Treasury Department, where, among other things, the fifty million dollar re- serve is kept. Besides this there are several cartloads of gold, silver, and greenbacks. People who have been admitted to the vault have, therefore, seen more money, or its equivalent, at one glance than it is possible for them to see at any other place in America, excepting the New York Sub-Treasury. It has long been the custom at the vaults to hand to each bride who entered it a package containing five million dollars (£1,000,000). They were allowed to hold it for a second. It was then carefully taken from them and put away. It has also been generally understood among the knowing ones that this five million dollar package, which has been the bridal portion temporarily of so many brides, did not contain much money; but it was never ascertained exactly what was in the package,until a few years ago, when the count of the treasure in the vault was com- menced. A despatch to the New York Herald says :—"lt was found that this five million package, which has been , so fondly handled, and over which so many endearing words have been said, was simply a huge joke, contain- ing three or four heavy old Government documents, such as would sell in a junk shop for two cents per pound. The package weighed fifteen pounds, and as old paper its value would be thirty cents. The package was carefully tied up •again, and it will continue to be used to make brides happy. It will suit them just as well as if it contained real money." CIGAR SMOKERS.—A gentleman who is a great smoker says that lie has philosophised about smokers with this result—" An even-tempered, quiet man never goes to an extreme in choosing his cigar. A nervous man wants something strong and furious; a mild man, something that smokes and nothing, more. There is a great deal in the way men handle their cigars. If a man smoke his cigar only enough to keep it lighted, and relishes taking it from his mouth to east a look at the blue curl of smoke in the air, set him down as an easy-going man. He has keen perceptions and delicate sensibilities. He will not create trouble, but is apt to see it out when it is once begun. Beware of the man who never releases the grip of the cigar, and is indifferent whether it burn or not. He is cool, calculating, and exacting. He is selfish, energetic, physically, but lives easily off those who perform the labour. The man that smokes a bit, rests a bit, and fumbles the cigar more or less, is easily affected by circumstances. If the cigar go out frequently the man has a whole-souled disposition, is an easy-going fellow with a lively brain, a glib tongue, and generally a fine fund of anecdotes. To hold half of the cigar in the mouth and smoke indifferently is a lazy man's habit. They are generally of little force, and their characters are not of the highest strata. A nervous man who fum- bles his cigar a great deal is a sort of popinjay among men. Holding the cigar constantly between the teeth, chewing it occasionally, and not caring if it be lighted at all, are characteristics of men who have the tenacity of bulldogs. They never forget anything or let go their holds. The fop stands his cigar on end, and an experi- enced smoker points it straight ahe'ad or almost at right angles with his course. Such have been my observa- tions with regard to smokers."

The National Health Society has published the following verses by Sir Alfied Power, who was mainly instrumental in establishing the present poor-law system in Ireland. Sir Alfred Power is now an octogenarian, and lives in retire- ment in Dublin :

There's a skin without, and a skin within, A covering skin and a lining skin ; But the skin within is the skin without, Doubled inwards and carried cdtnpletely throughout. The palate. the nostrils, the windpipe and throat Are all of them lined with this inner coat, Which through every part is made to extend, Lung, liver, and bowels from end to end. The outside akin is a marvellous plan For exuding the dregs of the flesh of man, While the inner extracts from the food and the air What is needed the waste of the flesh to repair. Too much brandy, whisky, or gin Is opt to disorder the skin within; While if dirty and dry, the skin without Refuses to let the sweat come out. Good people all, have a care of your skin, Both that without and that within. To the first, give plenty of water and soap, To the last, little else but water, we hope. But always be very particular where You get your water, your food, and your air; For if these be tainted or rendered impure, It will have its effect on the blood, be sure. The food which will ever for you be the best Is that you like most, and can soonest digest. All unripe fruit and decaying flesh Beware of, and fish that is not very fresh. Your water, transparent and pure as you think it, Bad better be filtered and boiled are you drink it, Unless you know surely that nothing unsound Can have got to it over or under the ground. But of all things the most I would have you beware Of breathing the poison of once-breathed air: When in bed, whether out or at home you may be, Always open the windows and let it go free. With clothing and exercise keep yourselves warm, And change your clothes quickly if caught in a storm. For a cold caught by chilling the outside skin Flies at mica to the delicate lining within. All you who thus kindly take care of your skin, And attend to its Wants without and within, Need never of cholera feel any fears, • And your skin may last you a hundred years.

div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1885. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- COTTAGE GARDENING I IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. CULTURF, to
At a recent rent audit, Mr. James Rankin, M.P., of Bryngwyn, Herefordshire made an abatement of 12f per cent, on the rents of his estate.

It is said that Mr. James Ashbury, late member for Brighton, has become a large landed proprietor in New Zealand. He has bought some 26,000 or 27,000 acres of land, upon which no corn will be grown save for station purposes, and which will be stocked to its fullest capa- city with oxen and sheep. CLOTTED CREAM.—I send "A Young Housekeeper" the following directions for preparing clotted cream:— Strain the milk into tins or brass pans; let it stand twelve or twenty-four hours, according to weather; place it over a hot plate or ordinary-covered stove, and scald it for about an hour. The heat must be gentle and steady. When the cream rises in small bubbles on the surfaces it is sufficiently done; if it boils, it is spoilt. It needs a little experience. Let it stand in the cool dairy twenty-four hours before skimming.—DEvoNuar. RENT AGITATION.—As an outcome of the existing agri- cultural depression, a meeting of the tenants on Lord Scarsdale's estate was held at Derby last week, when it , was stated that an application which had been made for a reduction in rent, owing to depreciation in the value, of live stock and all kinds of farm produce, had been declined, a conditional promise being made to allow 10 per cent, reduction in November. It kvas resolved that those of the tenants who could should pay the past half- year's rent, and if no return were received in seven days another meeting be convened. PASTITB.ES.—Att address on "Pastures and laying them down" was delivered on Monday by Professor Car- ruthers (Consulting Botanist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England), before the members of the Seven- oaks Chamber of Agriculture. Mr. Carruthers advocated a careful examination of the old pastures, which were too often full of worthless grasses and weeds. He be- lieved it would pay to break them up, and to introduce grasses for fat stock and to supply food for the most part of the year. He dealt more especially with laying down land at present 'cultivated with permanent pas- ture, pointing out half a dozen grasses which should be introduced into all good pasture, viz., cocksfoot, foxtail, meadow, and tall fescue, Timothy and rough-stalked meadow grass. To these he added the clovers. WARBLES IN CATTLE.—Mr. Duckham publishes the re- sult of an experiment against these pests in his herd. He says :—I had each cow dusted along the back with sulphur. The result is that only two cows had one soli- tary deposit each, the others are perfectly free, whilst there are several in the backs of their calves. To those deposits I have used carbolic acid mixed with hog's lard, in the proportion of one to twenty, with excellent effect. I may add that that mixture is also a safe and effectual cure for ringworm, which is often so troublesome with young cattle. Mr. Duckham adds that the use of mercurial ointment, as recommended in Miss Ormerod's remedy for the warble, is one that requires great cau- tion in using, or the remedy will be worse than the disease. A few years ago a neighbour of his dressed his young cattle for lice with a mercurial preparation; they licked it off and were poisoned. Such a result cannot follow his remedy, and he has proved its efficacy. FARMERS' ASSOCIATION FOR CROSTON AND LEYLAND DISTRICT.—At a farmers' association meeting, recently held in the room adjoining the Railway Tavern, Croston, it was considered desirable that the objects for which the association has been established should be fully ex- plained to the farmers and public generally. The assd- ciation has been established to afford the members easy and convenient means of meeting together to transact business or to discuss any subjects interesting to agri- culturists, as for instance the rating of farm lands and buildings, railway rates, and charges; the adjustment of tithe and other rents; the representation of farmers' in- terests in Parliament; the cultivation of land and rota- tion of crops; and the cultivation of waste and unim- proved lands, which would find employment for the labouring: classes; the best means of raising, grow- ing, and feeding stock; the ensilage question; the question of compensation to tenants for land required for railways and other works; and to advise with, 'and if considered necessary to assist, morally or otherwise, any member that may be deemed by the association to be suffering from the before-named or other causes; also to promote, by all available means, including lectures by scientific men, in conjunction with landlords, land- agents, and others interested in the prosperity and suc- cess of agriculture any object likely to be beneficial to the agriculture of the country. A large number of farmers and others interested in agriculture have already joined the association; a secretary has been appointed, and a large and influential committee, with power to add to their number, has been selected. The committee hope that agriculturists, \landowners, agents, and the public generally will unite in supporting the association.

WEST OF ENGLAND SOCIETY. Monday week was the opening day of the great show held at Brighton in connection with the Bath and West of England Society, the second of the more important agricultural associa- tions in the kingdom. This was the first occasion on which the society bad visited Brighton. The greatest increase was in the classes for horses for other than agricultural purposes, and for Jersey and Guernsey I cattle; but Devons, Shorthorns, Herefords, and Sussex cattle were about stationary, whflst sheep showed only a small increase. The nett result was to show 1,057 en- tries at Brighton against 792 last year. Poultry, on the other hand showed a considerable falling-off. Besides the livestock,e there was a large and varied exhibition of implements, machinery, and other matters of a more or 1 less miscellaneous kind of interest to agriculturists, whether on a large or small scale. One of the special exhibitions was the working dairy, a model of what the interior of a dairy should be—cool, clean, and comfortable, with great pans of milk settling calmiy into cream, in readiness for the experimental lec- ture with illustrations, when Miss Smithard ex- pounded the latest science of butter making, or Mr. James Long endeavoured to make an English audience appreciate the merits of his systems of making the soft cheeses of the Continent. Efere, too, the manager of the dairy on the Devonshire .estate of that warm sup- porter of the association, Sir T. D. Acland, Bart., M.P., illustrated the making of Devonshire butter and cream. On Wednesday Viscount Hampden presided at the an- nual meeting of the society. The report showed that, in order to meet the requirements of the time, the society had commenced making arrangements for ex- perimenting on the wheat crops of the coming season, and also proposed to test the advantages or otherwise of the use of artificial manures on corn and grass on land in ordinary farming condition, to examine any new pro- cesses for dealing with agricultural produce which ap- pear likely to be beneficial, such as the manufacture of soft cheeses, improvements in dairying, and storing green crops as ensilage; and further, to collect and pub- lish information on new systems of cultivation and routine of crops. FEEDING wen' SILAGE.—The report of the Ensilage Committee of the Highland and Agricultural Society, drawn up by Mr. Mackenzie, of Portmore, and published in the current number of the Transactions, details an ' expenment in .cattle feeding with totally different re- sults from those brought out at Woburn. Twelve selected cattle were divided into two lots of six each. To one lot was given a daily ration of 301bs. turnips and 141bs. oat straw per bead. To the other lot was given a daily ration of 281bs. silage, made partly from rye-grass and clover and partly from the product of a leafield hained. An allowance of mixed linseed and cotton-cake, at the rate of 44/lbs. per head per diem, was also givenl to both lots. The experiment extended from February 14th to June 17th, in which time the silage-fed anhnals showed a total average gain of 'cwt. lqr. 18ilbs. per head, while the turnip and straw fed beasts had only in- creased in the average of lcwt. 25ilbs. per head in the samerime. On the 14th of February the silage animals were on the average 81bs. heavier than those on turnip; on the 14th of April this difference had increased to 491bs. ; but, when turned out to grass on May 12th, the turnip animals had recovered Illbs. of the difference, and five weeks later, on 17th June, they had recovered Illbs. more. When killed (in August) those which had been wintered on silage were on the average 2st. 111bs. heavier in carcase than those which had been wintered' on turnip, and dressed 71.84 per cent, of their weight at the commencement of the experiment against 67.24 per cent, of the turnip lot. The latter fact, if substan- tiated in future experiments, must be reckoned of con- 1 siderable value. The daily gain appears to have been very irregular in the different months—from less than 11b. to over 21bs. per head per day—and for the whole period, even in the case of the silage fed beasts, it only' averages something like lillas. per head per day. It must be recollected, however, that the animals were not highly fed. Mr. Mackenzie's report goes on to state that during the past winter ensilage has been tried on its own merits in conjunction NI ith cake for fattening sheep. A flock of 110 three-year-old black-faced wethers was placed in a field which had been hained and 'cut for silage in September. They received a daily ration of cake (linseed and cotton mixed) at no time exceeding lilbs., and silage at the rate of 101bs. each pier diem was given them, in racks made of wire sheep netting. After they began to get fat this was reduced to 81bs. They throve very well upon this food, and to all appearance did as well, relatively, as another flock of black-faced wethers which were fed on cake and turnip. The mode of feeding the ensilage, however, gave rise to consider- able waste; so much so that Mr. Mackenzie expresses an opinion that a saving of 21bs. per head per diem might have been effected by feeding in boxes. It is a pity the sheep were not weighed at the beginning and close of the experiment.

Dap4st, 114 & 116 Southampton Row, London.—Advt. TERRIBLE MURDER IN Cox.—Michael Cashman was brutally murdered in Cork off Sunday in a lonely pathway within half a mile of Mil:-street. A party lay in wait for him, as it was known he would pass the place on his way home. His head was battered in with a large stone, which was found en the spot, his brain protruded,and his body was mutilated in a shocking manner. It is stated that he has opposed those in the locality who attempted to boycot cer- tain persons.

SEICDS, GOOD AND Ben.—Last year was exceptionally fine for maturing seeds, and as their coming up when properly sown must depend upon that, such a season is a boon to seed growers, seedsmen and the retail buyers or sowers. All honest seedsmen artificially test their seeds before sending any out to their customers and are consequently aware of the per cent,age that ought to come up. If this is small they add to the number of the seeds, or warn the sower to sow thicker than usual; if large they may add 10 or 20 per cent, of old seeds and no one is any wiser or worse off, as in nine cases out of 10 seed. 4 are grown too thickly. Our attention has been drawn this season- to several failures of seeds coming up, but in nearly every instance it was apparent that the seed had germinated but had either been crippled by the continuous cold weather during April and May, or were eaten off by slugs before they had come fairly above ground. It is a rare occurrence for us to have to com- plain of the quality of seeds, and we have received them from various dealers. In fact, we cannot recall an in- stance of any importance and with the recollection of the glorious season of 1884, we . never expected to ex- perience such an unfortunate incident in 1885. Two sorts of parsnips were soivn side by side, the student germinated as well as could be expected, but of the other, the Hollow Crowned, scarcely a seed has come up. It is, however, only fair to state that both were cheap, and one, decidedly "nasty" and were not pro- cured from a professional seedsman. Someone must have acted dishonestly in the matter._ Either the un- scrupulous wholesale dealer took advantage of the ignor- ance and incapacity of the retailer to test the seed and supplied him with old ones, reserving the good seeds of 1884 to mix with older or bad seed to be supplied to those whom he dare not clie,at ; or the retailer, having a quan- tity of old seeds, or may be only those of 1883, and thinking they would be all right (which they ought to be if properly stored), distributed them amongst his customers. Those who had only the one kind had their failure credited to their own ignorance or negligence. We learn two lessons from this occurrence: that cheap wares are frequently very dear, and in the case of seeds it is always wisdom if only an ounce of seeds is ordered, to have two sorts of half-an-ounce each.

THE Frtowr GABDEN.—Recent rain has made us very busy, pricking out or planting such flowers as Asters, Zinnias, Scabiosa, &c. Our method of planting these is to place one in the centre of the space and four more at equal distance round it; or, if the space is small, place three forming a. triangle. The patches of each sort are disposed of as nearly as possible the same distance apart, and those that are likely- to grow the tallest are placed at thh back or middle, just as it hap- pens whether we are dealing with a bed or border. All small plants as the above will require watering if dry weather sets in till it is seen that they do not droop during the day. Dahlias have been planted in holes already prepared for them, and each plant has been pro- vided with a stake. If the plants are small, these sup- ports need not be the full length at first, but others in proportion to the vigour of the plant should be inserted, and the plant securely tied to it; but anything like a strangled appearance should be guarded against. Much vigilance must be exercised, or slugs will soon devour every plant. When in a small stage, and in addition to a belt of lime or soot placed round each plant in the evening, they should be visited later on with a lamp, and every slug picked up and placed in a • vessel con- taining lime or salt, and an end will be put to their ex- istence.

WlNDOW.—Balsams if not kept potted will soon come to a stand-still. They delight in a rich compost, such as a little fresh horse excrement, rubbed so fine that it may pass through a quarter-inch sieve; two or three handsful are sufficient to add to a peck of soil. At each potting the plants should .be kept low down by Rutting less soil under than might be deemed neces- sary for the majority of plants, so that when they re- ceive their last shift the bottom side branches will be near the rim of the pot. If it is intended to exhibit these plants during August or September, and the plants are at present starved and elongated, we would prefer to start with others late as it is, as more creditable re- sults might be produced, especially if the seeds could be raised, in a greenhouse or frame, where they would germinate in less than a week. From that stage their tops must be kept close to the glass to prevent their growing long jointed. They may be placed out of doors at the end of this month in a warm sunny corner plunged in the soil, ashes, or any material of that kind. Any one living near a tanyard should procure a few barrow loads of spent bark, and supply their plants with bottom heat.

Tag, MorirragiAL Camts.—Lord Gassy:ELLE said: I have now to inform your lordships that Mr. Gladstone ten- dered his resignation and that of his colleagues to Her Majesty who has been graciously pleased to accept it, and to send for Lord Salisbury who is at this moment at Bal- moral. Under these circumstances, we shall not proceed , with any of the ordinary business, except the Redistribu- tion Bill.—Lord KIMBERLEY, in asking their lordships to consider repo., tof amendment to the Re listribution Bill, said be had the full concurrence of Lord Salisbury. A new clause had been introduced providing that elections should take place after the Ist of November.—Lord Caaxnaoox, on behalf of Lord Salisbury, consenting, the report was aged to, and the Bill was read a third time.—The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FaIDAT. The House met at four o'clock. , There was a very full attendance of members when the Speaker took the chair. Sir M. Beach and Mr. Gibson were the first to take their seats on the front Opposition bench. They were soon afterwards joined by Lord R. Churchill, James Lowther, Sir W. Hart Dyke, Lord John Manners, and Sir R. Cross. Sir S. Northcote entered at 25 past four' and was received with cheers. On the Ministerial bench were Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Childers, Mr. G. Russell, and Mr. Ashley. When Lord R. Grosvenor entered he was re- ceived with cheers. He was followed by Sir C. Dilke, and at half-past four Mr. Gladstone entered the House, and was received with very loud cheers. THE RESIGNATION OF THE GOVERNMENT. After a tew notices of motion had been given, Mr. GiLinsirona rose, and was again loudly cheered. He said he wished to communicate to the House what had taken place since he informed it that the Cabinet had made a dutiful communication to her Majesty. The communica- tion, it was perfectly understood, was the resignation of the Cabinet. The communication was sent to Balmoral on the 6th; it reached on the 10th, and on the 11th a cotnmuni- tion was received from her Majesty stating that she accepted the resignation tendered and that she had sent for Lord Salisbury. He stated that the resignation arose out of the vote on Tuesday. He had nothing further to state than that Lord Salisbury left town last night, and, under these circumstances, it was impossible for him to have communication with him. In ordinary circumstances, he should have moved that the House at its rising should adjourn until Monday, but there was mentioned on Tuesday the Redistribution Bill. It was necessary that that Bill should be censidered and com- pleted as early possilsle and it was now being considered by the House of Lords. There were no serious differences likely to arise, and therefore be reseectfully suggested that the amendments might be considered that evening.—Sir S. rapidly ycargas agreed that amendmentsthat thei Bill weresho notuld proceedyet printed, as and from communications he bad received he doubted possible. whether they could be considered that evening.—The sitting of the House was then eitspeeded. At ten minutes past five the Redistribution Bill was brought from the House of Lords —Sir C. Ditarz moved that the amendments be printed and considered on Monday next.—This was agreed- to and the House at a quarter past five adjourned until Monday. , _ HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mosmalt.

IThe Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. 'lna CHANGE OE GOVERNMENT.—ViECOBIIt CBANBROOIC, in the absence of the Marquis of Salisbury, and by his re- quest, moved that the House adjourn till Friday next, by which day he hoped to make a statement.—Earl Gnat/- VILLE agreed with the motion. The Burial Board (Contested Elections) tilt was read a second time. , The House rose at 4-35. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MosmAr. The Speaker took the chair at 3-50. Between that time and half-past four, when public busi- ness began, there was an entire absence of the excitement that marked the beginning of Friday's sitting, the only cheer being when Mr. Gladstone took his seat on the Treasury bench. A short time previouily Lord G. Hamil- ton had held a short consultation with Lord R. Grosvenor on that bench and afterwaids the noble lord had crossed the floor to speak with Sir S. NorthcAe. At half-past four the House was full, but the Strangers' Galleries were only ap- proaching that condition. On the , motion of Sir C. Forster,,the Standing Orders were suspended to allow of nineteen private bills being read a third time. NOTICES.—Sir G. CAMPBELL: J beg to give notice that on the first convenient day L hall ask the right bon. member for North Devon whether, its the event of his taking part in a new. Administration—(laughter)—if he Will advise his colleagues to consider if it might not be possible to save the country the burden of two enormous pensions to two Lard %ancellers, by inviting the present Chancellor to continue his non-political functions. (Loud laughter) THE MINISTERIAL CRISIS.—THE ALLEGED "ASSURANCES." MS. GLADSTONE said be had received authentic informa- tion that Lord Salisbury had undertaken the formation of a Government, and that it would be convenient if the House at this early stage of the proceedings adjourned until Friday. He therefore proposed that the House should agree to this, but should make an exception from the rule of not proceeding with any public business in favour of the Lords' Amendments to the Se its Bill, and also of the Princess Beatrice's Annuity Bill. There was also a capital sum granted in addition, but that would not be proceeded with, as the judgment of the House had net been passed on It in any form, until it could be introduced by a responsi- ble Minister. Sir S. Northcote having expressed his concurrence in this proposal, Mr. COLLINGS asked that an exception should also be madel in favour of his Medical Relief Bill, bat Mr. GLADSTONE! thought this inadmissible. , Mr. LABOUCHEBB Said: We have recently seen state- ments that there is some species of negotiation going on be. tween the leaders of the present Opposition and her Majesty's Government, and that the Government are about to give certain assurances to the Conservative party that, should they take office, they would not oppose them. ("Oh, oh ! ' from the Ministerialists below the gangway.) In the Standard It is stated that they must do this as patriots, because the Ministers have brought the country into such a deplorable state that they ought to be thankful to any one who gets the country out of that state. (Opposition cheers.) In The Times if is stated that Ministers ought to take this course, and indeed that they Intend to do it, and that without this course the present Opposition will not take office because the Ministers themselves committed a species of suicide. I think it desirable that these statements should be put at rest at once. Hon. and ri4ht bon, gentlemen opposite during the present session have done their very best to turn out her Majesty's advisers. They. were warned beforehand that if they did so they would have to accept office. Under these circumstances I would ask the Prime Minister whether there is any truth in the statements and whether anything beyond that aid will be afforded to the leaders of the Conservative party to carry on the Government which the Conservative party have afforded to her Majesty's present advisers during the present session. Mr. GraapsroNE: All I can say is that I have no cogni- sance of any such communications. I can commit nobody, I can promise nothing, I can refuse nothing. lam abso- lutely without any information. (Ministerial cheers.) The motion was agreed to, as was another motion that all Committees should have leave to sit notwithstanding the adjournment of the House. THE SEATS BILL.—REVOLT FROM SIR S. NORTH- COTE. _ _ _

- - -- On the order of the day for consideration of the Lords' amendment to the Seats Bill, Sir H. D. WOLFF moved the adjournment of the debate. There was no responsible Government or Opposition, and certain amendments entirely altered the character of the Bill. A new clause giving the judges the right to appoint additional revising barristers was indirectly an infringe- ment of the privileges of the House, which alone was en- titled to initiate any extra expenditure. These things had been done at the instance of a Liberal Government. Sir C. DILKE, noting the hon. gentleman's reflection on the Liberal Government, said the amendment for Accelerating the registration was put in the Bill at the instance of Lord Salisbury. The Government's intention was to introduce a separate Bill. Sir S. NORTHCOTE confirmed what the right hon. baronet had said as to the consultation with his noble friend. Mr. GORST found fault with the substance of the clauses, but said it was desirable that the introduction by the Lords of clauses not germane should not be drawn into a prece- dent There was no hurry for these provisions. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL assured the House that there was every reason for taking care not to lose a single day. If these clauses were objectionable the House could deal with them when they were reached. Lord R. CHURCHILL, who rose amid laughter and cheers, said the House was just going to set a precedent for which there was no justification. Were the Government prepared to contend that the delay of business for a few days— namely, till Friday—would really cause the country any inconvenience ? But with regard to the new clauses, it was obvious that the House oualat not to proceed. for the House of Lords had—no doubt igne.rantly—(laughter)—at the instance of the Government—(hear, hear)—imposed a pecuniary burden upon the people. In the absence of any responsible Government, such an extraordinary innovation on the constitution of the country was monstrous. But supposing that the country did suffer inconvenience from being unable to proceed at the present moment with the Lords' amendments, whose fault was it—wbo had thrown the country into this state of confusion ? (Opposition cheers and counter cheers.) Aye, not only thrown the country into this state of confusion, but deliberately and with malice aforetbought—Klepposition cheers)—prepared the inconvenience under which the House was now suffer- ing. (Laughter and cheers.) Was it not a notorious thing that the whole of the events of Monday night, the inconve- nience of which they were now suffering from—cries of " Order.") The SPEAKER said the noble lord was going beyond the question. Lord RANDOLPH Cretrnctum, would not proceed with his remarks. He ventured to say that there was ne precedent for proceeding with the bill without having at command responsible advisers. He trusted that the leaders of what was called the Constitutional party in this country—(Min- isterial laughter and ironical cheers)—would not sanction a precedent which some day or other might have most in- convenient and dangerous consequences. (Hear, hear.)

BRUTAL WIFE MURDER.—The wife 43, a farmer named Esaan, living between Horseleap and Kilbeggan, County Westmeath, was found dead in her house on Sunday morn- ing. The suspicions of the neighbours being aroused by stslinass within the house, an entrance was eff cteil, and Mrs. Eagan was found lying dead in a pool of blood, with several punctured wounds about the neck and body. A pitchfork lay on the floor near the body. and this was besmeared with blood.) Eagan was afterwards discovered sitting in a ditch on his farm. It is stite4 that for some time past he has been suffering from mental depression. He has been arrested.

THB DEVIL ON A WINDMILL. There are on the Con- tioent sotne spots in which the bicycle is still a novelty. One of these seems to be Northeril Denmark. A corres- pondent relates that he recently made a bicycle tour in Jutland ; and that, upon a second time passing through a small village near Viborg. he was told a story which for a day or two had much exercised the minds of the local gossips. On the occasion of his first visit to the neighbour- hood the bicyclist was benighted, and, having lighted his lamp, rode at topmost speed for many miles along a lonely highway in the dark. He was seen by a passing countryman, who, stricken with terror, fell upon is knees, and was found in that attitude by a belated letter carrier. "What is the matter ? " the postman asked. " What, in- deed I " stammered the peasant ; "for the devil has just gone by on a Windmill ; and God have mercy upon me 2"

Mr. GemasTwee sympathised with those who disliked the practice of inserting in the House of Lords clauses which do not impose charge directly, but which do so as a natural consequence. But it had become a settled practice. If, however, they were to be rejected, why not de so when they came te them. The main question was whether this subject should be entertained at all in the absence of a fully responsible Government. They asked for an adjournment until Fiday, and said there could be no very great evil in that. Their adjourning till Friday would very materially aggravate in inconvenience. But there could be no respon- sible Government on Friday next. (Hear, hear.) The ut- most that could happen was that Lord Salisbury and his friends through their proper agests should move certain writs for the re-election of certain members ; but until those gentleman had been returned and had taken their places, there would be no means of meeting the objection that there was not a responsible Government. That day fortnight would be the earliest day on which it was possible to entertain the question with a responsible Government fully installed on the Treasury Bench. He found no danger in the precedent, first of all from the extreme peculiarity of the circumstances, which could hardly recur; and secondly, from the general assent of the House. Sir M. HICKS-BEACH supported Lord R. Churchill's con- tentions. He said he maintained that in the difficult posi- tion in which the House was placed it should not be asked to take any contentious point. He thought his right hon. friend and others who had been in favour of proceeding had only done so with respect to business that was uncon- tested. (" Oh, oh.") Sir W. HARCOURT :—The right hon, gentleman has said that we are placed in a difficult position. Well, of course we are, because my right lion. friend has made a proposal to the House which has been accepted and approved by the leader of the Opposition—(Ministerial cheers)—and then the noble lord the member for Woodstock (Lord R. Churchill) gets up and denounces the proposal, and he is supported by the iight hon. gentleman the member for Gloucestershire (Sit M. Hicks-Beach.) (Ministerial cheers.) No doubt that is a difficult position, but it has not been created either by those who for the moment sit upon these benches or by the leader of those who sit upon the benches opposite. ([fear, hear.) I take it that if we are in a diffi- culty the responsibility rests with the noble lord the mem- ber for Woodstock and the right hon. gentleman the member for Gloucestershire. (Ministerial cheers.) The whole question, however, is one not only for the convenience of the House. but for the convenience of the country and the eonstitnencies. (M nisterial cheers.) Of course we are not in a position to dictate to or to put pressure upon the House ; but I think this is a matter which ought to he de- termined by the free vote of the House. (Hear, hear.) Then take on the one side my right hon. friend (Mr. Glad- stone) and the right hon. member for North Devon (Sir S. Northcote), and on the other the noble lord the member for Woodstock—laughter) —and the right hon. gentleman the member for Gloucestershire, and decide between them. (Hear, hear.) Well the reason why we, at all events, have recommended this course to the House is on account of the very great inconvenience which it is impossible to exaggerate, that will result from the delay of this matter for a fortnight. It was the facts brought before Lord Salisbury as to the great evils which would ensue to those charged with making up the registers which are to be the foundation of the future elec- tions, and upon which the rights of the constituencies rest, that induced 4rd Salisbury to ask us to take the course which has been taken, and that argument equally applies to our going on with the matter now. That, no doubt, is the reason why the right hon. gentlemen the member for North Devon, who has been—and I believe the right hon. gentle- man the member for Gloucestershire was not—(laughter)— in constant communication with Lord Salisbury in reference to this bill, approved not only of the introduction of the acceleration clauses in the House of Lords, but the taking into consideration these clauses to-night in order that the House of Lords may deal with it on Friday. We desire to carry out to the end the spirit in which this bill has been conducted from the commencement, and I sincerely hope that on one of the last stages of the measure in the House of Commons it will not be made the subject of a party fight (Cheers.)

Mr. RAIKES said that the Government, in asking the House to discuss at a moment of general excitement and confusion provisions entirely new to that House with regard to registration, had done their best to embitter the last moments of the bill. (Hear, hear, and Ministerial groans.) The Government, in dealing with this matter, were anxious to divest themselves of the responsibility which was at- tached to them as long as they sat upon the Bench oppo- site, and to shelter themselves behind the names of Lord Salisbury and Sir S. Northcote. ("114, no.")* lie booed it was not too late to postpone for a fortnight—(cries of Oh") —the serious questions which bad been raised. Mr. COWEN suggested, as a compromise, that the clauses of the bill proper should be passed, and that the new matter which had been introduced into it should be postponed.

Mr. LEWIS approved this suggestion, maintaining that the proposal as to the new registers coming into force on Nov. 7th were too hastv.—The hon. member's remarks were in- terrupted by Mr..DILLWYN, who asked if they were relev- ant.—The SPEAKER ruled that they were. Lord J. MANNERS regarded this suggestion from the House of Lords as a wise one; but nevertheless thought that, under present circumstances, the proposal of the hon. member for Newcastle (Mr. Cowen) might very well be acted upon. Mr. O'DONNELL wished the right bon. member for North Devon (Sir S. Northcote) to make an explanation in order that hon. members might know whether he accepted the views of the noble lord in the other House, or of the noble lord in this Reuse. (Laughter.) He (Mr. O'Donnell) was somewhat concerned for the unity of the future Govern- ment, because under present circumstances those who were to form it seemed nearly as divided as the united Liberal party. (Laughter.) Mr. RITCHIE, who rose amid cries of " Divide " from the Ministerialists, was very desirous to koow the views of the Government en the suggestion of the hon. member for Newcastle. Sir R. CROSS, speaking amid ironical laughter and cries of " Vote," urged the Government to give their opinion upon the suggestion. The House divided : For the adjournment Against ' 333-298 The result was received with loud Ministerial chee-s. The House proceeded to consider the Lords' amendment. —On a Lords' amendment which raised the question of accelerating the coming into force of the registers, Sir C. DILKEI moved that the House agree with the Lords' amendment —Mr. C. LEWIS said that it was impossible in many instances to get the revised lists ready for the 7th of November. Mr. GORST thought the two front Opposition benches— for there were now two Oppositions in the Hous3—(laughter) —were agreed as to the convenience of postponing these clauses. ' Sir W. HARCOURT said if there were two Oppositions, there was, it appeared, a third Opposition opposed to both, and re- presented by the hon. gentleman. (Laughter,) The Govern- ment adhered to the arrangement nude with Lord Salis- bury in this matter, and therefore had proposed to agree with the Lords' amendment. Sir S. NORTHCOTE explained that Lord Salisbury's sole ob- ject was to save time. That was a different thing from saying with regard to the clause that there should he any attempt to shorten discussion on what the House theughi right to discuss. It struck him that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Newcastle before the last division was a reason- able one, and that if the House thought proper when they came to the discussion, the clauses, if necessary, might be set aside.—The amendment was agreed to. The other Lords' amendments were all agreed to, with the exception of the lncarporation of Jedburgh with the Border Burghs, which, on the motion of Mr. TREVELYAN, was disagreed from; and another. changing the name of a division of Yorkshire from Spen Valley to Birstal, was also reversed.
_ _ THE PRINCESS BELTR/CE'S ANNITI TY BILL was read a third time.

DISFRANCHISEMENT BY MEDICAL RELIEF AND Copy. BOLD ENFRANCHISEMENT.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in pursuance of his pledge at an earlier period of the evening, moved that the House do now adjourn. This was object ql to by Mr. CoLuNas, on the ground that it would deprive him of the opportunity of introducing his bill abolishing disquali- fication for the receipt of medical relief. and after a long conversation, in the course of which the TreasurV B.nch disappeared en maw, the motion was negatived by 55 to 32. The Government Orders were gone through and post- poned seriatim, and after the first private member's bill. the Copvhold Enfranchisement Bill, had been committed pro forma, Mr. T. HILL moved that the remaining Orilsrs be postponed until Friday. This was carried on a division, after a long conversation, in which Mr. H. FoWLER strongly protested against legislation in the middle of a Ministerial crisis, and Sir S. NORTHCOTE supported the nnothn.—Mr. Collings then brought in his bill, which was read a first time. The House adjourned at 9-50 until Friday.
