THE POLITICAL CRISIS. LORD SALISBURY'S RETURN FAOM BALMORAL. BALMORAL, Starney.---The Marquis of Salisbury had an nudience of the Queen previous to leaving Baluaoral, and has accepted office. The Marquis left the Castle yesterday.

—Court Circular. The Marquis of Salisbury left Balmoral Castle about two o'clock on Saturday afternoon in one of Her Majesty's car- riages, and proceeded to Balloter, where he joined the "Queen's Messenger" special train, and arrived at Aberdeen at half-past four. the train has four stoppages between Ballater and Aberdeen, but only at Banff and Banchory was there any demonstration. At these stations a considerable crowd had gathered and raised a cheer as the train departed. As the train steamed into Grahamston station Lord Salis- • bury was loudly cheered. A stoppage of five minutes was made, daring which calls were made for &speech, but the Marquis simply bowed his acknowledgments, and the train moved on amid cheers and hooting for Salisbury, mingled with cries of "Gladstone for every" His lordship reached the Waverley Station, Edinbargh, at about a quarter-past ten o'clock. There also a crowd had assembled, in expecta- tion of his arrival, and upon the train drawing up he was enthusiastically cheered. His lordship on leaving the rail- way carriage walked arm in arm with Ur. Macdonald., dean of faculty, to the -east refreshment room, followed by the crowd, cheering and waving their hats. The throng 'fol- lowed into the refreshment room, which was aeon killed, and there were cries for a speech, but the Marquis retired into a side room. When he left he was again cheered and fol- lowed to the carriage, where theezrowd remained till the train left for the South at 10.40. At the Haymarket Station also a cordial demonstration was made in favour of the Conservative leader, and again at 'Berwick. The remainder of the journey was without particular incident until the train arrived at Hatfield at 8-25 on Sunday morning. Lord Saliabury's secretary, who arrived in 'London on Sunday afternoon from liatiAd, immediately proceeded to Sir Stafford Northeotefs hose, and subsequently Mr. Row- land Winn, the Conservative whip, had an interview with Sir Stafford Northcote. LordSowton also called upon Sir Stafford Nerthcote, and remained with him for a consider- oble time. The Duke of Richmond and Gordon, who be- fore Lord Salisbury's accession to the peeragetilled the post of Conservative leader in the Upper House, and the Hon. Edward Stanhope, who filled the post of Under Secretary for India in the former Administration, alsO,called upon Sir

Stafford. CONFERENCE OF CONSERVATIVES.—" A HAPPY FAMILY." The Marquis of Salisbury left Hatfield at a quarter past eleven o'clock on Monday morning, and arrived at the King's Cross Station of the Great Northern Railway at twenty minutes to twelve o'clock. He was there met by his nephew, Mr. A. J. Iletfour, M.P. The noble marquis drove in Mr. Balfour's carriage from the railway station to his town house in Arlington-street, where he arrived exactly at noon. The senior whipeof the Cosservative party, Mr. Row- land Winn, had reached Arlington-street about ten minutes previously. He remained there waiting in company with Sir Stafford Northcote. The Earl of Carnarvon arrived at twenty five minutes past twelve, and was shortly followed by Lord Harrowby, -Sir R. Cross, Lord Cranbrook, and Lord efohn Manners. Me. W. H. Smith arrived almost immedia- tely afterwards, and then came Lord George Hamilton and Sir M. Hicks-Beech. Although Mr. Balfour was at Arling- ton-street, he did not attend the meeting; neither did Lord Henry Lennox, who called, but stayed only a few minutes. The meeting did not occupy more than two hours, but the Duke of Richmond left shortly before its conclusion. Mr. W. H. Smith arid Lord Cranbrook left together, followed by Lord John Manners, Sir R. Cross, Lord George Hamilton, Lord Cranbrook, the Earl of Harrowby, Sir Stafford North- cote, and Mr. Rowlaed Winn. The last to leave was Sir M. Hicks-Beach, who walked to the Carlton Club, where a large number of the members of the party were waiting to hear the result-of the meeting. It wee a noticeable fact that the Duke of Northumberland passed by the residence of Lord Salisbury while the meeting was going on, and did not enter, although he held Cabinet office in Lord Beaconsfield's Government. Colonel Stanley was also absent from the meeting. The strictest reticence was observed as to the nature and result of the proceedings in Arlington-street; but it is stated they have not produced very encouraging results. The party is a good deal " split " on the question of the advisability of taking office at all, and there is even more disagreement on the question of the leadership in the House or Commons. It is reported that Lord Randolph Churchill has repre- sented that it would be impracticable, if not undesirable, CO attempt the passing of a Crimes Act for Ireland this session; whilst, on the oeher hand, several of those who are expected to hold high places in the neW Ministry, if one be formed, are no less emphatic in their opinion that such a measure is indispensible. It is said that the announcement in the Court Circular is too definite. The acceptance of office by Lord Salisbury, it is now understood in some quarters, was conditional. Meantime considerable surprise is expressed in the clubs and Parliamentary lobbies that Lord Randolph Churchill was absent from the meeting in Arlington-street. One explanation is that only members of the former Govern- ment were invited ; but there seems to be reason to believe that the relations of the Fourth Party towards Sir S. Northcote and his immediate adherents are somewhat strained. There are-serious differences as to the constitution of the Ministry. Lord Randolph Churchill is said to insist not only that he shall boa member of the Government, but that the whole of the fonrth party shall be taken into the Ministry. In order to make room for Mr. Goret,-Sir D. Wolff, and others, Lord Randolph Churchill suggested, at a private conference with Lord Salisbury, that Sit R. Cross, Mr. W. IL -Smith, and other members of the last AdmiBtra- tion should be shelved, either by being sent to the back benches or transferred to the Upper House. Lord Salis- bury on the other hand, wished to bring back to office as many of his old colleagues as possible. The personal com- position of the Government is therefore likely to give Lord Salisbury some trouble. But this is not the MA WHOM of his difficulties. The party is torn with dissensions on ques- tions of policy. Some of them do not want to take office at ell, while there is a serious split on the question of coercion. Lord It. Churchill has taken up a very decided position on this point. The Tory leaders are finding out, moreover, that to pass a Coercion Bill would be a matter of enorm- ous difficulty, and they may abandon the effort for that reason. In the House of Commons on Monday night the strained relations between the Conservative leaders and the Fourth Party developed into an open revolt against the Wishes ef Lord Salisbury, and Sir S. Northcote. Mr Gladstone re. i commended the House to deal with the Seats Bill and the measure ,providing an annuity for Princess Beatrice, and Caen adjourn until Friday. Sir S. Northcote assented to this course. Sir R. Wolff moved as an amendment that the debate on the Seats Bill be adjourned, and WAS sup- clotted by Mr. Gorst. Sir S.iforthcote pointed out that the provisions in the Seats Bill which the House had to consi- der had been inserted" at the suggestion "of Lord Salis- bury. But it did not matter, Lord R. Churchill and Sir M. Hicks-Beach ruteeed into the fray in support of Sir H. Wolff's amendment, caring neither for Lord Salisbury nor Sir Stafford. In the end a division was challenged. Sir H. Wolff and Mr. Gore were named as tellers as against the Tories. The motion for adjournment was defeated by 333 to 35. The Liberals made merry over the plight of the Tories, and Lord R. Churchill, having exposed himself and Lord Salisbury to derision, soon withdrew from the House, together with those of his comrades who were suspected of being disappointed place-hunters. The Daily Mies says :—Various explanations are car- rent with respect to the action taken in the House of Com- mons by Lord Randolph Churchill. We have the best reason to believe that the question at issue between the Marquis of Salisbury and the noble lord, of which Monday night's demonetration was an outward and visible sign, has nothing to do with Ireland or with any feature of the future policy of the proposed new Government. Lord Randolph Churchill has, we understand, demanded a thorough reor- ganisation of the Conservative Administration, leaving out at least half-a-dozen of the gentlemen whorl Lord Beacons- field had selected as colleagnes. A leading point in the de- mands Lord Randolph Churchill makes of the Marquis of Salisbury is said to be that Sir Stafford Northcote snail be removed to the 'Upper House, and that Sir M. Hicks-Beach shall be the leader of the Conservative party in the House of Commons. OPPOSITION IN THE HOUSE OF LORDS. The t..entral 3ToNs. speaking from undoubted authority ' says that Lord Saliebury's chief difficulty in accepting the reins of government at present lies in the action taken by his colleagues in the Upper House. While the members of the Lower Chamber are almost to a man anxious that their party should come into office, the Peers as a body strongly I object to this course The opinion among their Lordships is that, rather than for the sake of a temporary accession to Power and consent to perform the offices of what can at best be but a stop-gap Government" for a few months at most, they should wait until the General Election, and then take their chance of being returned to power _with the country at their back and a working majority in the Commons. They feel that as matters at present stand, with their party in the minority, their advent to office cannot hope to be a great success. QUEEN'S JOURNEY TO WINDSOR. The Queen left Ballater on Tu May at tea minutes to three o'clock. There was a considerable number of per- sons waiting at the station, who cheered her Majesty loudly. The Royal train arrived at Aberdeen at 4-22, and the jour- ney was resumed after engines had been changed. The order for the exclusion of the public from the station was withdrawn, by the Queen's command, and her Majesty ap- peared at the saloon window and bowed in acknowledgment of the cheers of the spectators. It was not until ten minutes to nine o'clock on Wednesday morning that the Queen, who was accompanied by Princess Beatrice, arrived at Windsor from Balmoral. The approach to Windsor was on the Lon- dos and North-Western Railway Tia Bushey. ger Majesty appeared much !aligned, having slept little during the [night, and was assisted by Lord Sidmouth to a carriage in waiting. Extraordinary precautions had been taken to keep the railway station clear of spectators, and neither repre- sentatives of the prees nor the public were permitted upon the platform until after the royal travellers had driven off to the Castle. Beyond the barriers a considerable crowd of persons had assembled, but there were Was no cheering, and they contented themselves with raising their hats, a saluta- tion which her Majesty acknowledged by bowing. Mr. Gladstone, who had been informed that the new Cabinet was practically completed, sent a special messenger from Downing-street to Windsor in the afternoon to ascertain leer Majesty's pleasure as to the time when she desired to

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1885.

give her retiring advisers an audience, in order to receive from them the seals of office. LORD SALISBURY AT WINDSOR. On Wednesday, keen public interest was shown in the proceedings at the town residence o: the Marque of Salis- bury, Arlington-street, where his Lordship received a num- ber of his future colleagues in the coarse of the day. The Duke of Richmond called at half-past ten o'clock, and re- mained until shortly before eleven. The next caller was Sir t Harding° Giffard. He remained but a short time, and then came the Earl of , Harrowbv who had a ten minute: inter- view. with the noble Marquis. Almost immediately after he had left Lord Carnarvon arrived, accompanied by the Hon. Colonel F. Stanley, who was unable to see his leaaer on Tuesday on account of having an engagement in Lancashire. Sir Richard Cross was the next ar- rival and with him was the Earl of Har- roWby, who had met the right hon. Baronet in Piccadilly, and returned with him. The later callers were Mr. Arthur Balfour, Mr. W. H. Smith, Lord George Hamilton, Mr. Gibson, and the Duke of Richmond, who re- turned on foot. These were followed by Lord Randolph 'Churchill and Lord John Manners, whose son, Mr. Henry ' !Canners, at the same time left Arlington-street. The last of the leaders to arrive was Sir Stafford Northcote, who walked up from his residence in St. Jarneereplace, with Mr. Winn, the senior whip of the Conservative parry. Mr. Bal- four left at a ,quarter-past twelve o'clock, at which time the leaders were engaged together in consultation, and re- maining in conclave until one o'clock. The Duke of Rich- , mond and Lord Cranbrook left before the coancil conclnded. Sir Stafford Northeote was the last to lease. Lord Ran- dolph Churchill drove to the Carlton Club, where there was a large attendance of members and keen anxiety as to the latest news, but the strictest reticence was 'ob- served as to the nature or the result of the consultation. Having received a message from the Queen, Lord Salisbury left Aelington-street at five minutes to three o'clock on Wednesday afternoon and drove to Paddington station. A special train, consisting of a splendid saloon, two car- riages, and a brake van, was there in readiness, and in it the noble Marquis left shortly after three o'clock for Wind- sor, accompanied by Mr. H. Manners, his secretary. Before ha left, the future Premier was cheered by the group on the station platform who had recognisediaim. The only other occupant of the special, in addition to his secretary, was Viscount •Bridport. The train arrived at Windsor at 25 minutes to four o'clock, ten minutes before it was expected. A Royal carriage was in waiting at the station, and in this the party were conveyed to the Castle. They were not generally recognised as they drove past. After an audience .6f 'Her Majesty, his Lordship, accompanied by Mr. Manners, returned to the station, and at five minutes to six the special train conveying them back to town steamed out of ttic •station, Paddington be- ing reached at 20 minutes past six. The South Afriean mail train had just previously arrived at an adja- cent platform, and the rush of passengers and the bustle amongst the vehicular traffic diverted attention from Lord 'Salisbury's arrival. There was an entire absence of specta- tors upon the platform, and only a few of the railway offi- cials were present to receive his Lordship, who at once en- tered the closed caraiage that was in waiting. Even as he -stepped hurriedly across the platform the Marquis suc- ceeded in escaping recognition, and only one solitary cheer was heard as he drove off. The carriage at once proceeded to his Lordship's residence in Arlington-street, and as it passed through the streets itadistinguished occupant was , again successful in evading observation. Arlington-street was reached in less than a quarter of an hour, and his ' Lordship was received at his residence by several of the , servitors of the establishment.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

THE SOUDAN.—LETTER .FROM THE MARDI. WADY IfeLFa, MONDAY.—The let Battalion of the Black Watch and the 2nd Battalion of the Essex Regiment have passed through on their way to Lower Egypt. The Heavy Cavalry are expected to-morrow. The arrangements for carryirw out the evacuation of the Soudan by the British troops have been well planned, and have worked very

smoothly DONGOLA, MONDAY.—A letter from the Mandi' which is believed to be genuine, has been received here. In this he declines to give up the Christian prisoners who have em- braced Islamism, and are unwilling to leave him, and he exhorts the English to become Mohammedans and to join him, otherwise he will destroy them. A letter has also reached Dongola, signed by .96 of the Mandi's prisoners, mostly Greeks, Copts, and t,yrians, in which they state that they are unwilling to leave the Mabdi, being no longer Christians. Among the signatures to the document are the names of Lupton Bey and Slatin Bey. DEATH OF PRINCE FREDERICK CHARLES, THE RED PRINCE. •

POSDAII, MONDAY.—Prince Frederick Charles died at a quarter past ten at his Castle of Guiencke. The Prince, who was the father of the Duchess of Counaught, had an apo- plectic fit yesterday morning, and lost the use Of the whole of his right side. The Prince was the eldest son of Prince Charles, second brother of the Emperor. and was born in ' 1828. He entered upon a military career at an early age, and commanded: in the war against Denmarlikin 1864. In 1866, in the war against Austria, he was placed in command of the First Army Corps, out-manceuvred the Austrian General Benedek, drove the Austrians to Sadowa, and, aided by the Crown Prince, won the battle of Koniggratz. His reputation was increased by his successes against France. At the close of July, 1870, he was on the Rhine frontier in command of the Second German Army, comprising 260,000 men and 500 pieces of artillery. On the 6th August he de- feated General Froissart at Speichern, and ten days later made a vigorous attack on the right of the (French position held by Marshall Bazaine between Doncourt and Vionville, , driving the French troops back to Metz. He closely inves- ted that fortress, which, after enduring a siege of seventy days, capitulated on October 27, when Marshall Bazaine i surrendered with 150,000 prisoners. Shortly afterwards he defeated the Army of the Loire (Nov. 28), recaptured Orleans (Dec. 4), and after a struggle, protracted ever six days, he took Le Mans and compelled General Chanzy to withdraw his troops northward (Jan. 13. 1871). He was created Field-Marshall Oct. 28,1.870. The Prince married, Nov. 29, 1854, Marie Anne, daughter of Leopold Frederick, reigning Duke of Anhalt, and has four claildren.—The Court will go into mourning for four weeks. FRANCE AND CHINA.—DEATH OF ADMIRAL

div.head: COURBET.
div.p: COURBET.

PARIS, MONDAY.—In the Chamber of Deputies Admiral Galiber announced, amid profound silence, the death of Admiral Courbet, from fatigue, on board the Bayard, on the 11th inst. The whole country would share the grief of the navy at the loss it had sustained. M. Floquot, the President, expressed the gratitude of the country for the services rendered by Admiral Courbet and the sailors under his command. The House then rose. Private ad- vices report that Admiral Courbet died from bilious fever. PRANCO•CHINESE TREATY RATIFIED.

' Pews, THIIIISDAY.—The Minister for Foreign Affairs received a telegram to-day from M. Patenotre announcing that the Court of Pekin has ratified the treaty of peace be- tween France and China. SPREAD OF THE ,CHOLERA IN SPAIN.

-- MADRID, SIINDAY.—Iwo fresh cases resembling cholera oc- curred here to-day, and 7 deaths. In Murcia during the last 12 hours 15 cases, 12 of which proved fatal, were re- ported, and 37 cases, including 16 deaths, in the province. Despatches from Valencia announce three fresh cases in the city and over 40 in the province. MADRID, MoNDAY.—Three suspicions cages resembling cholera occurred to-day, and two deaths. Telegrams from Valencia report three fresh .cases of cholera and one death in the capital, and 35 cases in the province. In Murcia, 60 fresh cases, 11 of which proved fatal, have been registered in ithe city, while 42 cases, including 15 deaths, are reported from other towns in the province. The exodus of families from Madrid continues. It is calculated that 12,000 persons have left the city during the week. MADRID, TUESDAY.—In the province of Castillo there I were 80 cases of cholera and 60 deaths Yesterday. Later re- ports from Murcia announce 64 fresh cases. There had been 39 deaths in the city, and in the province 50 cases, of which 16 proved fatal. The official Gazette of Madrid pub- lishes a declaration confirming the existence of cholera in ; \Valencia, Castillon, Murcia, and Madrid, and stating that official bulletins are to be issued daily during the prevalence of the epidemic. MADRID, WEDNESDAY.—The official bulletin issued this mailing gives the following report concerning the cholera yesterday :—Province of Castellon 58 cases, 28 deaths; ' Valencia kcityl 17 cases, seven deaths; Valencia (province) 146 cases. 88 death ; Murcia (capital), 98 cases 41 deaths; ' and in the neighbouring villages 136 cases and 63 deaths. Returns from other parts of the province give 35 cases and 11 deaths. One case of cholera is 'reported to have occur- red at Manju.z. THE AUSTRIAN ELECTIONS. • VIENNA. SATURDAY.—The returns of the elections to the Rrichsrath are now complete, with the exception of one constituency. Of the 353 deputies composing the House, 191 are Ministerialists, and 132 belong to the German Liberal party, the latter having lost 15 seats. The remainder consists of 22 Ruthenians, Italians, and Centrals, 4 anti-Semitic par- tisans, and 3 Democrats. THE AGITATION IN CRETE.

ATHENS, SATURDAY.—lntelligence received bete from Candia states that the Christian members of the Cretan Assembly have, in deference to the official intervention of the Consuls of the great Powers approved the nomination of &was Pasha as Governor of the island. ri he danger pf an insurrectionary movement has thus beensaverted. THE CASHMERE •EAR'FHQUIKE. SIMLA, SATIIRDAY.—Shocks of earthquake continue to be fait in Cashmere at the rate of from eight to ten daily, but their violence is abating. FALL OF A RIVER TUNNEL.

FRIDAY.—The new river tunnel on the Cincinnati Southern Railroad in Tennessee, about 100 miles from Chattanooga, fell in last night owing to the vibration caused by a train which was passing through. The tumid fell upon the cars, and nearly everyone in them was hurt, six persons being killed outright and twenty severely in- jured.

div.head: MEXICO.
div.p: MEXICO.

NEW Yoe, SllNDAY.—lntelligence from Mexico states that a waterspout burst on the night of the Bth inst. at Paso de Cuarenta, 20 miles from Lagos, causing great loss of life. One hundred and seventy bodies have been found. In• telligence from La Libertad etates that 2,000 Guatemalan troops have entered Santa Anna. AFFAIRS IN SOUTH AFRICA. A Blue Book containing correspondence respecting the fumes of the Transvaal and adjacent territories has been

issued. It appears that on March II Sir H. Robinson tele- graphed to the home Government expressing his disappro- val of certain points of Sir C. Warren's policy, and intima- ting that he would resign his High Cominission,hip if the settlement of civil questions were left in Sir C. Warren's hands. In consequence of this communication instructions were sent to Sir C. Warren on March 21, itistructiog him to refer to the High Commissioner all questions of policy whenever practica,ble, and observe special caution in all matters affecting the Dutch population. On March 23 Sir C. Warren complained of the difficulties which he expe- rienced in carrying out his duties as Special Commissioner in the later communications with the Home Governrhent. The cEspute between Sir C. Warren and Sir H. Robinson does not appear to have been settled one way or the other, but, on May 28, Earl Derby telegraphed to the High Com- missioner, requesting him to inform Sir C. Warren that her Majesty's Government highly appreciate the ability and success with which he has accomplished the objects of the expedition, but that they would be glad to know that the regular forces can be dispensed with and an armed police substituted; and to obtain information whether the Colo- nial Government would now propose to Parliament the an- nexation or protectioa of a part or whole of the protector- ate. THE PROPOSED TRANSCASPIAN RAILWAY. • THE MATERIAL BURNT. ST. PETERSBURG, TUESDAY.—The .7ournal Kaspi 'pub- lishes intelligence from Kizil Arvat announcing that a fire occurred on the 6th, in which all the material collected for the construction of the Transcaspian Railway, as well as 20 carriages, were destroyed. AUSTRIA.—RIOT AT BRUNN. BRUNN, WEDNESDAY.—In consequence of a dispute be- tween masters and men in regard to the hours of labour, a riot broke out at half-past six yesterday evening among the workmen in this city. The men collected in large crowds and attacked the factories of several firms by breaking the windows with stones and forcing the gates. At length it became necessary to call out the military who were com- pelled to use their arms to disperse the rioters, several of whom were wounded. DEATH OF FIELD-MARSHAL MANTEUFFEL. CARLSBAD, WEDNESDAY. Field-Marshall Matte off-I, Governor-General of Alsace-Lorraine. died this morning from a sudden attack of pulmonary congestion. THE EVACUATION OF DONGOLA. CAIRO, TUESDAY —DOngola is now completely empty. The police examined all the houses, and a few helpless old women who had been left behind were given conveyance northwards. These are absolutely the last of the refugees, of whom the grand total is now 12,600. All claims have been settled, and the people appear to be perfectly satisfied. —Morning Post. OPENING OF THE VICTORIAN PARLIAMENT. MELBOURNE, TRURSDAY.—Parliament wasiopened to-day by Governor Sir Henry Brougham Loch, who in his speech on the occasion congratulated the Legislature upon the flourishing condition of the colony. The bills announced by his excellency are of local interest only.. THE BLOCK IN THE SUEZ CANAL.

PORT SAID, TRURSDAY.--The work of clearing a new channel alongside the sunken dredger is being actively pushed forward, bat it is not expected that the canal will be re•opened for traffic before the 21st inst. One hundred steamships are now waiting to pass through the canal. RESIGNATION OF THE ITALIAN MINISTRY.

ROME, THIMSDAY.—In consequence of the narrow majority obtained by the Goverument yesterday in the division ,upon the estimates of foreign affairs, a Cabinet Council was summoned in the evening, when Signor Man- cini announced his determination to resign. His colleagues, especially those who are members of the Chamber of Depu- ties, however, objected to Signor Mancini leaving the Cabinet, and it was therefore decided to tender to the King the resignation of the whole Ministry. GENERAL GRANT'S ILLNESS. The Central News New York correspowdent telegraphed on Thursday morning :—A despatch sent from Mount McGregor late last night states that General Grant has had a relapse, the result or over-exertion in walking around and examining the country house in which he has just taken up his quarters. He is unable to speak, and has written a note to his family, informinz them that he feels death to be near. Dr. Sands, of New York, has gone down to see the General, whom he formerly closely attended.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

- --- Since the excitement attendant upon the publication of Lord Harris's letter to the Lancashire Executive has abated, the persecution against Crossland has taken another form. This time the Nottinghamshire Committee have gone a little out of their way to charge him with having failed to sustain hia residential qualification. The grounds for this—that be has not resided in the county during the past winter—are very slight. In every other county, when a man has once qualified himself to play, he is allowed to do so, as long as he is worth an engagement. Crossland is not the only one whom the :Nottinghamshire Committee have thus tried to prevent from playing in the county of his adoption, the other instance being Brown of the Cheshire Eleven. This hunting the elevens of the country for "Notts lads " and the subsequent objections, if not dis- continued, are likely to tell against the Nottinghamshire Committee, and to do them more harm than gaining the players would do them good. As might have been expected after Friday's play at Not- tingham, the Notts. County Eleven on Saturday gained a I decisive victory over the England by an innings and 48 runs. Although the weaknese of the England Eleven rob- , bed the match of its representative character, still the per- I formance reflect n great credit upon the Nottingham men, who were seen to advantage at all points of the gaine.—After a very close finish at Stockport, on Saturday, Cheshire ',eat Warwickshire by 15 runs. The losers had the bad luck to I be deprived of their best bowler during part of their oppo- nents' second innings, Mr. Rotherham being obliged to re- tire through an injury to his hand when the Cheshire total had reached 115, and be was also unable to bat in the second innings of Warwickshire. Whatmongh and Daven- port for Cheshire batted very well, and raised the score to 74 before the second wicket fell, but after that little was done, and the whole side were out for 139. Warwickshire Irequired 109 to win the match, but only Mr. Docker and Mor- gan reached double figures, and when the last wicket fell the total was 93, Cheshire winning, as stated above, by 15 runs.— At Vincent-square, on Saturday, the Westminster School team, in their annual match with a side picked from the Houses of Parliament, scored an easy victory on the first innings by 42 runs.—Before a large attendance, the match Surrey v. Essex concluded at the Lyttelton Cricket Ground, Lepton. the result being in favour of Surrey by an innings and 174 rune.-Derbyshire suffered a signal defeat in their match, ore Tuesday, with M.C.C. and Ground, which ter- minated at Lord's Ground, London, on Tuesday, the home club winning by an innings and 17 runs. So far thin season the performances of the Oxford Uni- versity Eleven have been of a most disappointing charac- ter, and on Wednesday, at Manchester, another one was added to their list of reverses, as they were beaten by a moderately good Lancashire team by nine wickets. Rain prevented any play on Tuesday, and on Monday Oxford bai4 scored a first innings of 176, and Lancashire had lost three wickets for 165. There was, therefore, little hope of success for the Dark Blues, but it was generally thought the match would terminate in a draw. However, the Lan- cashire men played up well, and gained victory within about an hour of time to draw. Briggs had a very large share in the performance, as in the two Linings of Oxford he took eleven wickets at a coat of only 60 runs. Sussex gained a victory over Gloaceetershire on Wednesday at Brighton, beating them in one innings, with two runs to spare.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.

div.head: MONDAY. ‘
div.p: MONDAY. ‘

On Monday morning the Select Committee appointed to inquiresinto the Ship Canal bill commenced its sittings. Mi. W. E. Forster presided, and the other members of the committee were Lord Eustace Cecil, Mr. W. Fowler, and Mr. Dalrymple. The promoters were represented by the same counsel as on the previous occasions, whilst a formid- able array of counsel was retained for the opponents. Be- fore the case was opened the Chairman stated that both he and the other members of the Committee were ignorant with regard to the question, not having formed any opinion upon it ; therefore they would feel it their duty in so im- portant a matter to hear all that counsel had to say. On the other hand they could not be blind to the fact that enormous sums of money had been spent on the inquiry in both Houses, and that much evidence had been brought before the Committees. The time which this session might last could not be long, and might even in the circumstan- ces be shorter than was at present supposed. They wished to state that, if the counsel on both sides could agree to refer to them any evidence which bad been given before either House, they would undertake to give it the same attention as if produced before them in that room.—Mr. Pember said he could not reply at the moment, but he would talk the matter over with counsel on the other side, and would state the outcome of the conversation in the morn- Aspinall said it was impossible to give an answer that day. It was desirable that they should discuss the answer they should give before Tuesday. Opponents were anxious to assist the Committee.—Mr. Pember assured the Committee that what had been said was satisfactory to all parties. The learned counsel then proceeded to state the the case of the promoters. He narrated the efforts which had been made in the past two sessions to obtain Parliamen- tary sanction to a scheme for constructing a ship canal from Manchester to the sea, and having described the dif- ference between the present scheme and that previou.ly projected, examined this year's scheme side by side watt that recommended last year by some of the petitioners' witnesses as an alternative plan to the proposal for taking the canal through the estuary of the Mersey. He explained that the promoters bad adopted the suggestion of their opponents, and had prepared their plans so as to carry out as far as they could the recommendations made last Year by Mr- ' Lyster, the engineer to the Mersey Decks and Harbour Board, and others. Cartoons of the two plans were on the walla of the committee-room, and Mr. Pember p inted out that they very closely resembled each other in all impor- tant respects. The general width of the bottom would be 120 ft., at the top 260 ft. to 1351 t ,with a large increase at the locks and sluices, and being further enlarged at each end of the canal. The total length would be 34 miles four furlon.pa, and the depth 26ft., the navigable width being twice that of the Suez Canal, providing plenty of room for two ships, each of 50ft. bearta, to pass. The canal would ac- commodate 99 per cent, of the steam shipping of the United Kingdom, and the water supply for the canal would be ample. In answer to a questian by Mr. Pope, he said he in- tended to call his commercial witnesses first. Answering the Chairman, he said he would take care in the present circumstances of the time not to duplicate that part of the evidence.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

_ In regard to the suggestion made by the Chairman of the Select Committee, on Monday, that some portion of the printed evidence given in the other House should be referred to the Committee, Mr. Pember stated on Tuesday morning that he had had a conference with Mr. Pope, representing the opponents, and offered to refer the whole of the comfier- cial evidence given on both sides. Mr. Pope, however, did nqt consider it consistent with his duty to make what was called any concession at all.—M-. Daniel Adamson, chair- man of the Provisional Committee of the Manchester Ship Canal, who was then examined by Mr. Michael, Q.C., gave evidence similar to what he gave before the other Com- mittees who have considered the scheme. He complained of the high railway rates between Liverpool and Manches- ter, the heavy charois of the Mersey Dock Board, and the great tax that was upon the cotton and other industries of Manchester:and other places. He detailed the advantages of the scheme, and mentioned, with regard to Runcorn, that the canal would tend materially to develope the trade of that place. The Runcorn Improvement Commissioners were of the same opinion, and they had arranged clauses with the promoters. The saving in carting, he said, would be very large. Be considered that the estimates for the making of the canal were ample. Mr. Pope, Q C., on behalf of the railway companies, said that they I did not intend to controvert the estimates as to the making of the canal. Mr. Aspinall intimated that the Dock Board did not intend to contest the estimates in the deposited plans, but they would submit that, when the canal was made, more works would be required than was set forth in the Bill. Mr. Dugdale, QC., representing the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Company, said that they did not intend to contest the cost of the actual making of the canal. Witness, in further examination, said be had no doubt in the world that the capital for the making of the canal would be raised. Cross-examined by Mr. Pope, witness said that the canal would take about 75 per cent, of the cotton traffic of an area of twelve miles round Manchester. He calculated that they would get 3,000,000 tons of traffic within that twelve mile area. The railway companies had asserted that the whole of the traffic between Liverpool and the area of twelve miles round Manchester did not amount to 3,000,000 tons a year, but he thought they were mistaken in that respect. The promoters had agreed to purchase the Bridgewater Navigation, which waterway they intended to make subveryient to the Ship Canal, leaving it to be a distributing and receiving source for the benefit of the canal...,

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

Mr. Pope, Q.C., on VifeTlOes—day, stated that it had been arranged between his learned friend (Mr. Aspinall) and him- self that in order to avoid needless repetition one counsel should go into a particular branch of a subject and cross- examine upon it.—Mr. Daniel Adamson, the principal pro- moter, was recalled, and further cross-examined by Mr. Pope. He had got the figues he had given as to rates from books of the railway companies. He could not say whether, in all the instances he had given, there was an actual trade in the articles mentioned, but he knew, for example, that some fifteen years ago there was a large quantity of cotton carried from Manchester to Hull.—The Chairman: The terminal charges are not chwged to you in any special account? Never.—lt is only your inference that they are so much? It is Mr. Pope's suggestion that they must be included in the total rate.—Mr. Aspinall said he would as a few important questions with regard to the Dock Board, and then Mr. Potter would deal with the com- , mercial evidence. Mr. Adamson, you know that previous to the year 1857 the Liverpool Docks belonged to the Cor- I poration of Liverpool? Witness: I don't know.—But you know that it was upon an agitation proceeding from Man- chester that the Dock Board was constituted in 1857 ? I know that there was some action taken by Manchester, and that Sir Joseph Heron spoke about it last session.—Don't you knew that it was because the Corporation of Liverpool had a right to levy dues that a great agitatien was got up in Manchester which resulted in the Dock Board being con- stituted and the town dues being abolished? Personally, I cannot tell you anything about it.—You know that the Dock Board was created entirely upon an agitation created in Manchester? I have no personal knowledge Mr. Aspinall : Have you any fault to find with the Mer- sey Docks and Harbour Board with respect to their manage- ment? I have no knowledge of the details of their man- agement.—Mr. Aspinall : Do you impute any mistake or mismanagement since the creation of the Dock Board ? Yes, the construction of the Liverpool docks at a cost of L 5,900 000 was a great misfortune, and it is a shame that that failure should be charged upon Lancashire trade.— Mr. C. T. Bradbury, of the firm of John Henry Hartside and Co., spinners, of Ashton-under-Lyne, gave evidence as to the transit charges on cotton, and the saving to be effected by the ship canal. His firm would save £3l a week by the canal.—That was compared with £5l a week Cost of carriage on the same quantity of cotton from America to L.verpool. If the cotton market were transferred to Manchester they would get rid of at least one of the brokers charges.

THURSDAY. At the sitting of the Select Committee this morning Mr. Pope, Q.C., representing the London and North-Western Railway Company, resumed his cross-examination of Mr. C. Bradbury, manaeing director of the firm of Messrs. Gart- side and Company, cotton spinners, Ashton-undsr-Lyne.— Answering the Chairman, the witness said the cost of bring- ing cotton from the ship side at Liverpool to his mill was 17s sid per ton, which was equal to one-tenth of a penny I per lb. In a mill of SO 000 spindles, with £50.000 paid-up capital, this was equivalent to a dividend of from 3 to 4 per cent. The estimated saving of 6s per ton in the transit would he equal to an additional 1 per cent dividend. The sav- ing of one brokerage would be equal to another 63 per ton or 1 per cent. more.-The Chairmaw said the latter was a matter of inference. It was distinct progress to have the (Aber state- ment admitted.-111r. T. Nickels, resin merchant, Liverpool, having been examined as to the Importations of resin.—Mr. Reuben Spencer, the managtng director of the firm of Rylands and Sons, Limbed, Manchester, said that in his previews evidence he stated that the firm would annually save (3,000 by the construction of the Ship Canal, but be now found that the saving would amount to near'V £3,000 per annum.—Mr. Bowman, senior partner of the firm of Messrs. Bowman, cotton spinners. Halifax, said the charge for the carriage per ton of cotton from Liverpool to Halifax, was Ll Os 3d; by the Ship Canal it would be 12s 10d per ton.—Mr. M. Spitz, cotton-waste merchant, Manchester, calculated that if the firm with which he was connected sent their cotton-wasre by the Ship Canal instead of by rail they would save 3s 91 per ton, or £l,lOO in the year, which would be equal to nearly one-half per cent, on their turn- over.—Mr. Charles Hold, corn merchant, Manchester, was also examined, and the Committee adjourned.

TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION: OVER 100 LIVES LOST.

About half-past nine o'clecte on Thursday morning / dreadful explosion occurred at the Lumps Pit, belonging to the Clifton Hall Colliery, the property of Messrs. Andrew Knowles and Sons, Peudlebury. The accident occurred in the Trencherbone Mine, the lowest of the seams now being worked. There were about 170 men and boys in this par- ticular seam, none of whom have as yet been reached, and it is feared that none of then] may be e:ot Out alive. Alto- gather, getween 300 and 400 men and lads were at work in the mine at the time, but the remainder were working in the two higher seams, the " Dow " and the "Five Quarters." It is from these workings that the men have been brought to bank at the Ageeroft shaft, distant from the Lumps Pit about threemuarrers of a mile. The force of the explosion was felt for some distance, and the report, like that of distant artillery, could be heard as far as Kersal Moor. The effect of the explosion at the pit's mouth was terrific. • Flames shot up a great height. The iron plates covering the pit's mouth Were buried upwards and the gearing damaged. An attempt was made shortly afterwards to descend by a volunteering party, under the management of Mr. Jonathan Hall, a certified manager, but, owing to the injury to the sides of the pit, they were unable to reach the bottom, and had to be drawn up. Attention was then directed to the Agecroft shaft, where a descent was quickly made by the manager, Mr. John Crook, accompanied by a party of willing volunteers. They are unable to reach the encherbeneMine, owing to the fall of earth, Sic" and were compelled to direct their efforte to the recovery of the teem in the other workings. By half-past twelve o'clock 123 men and boys had been brought to bank, all of whom were more or lees injured, but none killed, though cne boy,' named Jackson, died shortly afterwards at the nearest hospital, to which he was removed. The other sufferers were taken to their own homes, and toe more serious cases to the Salford Hospital. The discovering party have. found a depth of about two feet of water in the part of the mine nearest where the accident hanpened, extending for a considerable distance. As soon as the accident happened medical help, cabs, carriages, and all available help was sent for. While the operations detailed above were proceedings at Agecroft, attempts were being made at Clifton Hall to reach the men in the workings. An early effort of the kind preyed futile, but subsequently Mr. Hall, the manager, and a party under his guidance, succeeded in reaching the level channel at the bottom of the shaft leading to the deem quarters. Knowledge of the fact that communication had been here established soon got about, and a dense crowd assembled at the colliery. The grief of many of those collected was pain- ful to behold. It was a matter of certainty by this time that actual loss of life had occurred, and there was every reason to fear that the number of victiins would be great. It was sad indeed to see poor women sobbing silently and helplessly. I Tbeir grief was subdued but intense. Th 3 police kindly but firmly kept the crowd outside a barrier which had been I placed for the purpose. Perseus eager for tidings of those near and dear to them did not altogether approve of this arrangement, perhaps, but otherwise serious impediment would have been offered to the organised efforts of those upon whom the real work devolved. Information of the disaster was given by telephone at the County Police Court, ! Strangeways, very soon after the explosion ocurred, and a I body of constables in charge of Inspector Kelly was told off to keep order. Inspector Stantoo of &Ilford. eves also lon the spot with a contingent of officers. By about half- past one o'clock 75 persons had been brought to the ear. , face, of whom eleven were dead. The proportion of in- jured Was considerable, and several of them were badly I scorched. I It is known that 349 men and bays went down the Clif ten Hall mine on Thursday morning. Of this number 182 had been brought out of the workings alive—many of these suffering terrible injuries—up to six o'clock in the evening, I and 22 (sine from the Agecroft pit and 13 by the shaft at Clifton Ball) were brought up dead. One of the injured died after his removal home. There still remain 144 men and l'boys below, and there is unhappily too great mason to fear i that all have perished. With such an appalling possibility before them those engaged in the operations worked with untiring zeal, and risks of the most hazardous kind were run alike by the workmen and the responsible managers in the forlorn hope that some, at least, of the-entombed men might be at length rescued. NARRATIVES OF SURVIVORS. , Some of the men who were rescued had remarkable es- capes. When the explosion occurred they were for the most part engaged in taking their breakfast, and the disaster came upon them most unexpectedly. Consternation seized I them all, and they hurried to the pit mouth. Before they ' could reach it, however, some were overcome by the after. damp, and fell exhausted under its tertibie influence. Their bodies were afterwards found by the explerers. A few men i escaped with the utmost difficulty, though some of these were in so serious a condition that feats were entertained I that they also would eventually succumb. Thomas Morgan, a miner, residing at Worslem Fold, Pendlebury, stated that at the time of the explosion be rat I seated with his fellow workers eating his breakfast. Every- thing appeared as usual, and none of the inen had observed the slightest indications to lead them to apprehene any disaster. He regards his escape from death as most marvel- lous. The place where he was working was in what is known as the "Five Quarters." The first intimation he received that anything had happened was a bright flash of light, I followed almost immediately by a rumbling sound. Greatly ' alarmed he and those with him sprang to their feet, Morgan exclaiming, " Something is wrong." With his terrified I companions he hastened with all speed in the direction of I the pit "eye." On their way thither they found them- selves in deep water which gradually grew deeper until it reached their breasts. Through this they waded, and the scene here was dreadful io the extreme. The young and weak found it impossible to struggle against the force of the waters, and the deadly effects of the after-damp, and their cries and entreaties for help were inset piteous. Mor- gan himself had a narrow escape at this point. Another miner clutched him desperately, and it was with the utmost difficulty that after strtugling with the unhappy man for what appeared to him tally five minutes, he got clear of, him and thus escaped being dragged down into the water,. lin which case both woald have perished exhausted with the 1, struggle, and overcome as he was with the terror of the , surroundings, he still pressed forward, and presently suc- ceeded in reaching dry ground, where he fell unconscione. He remembers nothing more until he found himself on the pit bank. He was subsequently taken home, where he re- ceived every care and attention, and is now doing fairly well, lie remembers that after the explosion the course of the air seemed to be reversed more than once. Al to the mine itself he had always considered it exceedingly well ventilated. The velocity of the air current was something remarkable, and, to use bis own expression, whenever they were using naked lights the air "swelled " the cantele away. Samuel Lambert, residing at Fendlebury, a miner, erne anether thrilling account of the peril which he underwent, and the narrow escape be had from death. Like Morgan he also was startled with the fl ish and the rumbling poise ee the explosion, and at once hurried towards the pit eye. it was with great hardship that he battled his way through the water, and while thus engaged he endeavoured, though unfortunately without success, to sive the life of one of the lads employed in the pit. He says he found a little bay who had fallen beneath the wheels of a waggon and was app trently much hurt.. In response to the heartrending ap- peals of the lad for assistance, he paused in his rush for the pit mouth, took him up and carried him a considerable di tance through the water. Before reaching dry ground he found that 1118 strength was failing him, and it became a question of leaving the boy or of their both sinking. He was, therefore, most reluctantly compelled to abandon the youth. The next moment he himself fell, and almost en- tirely lost consciousness. He could, however, distinguish the voices of the exploring party as they approached him, and was brought out in safety, though for some time he remained in a precarious condition. The cries of the im- prisoned miners were, he says, appalling. Such a scene he will never forget. As he called it to his mind his eyes were Suffused with tears, and his quivering lips gave token of great anguish of feeling. Joseph Whittingham, who is an inmate of the Selfc"d Royal Hospital, suffering from serious home abo at the face and arms and other parts of the body, says he wee suddenly enclosed as it were in a vast sheet of flame, and then dashed with great violence against some iroh portions of the wee.- gen way. Ile was near the entrance to the TrenCherb3tlo tiiitetdl ud anti to i s thenv.ay seam, and, therefore, felt almost the full force o.e, a f the explo- se lobsitcooinf scious iakcil. He overing ms to the place of exit, and fell in with one ef the rescuing parties. somewhat,nes3 f o rhe a r

div.p: 'HIE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1885.

th THR success of the Tory party in destroy- the Government on the question of a tax J3eer or on Tea has been a trouble to them. thlteY were wildly jubilant when they found thetoselves for once in a majority; but since theen it has been apparent to everybody that Y are not happy- They recognise their ICtn rY as the worst defeat they have yet sus- th fled; for, whilst it has more or less split % up as a party, it has thoroughly united Lee .Liberals. Mr. LOWTH. E.R says they have led into a trap, but a's a trap which have themselves baited. They dug a A: for others, and somehow find themselves totiudering in it, whilst the others" have n:tlPlacently walked out. Sir W‘ M.IIARCOIIRT, ti Tuesday night, effectually strangled what called "the wretched fiction" that the itievernment had planned their own defeat. It %evidence of the deplorable state into which Tory party have fallen when, after defeat- .lll° the Government, they are "of all men miserable" that they are called upon to tCer office and confront the difficulties of situation. They are beginning to realise kilt a plight they are in when, without tpli`cY and without principles, they are re- hn:rieri to act as if they were possessed of tial• It was as music to their ears the other when Sir MICHAEL HIcKS-BEACH tIS ,s-ered at Radical teetotallers, and boldly rigested that the Government ought to tax %la rather than Beer. But there is some- o' like weeping and wailing and gnashing teeth at the thought of being committed to ' aYin 4, tan. g a burden—not upon the Radical teeto- and'r only, but upon the pothouse ' the whole nation—by taxing tea. rea,4 Snrt i they are disposed to back out, f _any ts have been reminded by a formidable leafi°f opportunity be given them. Tory I as t-Otion that there is such an organisation ciet'e Church of England Temperance 'o- ten-IY. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, writing in trxey to this resolution, says Sir MICHAEL ai,i(S"BEACH "did not intend to recommend Nvb"'„ on tea." But what everybody knows is that, ''ever Sir MICHAEL "intended," that is actl What he did. It is a poor way of InR the issue, to try to separate actions intentions ; and it would,. we fear, to D.4e confusion worse confounded" to seek et at what was really in the mind of the in rher thfor Gloucestershire, when he argued tiolTur of a further tax upon tea. Ques ria the ed himself on the subject, he" deprecates sitio'Sina which turns an economic propo- to sa4 into a political party question ;" that is or rather suggest, that when he was kingb the Government for taxing spirits Dart, eer he hadn't the remotest thought of Politics. But it won't do; the Church tilietland Temperance Society are not to be With such a flimsy pretence. Nor does

Sir MICHAEL mend the matter by adding that "the resolution he moved did nots advocate 1 the increase of the duty on tea." Nobody says it did ; that is not the charge that is brought against him. What is complained of is that tile objectionable •proposal was apart of his speech --a part of himself rather than of the resolution. He had better dodge ag tin, or keep out of sight altogether, if he does not want to be hit. But the Tories are coming in, whilst the Liberals are going out—out gf office but not out of power. This latter consideration is one which should set at ease Liberals throughout the country, who may be deplor- ing the prospect of a SALISBURY-CHURCHILL Government. With a Liberal majority in the House of Commons, Lord SALISBURY, self- willed and imperious as he is, will not be per- mitted to do such mischief as was wrought during the BEACONSFIELD Administration. He will run in heavy harness, and with such a bit in his mouth as will pull him up if he attempts to play pranks. It is bad that he should be in office for six months; but better this than that he should be in office for six years. As things were going amongst such shabby Liberals as those who were absent from the House without just cause on Monday night week, it was a contingency to be feared that Mr. GLADSTONE might, at the natural death of the present Parliament, be so worn and wearied as to feel the n&cessity of retir- ing from public life. As it is. he is set free for a period of rest which will enable him to formulate the programme of the future, and, when the hour of battle comes, lead the party on again to victory. It is satisfactory to know that he has felt it to be desirable to forego the honour which the, QUEEN has sought to confer upon him by making him an earl, and burying him in the House of Lords, as if Queen and country were not themselves honoured and ennobled by the name of WILLIAM EWART GLADSTONE ! Let the Tories come in ; things are working together for good. Let the nation for a brief space witness the spectacle of the members of a Tory Government night by night eating tlmir own words in order in soma degree to recon- cile the past with the present; flying at each other's throats because of personal differ- ences arising out of thoughtless language and foolish vanity meddling and muddling abroad, and plundering and blundering at home; and the result, ere long, will be that the people will cry out as with one voice— .,Take away this Government of Shams, and give us back the Government of the Grand Old Man."

LAST night the proceedings in both Houses of Parliament were brief but interesting. The Tories are in a fix, and there is an adjourn- ment until Tuesday to give them time to get out of it. They have hungered and thirsted not after righteousness, but office, and now when office is within reach they are afraid to enter in unless they can have an assurance that they will be treated better than they have treated their piedecessors. They want the rose without the thorn, and may be ex- pected next to cry for the moon. In the Upper House, Lord SALISBURY, after his wont, did not give the real reason for asking for an adjournment. At any rate, if he was serious in what he said, he requires to be specially watched. He objected to going forward with the Redistribution Bill on the grohnd that, as it stood, it took away the p3wer to dissolve Parliament from now till November next. But this surely is a most reasonable thing. Does Lord SALISBURY want a General Election on the old register? Is he, at the last moment, disposed to try the old trick of forcing a dissolution and flouting the Two Millions of new electors by not taking them into account ? We rather think it is too late in the day to play a game of this kind. In the House of Commons, Mr. GLADSTONE, in response to an inquiry, made it clear that the adjournment was asked for because Lord SALISBURY is not in a position, as yet, to accept office. He is seeking some assurance, a Tory organ says, that the Liberals will " not oppose the business necessary to the winding up of the session, especially in regard to the mat- ter of finance." Was there ever anything so humiliating to the leader of a great party? The Conservatives have overthrown a Liberal Government on the question of taxation, and now, forsooth, when the problem of raising money confronts them, they would ask the Liberals to help them out. of the difficulty. What do they want? Have they not a . heaven-born Chancellor of the Ex- , chequer in their new leader in the House of Commons, Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH? What has become of the brilliant proposal he made the other night to tax Tea in pre- ference to Beer ? Does it not look well in the light of day; or does he want the as- surance of the Liberal party that they will offer no opposition to whatever he may pro- pose in the matter of finance ? What "measureless audacity !" The Tories will get no such assurance from the Liberals; they do not need it—they have " assurance" enough for anything.

THE Early Closing Movement seems to be making progress in the metropolis. Sir CHARLES DILKE, who presided over the an- nual meeting on Wednesday evening, spoke of the "rapid advance in the power, work, and authcrity of the society." A letter Was read from PRINCE ALBERT VICTOR expressing his sympathy with the objects of the associa- tion, while Cardinal MANNING was present, and addressed the meeting in support of a resolution. There can be no question as to the need for shortening the hours of labour amongst shopmen ; the difficulty is to bring ,about the reform by means of early closing. There is naturally a teluctance to appealing to the legislature; for Parliament is jealous of interference with trade regulations. Em- ployers for the most part express themselves as favourable to the movement; it is the public that seem to be callous 'on the ques- tion. People are accustomed to shopping at all hours of the day and night, and think more of their own convenience than of the comfort of those who serve them. If trades- men would show themselves united and reso- lute, the battle would soon be won; but there are employers in every branch of business who delight in turning over a penny after a neighbour has locked up—especially if they think the penny would otherwise have found its way into their neighbour's till—and these are amongst the chief enemies of the early closing movement Looking broadly at the question, it cannot be doubted that business would be done as well as it is, or even better, if the hours of labour were re- duced. "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy"; and we need hardly add that the dull shopman cannot .do justice to his em- ployer. The latter, by-the-by, in the slack parts of the week can occasionally devote a few hours to recreation; but the shopman is kept to the counter from week end to

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1885.

week end, with altogether too little time for leisure. The condition of the artizan class has greatly improved during the past twenty years, and it is not the least of the boons they have obtained that the hours of labour have been reduced. They are all the better for it, and trade is no worse for it. It is high time that a similar benefit should be ex- tended to the sbopkeeping class.

A WIDNES ScuLrron.—Mr. William Sadler, son of Mr Thomas Sadler, builder, of Widnes-road, has just executed a bust in marble of the late Mr. Tnomas Verdin, for Mr. Jos Verdin, of Brocklehurst, Northwich, brother of the deceased gentleman. This is the second commission Mr. Sadler has carried out for the Verdin VICTORIA-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—In aid of the funds of Lacey-street Sunday school sermons were preached in the above place of worship on Sunday morning and evening, by the Rev. C. W. L. Christian, of Sale. In the afternoon Mr. J. R. Frith, of Runcorn, delivered an ad- dress to the scholars. Hymns specially selected for the occasion were sung during the day. The collections amouated to .147 5s 4d. CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROPRIArENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.— The members had their first ramble of the season on Satur- day afternoon, when they visited Duke's Quarry. They were accompanied by Mr. Leach, who delivered an interest- ing lecture on geology, and succsssfully fired a blast. An interesting half-hour was also spent at the Stone Hills. Mr. Leach was cordially thanked for his kindness. Norton Priory, Chester. and Widnes are to be visited. ACCIDENTAL DEATH AT WIDNES —A jury, presided over by Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Monday, held an inquest at the Main Top Hotel,. Widnes, concerning the death of an infant son of Wm. Owens, labourer, 15, Beamont-street. On Thursday night Mrs. Owens tool; the deceased, which was ten weeks old, and another child aged 18 months, to bed with her. Daring the night she had to suckle the infant, and in the morning when she again awakened, he was resting upon her right arm, with his face against her breast. His face was partly black. A verdict to the effect that death probably occurred through acciden- tal suffocation was returned. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, PRESTON BROOK.—The an- niversary 'services of this school were held on Sunday, wben congregations of large proportions testified to the sym- pathy of the public with their claims. The Rev. S. Mees occupied the pulpit both afternoon and evening, and direc- ted his remarks to the training and education of children. Hymas of a special character were sung by the choir and scholars, Mr. John Frodsham acting as conductor and ac • companist. The amount realised V the services was about £l2, including a sum of nearly £5 collected by MT. Prod- sham, for which the committee of the school tendered their cordial thanks. The magistrates at Newton, on Saturday, were rather hard on a boy named EDWARD UNSWORTH in fining him—or rather his parents-5s including costs for doing damage to a field of wheat, at Haydock, whilst chasing a butterfly. There was undoubtedly a trespass, and evidence was given that damage was done to the amount of sixpence, but surely the penalty was out of all proportion to the offence? It is Mrs. HEMANS, if we remember rightly, who speaks of June's brightest days "when bee, and bird, and butterfly are on their lightest wing ; " and on such a day what boy who is a half a boy that would not chase a butterfly over a common, or a wheatfield, or, for that matter, into "my lady's bower ? " We would not give a brass button for a lad who, in " the excitement of the chase," could stop and calculate the consequences of a summons. He would be too good for this world, or else so radically bad as to have already become a designing young knave. It is, of course, very wrong to trespass. or to damage wheat—just as it is wrong in hunts- men to break down fences and gallop through gardens; but, if it is sufficient for the man it ought to be sufficient for the boy, to be "let off" on making good the damage. It is not unlikely that in this case the lad has had to suffer not only for his own, but for others' misdoings. He has been "made an example of," for before he was brought before the awful bench of magistrates he was stripped to the skin and beaten by his mother. The other boys who have chased butterflies amongst the wheat cannot take a share of EDWARD'S thrashing, but they can club to- gether and pay the fine. Poor EDWARD! he has had to sm4rt for chasing that butterfly. It ought to have been " a king's drummer," and we hope he caught it at the time. There can be no question as to his having "caught it " afterwards. •

Ridgway, coroner, held an Inquest at the Barley Mow public- laouse on Tuesday, touching the death of Jeremiah Bennett. six years of age, son of John Bennett, waterman of 15, Queen-atreet. On Saturday the boy crossed the lock at the Welsh-row basin, in company with about eight other lads. ' On the watehman making his appearance they returned in haste, but the deceased, who was last, caught his foot in a rope attached to a narrow boat, slipped, and fell into the water head first. His dead body was recovered a quarter of an hour later. Evidence was given by the father, Mrs. Elizabeth Martin, and P.C. Kelly. Mr. T. Simister repre- sented the Bridgewater Navigation Company, and stated that the public had no right of way across the lock. A ver- dict ef " Accidentally drowned "was recorded. , DEATH OF Mn. Wm. BERRY, OF DITTON.—The remains of Mr. Wm. Berry, of Dittoo, were interred at Hale Church on Thursday. The deceased, who was a gentleman of inde- pendent means, and the waywarden for the township, was in his 75th year. On Monday afternoon he visited a ' house in Hutchinson-street, Whines, and whilst there was seized with a fit. Mr. Saul, assistant to Dr. Booth, was sent for, and on his arrival prescribed, and advised the patient's removal home in a cab. By a mistake he was conveyed to Halebank, arid several lours elapsed before he arrived home. He died shortly afterwards. RUNCORN POLICE Cot:rem—Before Mr. James Handley. on Thursday, Jane Dean was charged with stealing several articles of wearing apparel belonging to Mrs. Emma Ad- kins, of Suffolk-street.—Superinsendent Leah stated that the prisoner had been employed as charwoman to Mrs. Ad- kins, and whilst thelatter was ill in bed the prisoner bad stolen and pledged the articles. As the prosectetor was un- able to appear the prisoner was remanded for seven days. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Robert Neil and George Jackson, men of bad character, from Nottingham and Sheffield respectively, were charged with stealing I. briar pipe and case,. value 20s, from F. Boyd, commercial traveller, Cotswold-street, Liverpool.—Mr. Peers, pattern maker, of Kaludah-terrace, Widnes. deposed to seeing the prisoners commit the robbery at Farnworth sports on Satur- day afternoon.—The prisoners were remanded for seven days. Setoceeterq ASSAULT AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. H. S. Hall and Mr. H. Gaekell, junr., William Henry Leach, an engine fitter from Leeds on "tramp," was charged with indecently assaulting Bessie Price, seven years of age, in Lugsdale-road on Sun- day..—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour, and was also committed for an additional week in default of paying a fine if Sc and costs for beieg drunk on Monday evening. MALICIOUS CONDUCT AT WIDNES.—John Kelley, a middle aged man, who is ernployed'as a labourer, was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, charged with wilfully and maliciously breaking two plate-glass windows at the Norton Arms Hotel, Lugsdale-road. kept by Mr. Jas. Tilley, doing damage to the extent of £B. The prisoner entered the bar of the public-house about ten o'clock on Saturday ni&ht, but as he was then plainly in an intoxicated condi- tion, they refused to serve him with any liquor. Upon this the prisoner went outside, picked up two stones, and sent them stashing through the windows.—The prisoner was commit- ted to Liverpool Quarter Seseions for trial. CURIOUS INCIDENT AT FARNWORTH SPORTS.—On Satan. day afternoon the person in charge of the chief ticket office at Faroworth sports discovered that a basin containing be- tween gs and £lO had been abstracted from the place. His son asserted that he had seen a inan insert his hand through an aperture in the structure and bring forth the bowl, which he subsequently handed to a confederate. He gave chase to them, but they eluded him. Afterwards he pointed out one of them to the police, who apprehended him. Only 3e 93 was, however, found upon him. Strange to relate, the missing money wa- a few minutes later found lying in an old cap on the ground between the entrance gate and the ticket office. The police were convinced their prisoner was innocent and released hip. THE FRAUD ON CHESHIRE MAGISTRATES.—John Win. Rigby, alias Thomas Mottersheid, alias Whittaker, was brought up at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, charged with obtaining money and clothing by false pretences from Mr. Henry Stanton, J.P., Thelwall, Jos. Marson, J.P., Hill Cliffs, and Mrs Hazlehurst, Beaconsfield House, Higher Runcorn. The facts have previously been repo, %eel in this journal. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and made a long rambling statement tn the effect that the woman with whom he had lived for the past six weeks had berm the cause of his conduct.— Supt. Leah said the prisoner had a wife and several children in Manchester workhouse. He had deserted them.—The Bench sentenced the prisoner to three moethe hard labour. WIDNES LAW CASE.--In the Court of Appeal on Setur- nrday, before the Master of the Rolls and Lords Justices Baggallay and Bowen, the appeal case of Banner v the Widnes Alkali Company, Limited, was heard. The plain- tiff was Mr. John S. El. Banner, trustee of the property of Tobias and Co., bankrupts of Liverpool. The case was tried before Mr. Justice Smith, at the Liverpool Assizes without a jury. The plaintiff claimed £1,615 143. 61. for breach of contract. The defendants agreed to supply the plaintiffs with 600 tons of bleaching powder, at the rate of 80s. per ton, for 12 months, and with 500 tons of bleaching powder, at £5 23. 63. per ton, per month, com- mencing in the mouth of April, 1884, and terminating in January in the present year. Messrs. Tobias and Co went into bankruptcy, and the defendants failed to supply the bleaching powder according te centiact, and the action was brought to obtain the difference between the con- tract and the market price. The learned judge found for the defendants, and from this decision the plaintiff now appealed. Mr. Henry Collins. Q.C. , Mr. Sinnot, and Mr. Wr H. Cross appeared for the appellant; and Mr .Gully, Q C., and Mr. W. J. Walton for the respondents. The Master of the Relic, in givieg judgment, said that the defendants had stipulated by their contract not to supply Tobias and Co. if they went into bankruptcy with bleaching powder, and consequently the decision of the learned judge in the court below muet be upheld. The appeal was therefore dismissed with costs. SELLING BUTTERINE FOR BUTTER AT RUNCORN.—Before Mr. W. Benkes and Mr. Henry Reynolds, at Runcern Petty Sessions, on Monday, Edward Johnson, grocer, of St. Helens, Warrington, Widnes, Runcorn, St c., was summone i on a charge of unlawfully selling food which was not of the nature, substance, and quality demanded. The defendant pleaded not guilty. On the sth May P.C. Harper entered the defendant's shop in Bridge-street, and according to the instructions of Super- intendent Leah purchased 21bs. of sugar and 21bs. of lard. He then asked for 21bs of butter, and the shopman inquired what price he would have it. He saw a card upon some butter marked "Splendid Is," ant said he would have 21be. of that. The butter was served to him, and subsequently Superintendent Leah told the shopman that it was pur- chased for the purpese of analysis. A. portion was for- warded to the public analyst, who certified that the butter was adulterated with 80 per cent, of foreign fat, The de- I fendant said the ticket had been marked butterine, but the manager had washed it off in cleaning the ticket. Persons whe only paid Is knew that they were not receiving butter, as it could not be purchased for that price.—Owen Qainn, the manager, corroborated this statement. He did not tell the officer that it was butterine, because he was just about to close the shop and was very busy. The price of the butter in the shop was is 41. Superintendent Leah asked the witness if he knew that pure butter could be purchased at the time for Is per pound, and that butterine containing 80 per cent, of foreign fat only cost 41 per lb. The defen- dant (sworn) denied that at the time that sample was pur- chased pure butter could be bought at Is per lb.. and the sample analysed cost him 841 per cwt., or 9d a pound, besides carriage. His managers had thorough instructions how to deal, and it was rather hard that he should be brought there through the negligence of one of them. Superinten- dent Leah handed ins certificate to show that he purchased on the same night pure butter at Is per lb. The Chairman said there was a long list of offences; against the defendant, and a fine of £5 and costs, £1 14s 91, was imposed. The defendant said he had 14 shops in various towns, and it was a hard case if he were to be made to suffer in this fashion through the negligence of a manager. Mr. Bankes said the fact of a man asking for butter and being supplied with butterine of such a low quality was enough to show the Bench that they were not wrong in inflicting such a penalty. OFFER OF AN EARLDOM TO MR. GLIDSTONE.—The Queen has graciously intimated to Mr. Gladstone her wish to offer him an earldom in recognition of his services to his Sovereign and his country; but while intention, appreciating her Majesty s gra- cious Mr. Gladstone has asked to be allowed to forego the high honour which her Majesty was ready to confer upon him. SIR R. A. Cnoss's RETURN TO OFFICE. The acceptance by Sir R. A. Cross of the office of Home Secretary in the new Conservative Government will necessitate on his part an appeal to the electors of South-West Lancashire for re-election as one of the members for that division of the county. It is be- lieved in Conservative circles that, in view of the short time which will elapse before a general elec- tion takes place under the new Reform Bill, there will be no opposition to Sir Richard at the present time, and the feeling among the Liberals in the. division is that it is not, under the circumstances, worth their while to contest the seat. It is not ex- pected there will be any opposition to the re-elec-. tion of Colonel Stanley for North Lancashire. PRESENTATION TO MR. JOHN WALICER.—At their usual tent meeting on Monday evening, at which there was an unusually large attendance, the mem- bers of the Ebenezer Tent of the Independent Order of Rechabites made a presentation to Mr. John Walker, late of the Blackburn Times and one of the trustees Of the tent.—Bro. J. IValmsley (the chief ruler) said their business was to make a presenta- tion to a very worthy Rechabite, and one of their hard-working trustees. Duty called him away from Blackburn, and he was sure they would all wish him success and prosperity at Warrington.— Mr. James Hadfield (one of the secretaries of the tent) read a short address to Mr. Walker, alluding to his many and valued services. Accompanying the address was a water-colour drawing by Mr. .1. Clinton Jones, and entitled "A View of Blackburn from Pleasington." The picture was supplied through Mr. L. S.Walmsley, by whom it was mounted and framed.—Bro. Dobson made the presentation, and in doing so gave a very interesting account of ' the life of Mr. Edward Walker,. the father of Mr: John Walker. Bro. Dobson said Mr. Walker had ' come to be looked. upon in Blackburn as a leader ' and representative of the working classes. In. 1875, when a fresh Act of Parliament was passed, Mr. Walker spent many weeks in preparing a fresh code of rules for the tent, for which services. he never received a penny. In his office as trustee, he had always taken care to see that the money was carefully and safely invested. If the investment was not good Mr. Walker had always the courage to tell them so. (App)ause.)—Bro. Roger Ilaock en- dorsed everything Bro. Dobson said.—Dro, John Graham, a fellow trustee of Mr. Walker, spoke in high terms of him, and bore, testimony to the great assistance he had been to him (the speaker). in his office as trustee.—Bro. John Walker thanked them heartily for their kindness, though he could not see that he had done much to deserve it. Re had, certainly done what little he could to assist in the work of the tent, and had spent a great deal of tin* on the rules. He thanked them most heartily for the picture, upon which was sketched so faith- fully a view of the hills of his native town; and he accepted it in the Berne kindly spirit in which it Shad been given. (Applause.)—BiacHurn.:Times.

A WAntaNGTON MILITIAMAN'S RAILWAY BS- cA.EADm—Before Mr. T. S.Timmis, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Peter Walsh, a militiaman, was charged with travelling on the Clleshire Lines Rail- way from Warrington to Farnworth without a ticket. William Hewitt, a porter, saw the prisoner and a companion, also a militiaman, alight from a Warrington train on Saturday afternoon. They jumped over a wall, and he followed and captured the prisoner. The other man escaped. A fine of 5s and costs was imposed. An order was also made for the payment of the fare.
