BURNING EFFIGIES AT Sr. HELENS.—LIVELY SCENE.—On Tuesday afternoon a lively. scene was, witnessed in the neighbourhood of Parr, St. iHelens, where some hundreds of women and children burnt the effigies of a glass-maker and the-wife of a chemi- cal labourer who live in the neighbourhood. It was suspected that the two unknown to their respec- tive partners in life, had formed an intimacy, and the house of the woman was watched: On Tuesday morning several neighbours saw the two leaving the house together and going to a neighbouring public-house. They were hissed and hooted, and the protection of the police had to be sought. Later in the day the glass-maker was again seen in the house of the woman. A crowd collected, and, amid a scene of considerable excitement, old clothes and straw were produced, and so-called " effigies " of the " pair ' made and burned, amid the beating of tin pans and kettles and the hissings and hootings of women and children. The man, fortunately for himself, made good his eecape over the back wall, and the woman bolted the door and drew down the blinds. The crowd was afterwards dispersed by the police.

RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL. IMPORTANT CLAUSES 013 TAINED. AN EXPLANATION. A special meeting of the Ranoorn Board of Cemmission- ers was held on Wednesday morning at the Town Hall. Waterloo-10.d, to receive and consider a report of the Par- liameotery and Legal Committee with reference to the negotiations with the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal. Mr. B. Shaw presided, and there were present Messrs. Norman, Dobson, Timmins, Grice, Lake, White, Lightbnen, Whittaker, Meadowcroft, Taylor, Speakman, Harris, Pritchard, Linaker (law clerk), and Marshall (Beare- tary).—Mr. Pritchard said the result of tile committee's negotiations with the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal had been such that they now recommended for the Board's approval an agreement and clauses wnich had been formulated ta protect the trade and port of Runcotn. The- committee had always been ready to entertain proposals that would reasonably meettheir requirements, but to within the last month they had had no overtures made to them that could be entertained as forming the basis of an agree- ment. The evidence laid before the Committee of the House of Lords, and the fact that should the Bill pass the promoters were to acquire the Bridgewater undertaking, had no doubt been the motives which had induced the promo- ters to consider the Commissioners' case, and to offer to meet their reasonable claims. They could not say that the Committee of the• House of Commons would give them more than they had attained; in fact, the committee might concede less. Under these circumstances the committee considered the arrangement fairly reasonable.—The Law Clerk read an agreement, in which the promoters of the Bill undertook to construct a lock 450 feet long and 45 feet wide opposite the pumping stition to enable vessels to pass from the canal to the estuary, and from the estuary to the canal, in addition to the one shown on the deposited plans opeosite the Fenton Docks. He also read the following clauses : (1) During the construction of the canal near the exist- ing docks basins and navigation at Runcorn forming parts of the Bridgewater undertaking (in this section referred to as "the said docks basin and navigation") and until the lock or basin work number 1 G. (c) is open for the passage of traffic to and from the said docks basins and navigation from and to the estuary of the Mersey all traffic destined for or coming from the said docks basins and navigation shall be allowed to piss up and down so much of the canal between Runcorn and Easthain as shall for the time being be open and available for traffic free of any ship dues or canal or lockage tolls. (2) From and after the opening of the said lock or basin work number 1 G. (c), for Runcorn traffic the company shall afford all such facilities for all vessels and bargesl which shall on any tide be ready to leave the said docks basins, and navigation, and which but for the construction of the canal and works thereof could have left Runcorn over the existing sills of the said docks, basins, and naviga- tion, and proceeded down the estuary on the same tide as ' will enable such vessels and barges to cross the canal and pass into the estuary in time to proceed down the estuaryl on the same tide, and any such vessels or barges to which such facilities are not afforded by the company may pass down and out of the canal free of any ship dues or canal or lockage tolls. Section 31 sub-section 4 further states— "The company shall provide and work free of charge dur- ing each tide the necessary motive power for towing all barges and sailing vessels to and from the docks at Elles- mere Port through work number 1 B B, and to and from the docks at Runcorn through work number 1 G, (c), and the bye-laws regulating the traffic destined for or coming from those docks shall be such as shall secure for such traffic whatever precedence shall be found necessary to enable the same to pass between such docks and the river Mersey, and to proceed to Liverpool or vice versa on the same tide in all cases in which such traffic would have been able so to pass and proceed if the canal had not been made." (3) By elause these it is provided that any disputes respecting any of the matters aforesaid shall he referred to tbe arbitrament of an arbitrator to be appointed by the Board of Trade. (4) In the event of the company acquiring under the powers of the act the Bridgewater undertaking they shall not levy or charge any higher tolls rates or charges for the use thereof respectively than are at present levied and charged by the Bridgewater Company to the public generally. (5) No canal tolls shall be demanded or taken by the company for any farm yard or stable-dung or for any marl, nightsoil, ashpit,xefuse, cinders, or street-sweepings carried by the Commissioners or any of their contractors, servants, or boatmen on tlie canal. (6) All vessels carrying salt only and not exceeding 450 tons gross register and carrying not more thee 500 tons and passing from. the said docks, basins, and navigetions, down and out of the canal shall be exempt from the pay- ment of all ship dues and canal and lockage tolls. (7) All vessels whether light or in ballast not exceedisg 450 tons gross register and destined for the docks, basins, or navigation for the purpose of loading salt may enter and pass along Work No. 1 without payment of any ship dues or canal or leakage tolls for such entrance or passage. (8) All vessels destined for the said docks, basins, orl navigation whose cargo consists only of flints, felspar. china-stone, china clay, or bones for use in the manufac- ture of pottery and not exceeding 450 tons register and not carrying more than 500 tons may enter from the estuary of the Mersey and pass along Work No. 1 to the said docks', basins; or navigatien on the payment of half the ship dues, and such cargo it destined for the Staffordshire potteries shall be liable only to the payment of half the tolls pre- scribed by this act. (9) If the company make any exemption from any portion of any dues payable under thie act in respect of any vessels or cargo heyond that confined by this section, they shall make the like exemption in respect of all vessels and cargo destined for the said docks; basins, or navigation falling. within the same class or description. using or carried upon.. the same section of the canal and subject to the same dues. and in the like circumstances. (10) In the event of any alteration in interference with et damage, or obstruction to any street, road, footpath, sewer, or drain belonging to or under the control of the Commis- sioners, being at any time caused by the operations of the I company, the company shall forthwith make good the same at their own cost to the reasonable satisfaction of the Com- missioners, and the company shall also be liable in convert- sation to the Commissioners for any damage, injury, or loss occasioned to them thereby, such compensation being in case of diepute determined by aebitration in manner pro- vided by the Lands CI IUSOS Act. (11) Notwithstanding anything in this Act contained or shown on the deposited plans to the contrary, the company shall not, without the consent of the Commissioners, in any wise interfere with the free flow of the sewerage of the dis- trict of the Commissioners into .the river Mersey, or the estuary thereof, unless and until the company shall have provided at their own expense, and to the reasonable sat- isfaction of the Commissioners, and in case of any differ- ence between the company and the Commissioners of the Local Government Board and vested in the Commissioners ell proper and sufficient outfalls and works for conveying the sewerage of the eaid district under the canal and into the river Mersey or the estuary thereof as efficiently and to the same extent and amount as at present and the company shall compensate the Commissioners for any increased expense incurred by them in maintaining and woriling any such new sewers and works over and. above the expenses of maintaining and working their present sewers, and the amount of such compensation it not agreed between the company and, the Commissioners, shall be settled by the Local Government Board on the application of either

party. • (12) The company shall at all times afford to the Com- missioners all reasonable facilities and accommodation for carrying through or under the property of the company any 1, woven, drains, or sewer outfalls which may hereafter 13e necessary for the proper drainage of the district, and the corapavy shall allow such Rowers, drains, and sewer outfallt

to be so carried through or under their property tzpon such terms as to wayleave and other matters as the Local Go- vernment Board shall determine, having regard to the facili- ties which the Commissioners at present possess for carrying out and exemiting works for the sewering of their district. Provided that any work executed under this isubw.ctlon shall when so far as they afLmt the canal, or works, or other property of the company be carried out according to plans and specificatioss previously Submitted to and ap- proved iewriting by and under the superintendence of the company's engineer, and shall not interfere with or affect the working of the canal or the future improvement thereof, and if the canal works or other property of the .company shall sustain any damage or injury by or in consequence of the execution of any such works the Commiasioners shall be liable in compensation to the company for each damage or injury, each compensation to be determined in case of dispute in the manner provided by the Lind Clauses Acts. Provided that should any dispute arise between the Com- missioners and the company respecting the necessity for any works proposed by the Commissioners, or should the company require the Commissioners under this sub-section to execute any works whim the Commissioners may con- sider to be unnecessary or urareAsondble, the Local Govern- ment Board shall on tle application of either the company or the Commissioners determine the question as to whether such works are necessary or whether the requirements of such company are necessary or reasonable, and to What ex- tent.

(13) The company shalt provide sufficient accommodation by a ferry or other means to enable persons to pass across the the -canal to or from thetown of Runcorn from or to the river Mersey with suitable means of access thereto. (14) 'Provided that the company shall not under this sec- tion demand or take in respect of any cargo carried in any vessel on any part of the canal between_ the existing docks and basins at Weston Point and the Old Quay Canal at Runcorn; any higher toll thaw one penny per ton oa lime, one halfpenny per Lou on coal, and threepence on any other desdription of cargo. (15) Except as expressly provided by this Act nothing herein contained she?! prejudice„ alter, abridge, or affect any rights,. powers, privileges, or authorities of the Corn- missoners under any Act of -Parlierneet or otherwise. Mr. Pritchard moved that the action of the deputation be approved and confirmed, and that the seal of the Board be affixed to the agreement, and that the petition against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill be withdrawn. .
Mr. Lightburn thought it would be better if that resolu- tion emanated from a inemb.-!r who was not on the deputa- tion.
Mr. Lake said the first part 04 the resolution hsd better be left oat. They might have something to say about the conduct of the deputation. h. Light
• Mr. Pritchard acted upon this suggestion, and Mr. ,Lightburn then seconded the motion,. which was carried antnimously..

Mr. Lake pointed out that previous tombtaining power to oppose the hill repeated promises were ,nade to the rate- payers that no opposition should be ofnred to the princi- ples of the bill, their only objec.', being•to obtain protection to the interests of Runcorn. The retepiyers were subse- quently very much surprised to read that the counsel engaged by the Parliamentary and Legal Com- mittee not only pleaded very tenderly for Run- corn, but wound up his speech l)e, opposing the Bill tooth and nail. The pliblic considered this a breach of faith, and an explanation was very desirable. Mr. Lighbura said he wad astounded when he heard th e counsel's statemeot that the people of Runcorn were op- posed to the Ship Canal scheme if it could: not be proved that it would be a financial and commercial success. He was not at the conference when ceunsel was instructed through no fault of his own, because he had no knowledge of the meeting. These gentlemen take the bit in their own mouths and did their work in their own way. If he (Mr. Lightburn) had known that it was counsel's intentlou to oppose the bill in that fashion he should have strenuously opposed it. He expressed himself strongly at the time upon the subject. He himself had previously advised the witnesses, Captain Shaw aid Captain Hill, to use their dis- cretion and professional ability in giving evidence, but that. they were on no account to oppose the Ship Canal as a scheme. He could assure the Beard and the public that the Parliamentary and Legal Committee had worked anxiously, and he might say with intellieence, and he did not think anyone would be more pleased than they were that the work had been accomplished with so much 811CCP139. Mr. Like wished it to be clearly understood that he did wot wish to cast any reflection on the work of the commit- tee. In his opinion, they were entitled to the most hearty thanks of the Board for the efficient way in which they had concluded their business. He only desired an explana- tion. The Law Clark said the brief which was placed in the hands of Mr. Littler, the counsel, did not contain one word n reference to opposing the bill on its merits. It simply re- ferred to cleuses for the protection of the town and port of Runcorn. That brief was in existence and could be pub- lished if theired. Mr. Littler had a consultation with the promoters but they said that they would have nothing to do with the Board of Cemmissioners.. The Commissioners would have to fight them. Mr. Littler went into court and did not state what his intentions were. He afterwards ex- plained to Mr. Linaker and his Parliamentary agent that he in his discretion thought it advisable to take a strong objec- tiotato the bill upon its merits, not that the objection would do any injury to the promoters of the scheme, but because it would pat the Conunissiocers in a better position for ob- taining clauses for the protection of the port from the Com- pany. The Chairman remarked that the Committee was quite as much surprised as anyone else at the course taken by the counsel. They never deviated from the intentions I expressed before the Board or the ratepayers in any shape or form. The evidence given would prove that statement. ' The members then separated.

_ The annual meeting for the election of a chairman was held on Wednesday morning, in the Town Hall, Waterloo- road. There were oresent—Messrs. R. Shaw, T. Norman, Doabr rises. Taylor, , 'aimylmori,"' I'rhGirticcea' Whittaker, Williams, .Speakman, H rd, Meadoweroft, Linaker (law clerk), and Marshall (secretary). The Law Clerk took- the chair.
THE ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

Mr. Meadowcroft said the prat year had been a very ardu- ous one for the late chairman. His responsibilities had been unusually heavy, and the difficulties he had passed throrigh had been very trying, and only such asa gentleman of ability and experience could have gone through. His great desire had been throughout to administer the affairs, of the Board and the duties of his office to the very best of his ability, and in the interests of the ratertayers of the town. He therefore took upon himself the pleasure of fol- lowing past precedents, and of proposing a resolution for their favourable acceptance—that Mr. Shaw, be re-elected chairman for the next twelve months. There Was a feeling entertained by many members of the Board that the office of chairman should not be filled two consecutive years by the same gentleman, and an understanding,to that effect which would, he believed, be carried out in future was ar- rived at a meeting on the previous evening. But looking at the very eminent services which Mr. Shaw had performed for the town during the last twelve mmtlaa, and at the fact that he had ;roved himself so exceedingly efficient, and att all times minifesied a keen desire for efficiency, economy, and a judicious administration of the finances of the town ; that everything they did should be strictly straightforward and above board ; that there ehouli be nothing withheld from the ratepayers in any form whatever ; and further that he had inaugurated many reforms in the several depart- ments of the estab!rshment which it was desirable be should, see carried out to a satisfactory conclusion—for these reasons he ws of opinion they should re-elect Mr. Shaw. He trusted the Board would .do so unanimously as some re- cognition of the valuable services he had rendered to the town.—Mr Timmins seconded the motion There was an important measure going through Parliament which affected Runcorn very much, and he thought it would be enwise remove Mr. Shaw from his present position until that mea- sure was passed. He referred to precedents for re-electing a chairman a second time.—The motion was carried unani- mously.—Mr. Shaw then took the chair, and observed that he could testify that during the past year be received that support, assistance, confidence, and counsel which he expected from the members when they asked him to take the office, without which no gentleman could properly discharge the duties of a chairman. He had been mindful of the fact that they could only give him that sup- port of counsel so long as he discharged the duties of the office with perfect fairness and to their saUfaction. That had been his object throughout the year, and he took it that the confidence they had DOW shown in him by asking him to take the position for another yearovas an evidence that be had in some measure achieved the object he sot before himself twelve months ago, viz., that as far as pos- sible he would transact the business of the Board!, with per. feet fairness to each member, so that the business might be There, carried on in a satisfactory manner. (dear, hear.) s was another inttter to which he perhap ought to refer— that was the changes that had taken place during the last two years in the business of the 13').:d He thought it would be admitted that up to that time the responsibility of carrying out the instructions of the Picard had rested mainly upon the officials, and complaints were made from time to time that the work had not been performed as. it ought to be. Tke committeeshad now undertaken to bee that the work was properly discharged, and in a great measure they had fulfilled their trust. He specially mentioned the ad- mirable labours o; the Health Committee, and said that this system was an important advance which he hoped might continue. He was sure that the town would rasp the bene- fit. Be again thanked them for the honour thay had con- ',erred upon him that day. The meeting then terminated.

Mr. Thomas Glbb-ms' work has our very warm approval. The author not only pos.esses rare talegt for collecting curious and interesting informatio ; he is a traveller of considerable reputation, and has had foreign experiences that fall to the lot of very few.—Liverpool City News. Mr. Gibbons visited these countries, and presents the result of his study and observation in a very graphic and scholarly manner.—Erening Transcript, Boston, U.S A.. His papers are full of information, exceedlngly well-written, and very entertaining. Mr. Gibbons is evidently a practical writer, and his graphic descriptions of foreign countries and peoples are both in.eresting and amusing.—London Figaro.

Mr. Thomas Gibbms has travelled widely, and observed aeutely ; and, while there is mu-h in his writings to ihterest the schllar, the general reader will be attr4cted by the fresh- ness and vigour of his style, and the numerous amusing anec- dotes with which he illusttates his subjects.—Soclety.

MISCELLANEOVS.—The following were deft with for drunkenness :—John Urey. in Church-street, was fined 5s and costs; John Rowan, in Irlam-street, tined 103 and costs; Wm. Moran and James PAter, in Scotland-road, each fined 105 and coats; Margaret Hector, in Winwick-street, fined 10s and costs; Sarah Alice Jowett, in Irlam-street, dia. missed with a caution, the Bench directing that Ler fare to Liverpool should be paid; Charles Pollard, in Church- street, fined 103 and costs; Thos. Taylor, in Silver-square, fined 5s and costs.—Thomas Wilson, for bcgging in Bridge- street, was sent to prison for seven days ; and John Hart- ley, Armley, charged with begging in Sankey-street, was dismissed on promising to leave the town.—James Willey, who admitted being a deserter from H.M. let Battalion Scots Guards, was remanded to Walton to await escort. Scam. ATTENDANCE CASES—Thorn IS Rutter, forge- man, Oliver-street. was summoned for failing to send his 11 son, Benjamin, regularly to school.—Mr. Riley, school at- tendance officer, said the, present was the 12th summons with which the defendant had been served. He was weary of bringing the case before the magistrates.—The Chief Constable said he had received a communication from the authorities of the ship Clio to the effect that there was now a vacancy for boys, whereupon Me. Riley asked the magis- trates to send the boy to the C.io.—The magistrates made an order to that effect.—ln the case of Charles Higgin- son, labourer, Stamford-street, it was stated that his son, James, was a companion of the lad Rutter, and had been several times brought before the Bench for irregular atten- dance at school; and the magistrates also decided to send this offender to the same ship.—The following persons were also dealt with as under for neglecting to send their chil- dren regularly to school :—Bartholomew Carley, fined 5s ; Thomas Walmesley, Se; Enoch Jones, 5s ; Robert Belles, 59; Joseph Wilcock, ss; Kate Higgins, 2s 6d; John Towey, 5s ; Ann Leach, 53,--In the case of Arthur Jones, of Ellen-street, the magistrates were satisfied that the lad was Incorrigible, and the Bench decided that he should re- ceive 12 strokes of the birch-rod. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks and Mr. E. J. Guest. MISCELLANEOUS —Walter Atherton, a person under police supervision, was charged with failing to report himself to the police. He was ordered to be imprisoned for 48 hours. —James Frainey, charged with being drunk in Bridge- street on the previous evening, was ordered to pay Is costs. —Wm. Hill and Richard Welsh was sent to prison for seven days each for begging on the previous evening.— Sarah Ellen Wilkinson, charred with being drunk and dis- orderly in the neighbourhood- of the Bridewell, was dis- missed on promising to go to the workhouse. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley. MISCELLANEOUS.—Hugh Drury, for being drunk and dis- orderly in Winwick-street, on the previous evening, and for assaulting a boy named Archer, was sent to prison for 14 days.—William Scott watt sent to prison for seven days for t begging in Gladstone-street and Walker-street on the pre- vious evening.—Patrick Kennedy, a deserter from Her Majesty's 65th Regiment Light Infantry, stationed at New- castle-on-Tye, was remanded to await escort.—Michael Dowd, charged with being drunk in Wilderspool-road, was cautioned and dismissed. IDLE VAGRANTS.—WiIIiam Johnson and William Ed- wards were charged with refusing to perform their tasks of work whilst inmates of the vagranteward of the Union Workhouse.-L-Prisoners said they did not know they should have to remain so lorg in the House, and Edwards said that he was in a respectable position, but had been to Newton races and lost all his money.—They were each sent to prison for seven days. THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. BEGGING.—George Wilson and Frank Wilson, cousins, were charged with beoging in Howley-lane and Greenall- Street. on the previous evening. They were dismissed on promising te leave the town. VIOLENT WOMEN.—Anne Hodgson and Mary Coyne were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-street en the previous evening, and with assaulting P.C. Johnson. That officer stated that Hodgson, who only UM out of prison on the previous morning, Was very drunk, and as she refused to leave the street he took her into custody. When near Academy-street Coyne came up and interfered. Hodgson then struck the constable, and Coyne tried to hit him on the head with her elm They pleaded hard for mercy, and were dismissed on making premises to reform their conduct. &Hoot. ATTENISANCE.—John Reams was summoned by Mr. Shearer for not sending his daughter to school regu- larly.—A fine of 55 was imposed. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes and Captain Reynolds. ASSAULTING A WIFE —Joseph Birchall, engine cleaner, was charged, under a warrant, with having assaulted his wife and was bound over to keep the peace, himself in £lO and two sureties in £5 each.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SLSSIONS. WEDNEsDAY.—Before Messrs. Ziba Armitage and James Matson. • MISCELLANEOUS —Patrick Mnlaney was fined 53. and costs for being drunk in the highway at Eurtonwood on the 6th inst.—William Lee. charged with damaging oats in a field at Great Sankey, belonging to John Hatton, was dis- missed with a caution.—Henry Antrobus was fined is. and costs for allowing an ass to stray at Poulton, on the sth inst., and Edward Marshall, for being asleep whilst in charge of a lorry on the 6th inst. was fined 55. and costs.—Daniel Allen was fined 58. and costs for riding on a cart whilst asleep at Great Bankey on the 6th inst.—Patrick Finerty and Isaac Fryer were charged with sleening out on the previous night. Fryer was ordered to pay 43. 6d. costs, and Finerty was sent to prison for a month. ALLEGED ASSAULT —Thomas Austell, fustian cutter, was summoned by Willi.m Perrin for assaulting him at Rixton on the 6th June. Perrin had been to a club meeting at the Eagle and Child, and alleged that on coming out Anstalt struck him and otherwise assaulted him. For the defence Mr. Jenkins said that the complainant was the aggressor. Witnesses having been heard on both sides, the Bench fined Anstall ss. and costs.
LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Brfore Messrs. Stanton and Allen.

MISCELLANEOUS.—George Oakes, a young man, was charged with not having proper control of a horse and cart of which he was in charge, at Warburton, on the 22nd May. P.C. 73 proved the we. Defendant was fined 53. and costs.—John Longshaw, Warrington, was summoned for causilag an obstruction at Lynam, on the 12th ult ,by leav- ing a carriage standing in the road near the Spread Eagle for an unreasonable time, viz, half an hour. A fine of ss. and costs was impos.d —John Platt pleaded not guilty to a charge of being drank and disorderly at Booth Hill, Lymm, on the 31st May. The case having been proved, he was fined 15s and costs, or an alternative Øf one month's im- prisonment With hard labour.—Thomas Moss, for being drunk and disorderly at Broom Edge, Lymm, on the 7th Inst., was fined 2s. ed. and costs. CRUELTY TO A tionsa.—William Dale, boatman, Patri- croft, failed to answer a summons charging him with ill-

treating a horse on the 13th inst.—Sergeant Bossons stated that on that day he saw dqfendant in charge of a black mare, attached to a heavy coal flat. D4endant was work- ing the horse severely, and lashed it cruelly.—A fine of 10a and costs, or one month's imprisonment with hard labour, was imposed. FIIBLIC•HOUSE GAMlNG.—William Owen, landlord of the Jolly Thresher, Broom Edge, Lymm, was charged with allowing gaming to be carried on on his premises.—Mr. Wallhead, from the office of the Town Clerk of Warrington, appeared for the defence.--Richard Kirkpatrick, joier, Broom Edge, stated that on the 4th April he took part in a game at dominoes, for beer, at the house of the defendant.— Hugh Collins spoke to seeing the game played, but said that Ihe heard nothing about beer being played for.—The Bench, after hearing the evidence, dismissed the case without calling upon Mr. Wallhead to address them for.the defence. MISCHIEVOUS BOYS.—Five boys named Clayton, Rowell, Read, Chorlton, and Dixon were charged with damaging hay-grass on enclosed land in the occupation of Jane Woodall.—On the 6th inst. they had been bathing in the canal, and afterwards trampled on the erass.—They were dismissed on promising not to off end again, and to pay the costs, 5s 6d each. A FEROCIOUS DOG.—William Johnson, who did not ap- pear, was summoned for allowing a dog to be at large, and not under proper control, on the 30:h March, in contraven- tion of an order that has since expired.—P.C. Chatterton, who proved the case, said that the dog was a ferocious one, and had bitten several people. It was not fit Vi be at large at any time.—Defendant was fined 5s and 13s 6d costs.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. Henry

Reynolds. MISCELLANEOUS.—Thomas Yond, for using profane lan- guage in Fryer-street on the Bth June was fined 103 and costs.—Patrick Smith, Patrick Coffey, and Thomas Oul- tram were each fined for drunkenness. -

NEWTON, HAYDOCK, AND GOLBORNE BUILDING SOCIETY. A LIVELY MEETING. The twenty-fifth annual meeting of the shareholders of the Newton. Haydock, and Golborne Permanent Benefit Building Society was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday evening. The meeting had not been publicly an- nounced, but was called by circular. There was a fairly good attendance. The chair was occupied by Lieutenant- Colonel George McCorquodale, J.P., and there were also present Mr. B. B. Glover, Messrs. Davies and Kirkconnell (solicitors), Prescot, Frost, Farrow, and other gentlemen.

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: THE REPORT.

The directors in their annual report stated :—" The amount now outstanding on properties in band is £18,072 3s 11d, which includes £216 3s 3d spent on street making during the present year. Efforts have been made to sell some of the properties by private treaty, bat the market still remaining so low, the managers have not been success- ful, and have thought better to keep them for the present rather than make a sacrifice; and in the meantime to main- tain them in an efficient state of repair, which has been done. Five mortgages on properties not in hand have been paid off during the year, amounting to £2,399 18s 86, and the ordinary repayments are £1,176 Sc Bd, leaving the net BUM of £20,624 18s 46. outstanding on the properties. The liabilities to the members on invested shares have been re- duced £3,822 14s 3d, that is from £40,338 5s 7d to £36,515 lie 4d. The profits for the year (including £3Bl 18s for- feitures of 15 per cent. on final settlement with withdraw- ing members) are £2,032 us 6d. A dividend of £3 per cent. per annum has been declared, which will take £1,016 Os 2d, leaving £1,014 us 46. to be carried to the contingent account, which, with the balance of £1,740 5s 3d in band last year, make the contingent account £2,754 16s 7d, which is over 15 per cent, upon the reduced value on properties in the society's bands. The society consists of 444 members, bolding 3,406 invested shares, and 4,566 purchased shares. Also 159 persons who have withdrawn. and left 20 per cent., amounting to £2,571 lds 4et," The general statement of accounts showed the liabilities to be £40,300 6s 26, including £2,032 us 6d as "balance- profit for the year," and the assets £38,716 4s 7d, with cash in bank £1,584 Is 7d. 'lles profit and loss account showed the receipts from all sources te be e£2,235 lOs 96, and the expenditure, including £l,OlB On 24 as "dividend at 3 per cent., £1,220 19s 56, leaving £1,014 11 46 to the con- tingent fund. The Chairman then addressed the meeting. In contrast- ing the balance sheet with one they had a few years ago, he said it showed the society to be in a favourable and satisfactory state. Of course there was one thing he was sorry for, and that was that they were in a state of liqni- I dation, instead of going on in a flourishing manner, but it I was only the state of many other building societies. He had an extract from "Truth" in his hand which showed that societies generally were in a very bad state, having vety little reserve in band. (Hear, hear.) He had been requested to point out that a good number of properties that had been mortgaged to the society had after a while been withdrawn, and the owners had been able to get mortgages on very favourable terms outside, and that seemed a pity when the society had nearly £1,500 lying in the bank at very small interest; but perhaps Mr. Davies could propose something to enable them to save their property and benefit their old friends. There was another thing they very much regretted, and that was the loss sustained by their friends withdrawing their shares. They had kept 20 per cent., as they knew, and many who were still in the society would lose in all about 15 per cent.,.and he did not thick they could do any- thing but finally settle with those who required settlement, for 15 per cent, instead of 20. The properties in hand could not well be sold yet; they were waiting for better times, and they had been kept in good repair. The other proper- ties they ha': not in hand were getting less ; five mortgages had been paid off during the year amounting to £2,399 18s 86. (Applause.) Mr. R. Brierley then proposed that the accounts be passed, and Mr. J. S. Entwistle seconded the motion. Mr. J. PRESCOTT (Earlestown) said he found something like £lB,OOO worth of property still in hand. How much of that property was insured against loss by fire ? He would like to say a few words as to what he would call the extravagant management. It was not mush consolation to the members to come there to be told that the society was doing fairly well, and as good as other bankrupt societies, and they were only getting 3 per cent, whilst the officials were feathering their nest. There was the secretary's salary. It had been said that Mr. Adams had taken away the pro- f fits of the society, and whilst he was doing this, he would guarantee he had not more than £lO in the society, which he was bound to have according to rule. He was not afraid to say this before Mr. Adams' face. £3O or £4O of the salary was virtually thrown away. Let them have it in their dividends. The printing and stationery item was ten per cent more this year than last. Another item was two guineas to Mr. Frost for attending audit. That was a new item. So long as they as shareholders were receiving three per cent instead of five, they had a right te insist upon these expenses being cut down. (Applause). Mr. J. Farrow said there was an item of £3OO "Final Retentions, 1883," but he could find no trace of it in last year's balance sheet. He maintained that the managers should give them a tabulated statement of the properties they had in band. They found that the property repre- sented art amount of £lBOOO, with a rental of enly £643, and he thought there must have been an extraordinary amount of expenditure, which in the present mode of keep- ing accounts was "burked." (Hear, hear.) The Chairman said he might tell them that the property was well protected. It was the duty of the solicitor to eee that all properties mortgaged to the society were properly insured. Respecting the secretaryship and the exp,nee attending it, he thought this question had been satisfactorily arranged in previous years. Mr. Prescott said as the receipts were small and the expenses heavy, the secretary's salary should be reduced. Ile (the speaker) thought they were getting on remarkably well. With regard to the question of printing, he did not think there was anything remarkable about that. He was a great advocate for expenditure in printing. (Laughter.) Mr. Davies (sot citor), in response to a request, read a I minute which was to the effect that the secretary's salary tENould remain as it then was namely, £BO a year. . That resolution was carried with only one dissentient. Mr. Prescott : That has just brought out what I wanted to know. I find Mr. Bridge was the only one in favour of the reduction, and I shall move that be be returned on the Beard. Mr. Glover defied either Mr. Prescott or anyone else to prove that either he or any other of the managers were feathering their nest out of the society—(cries cf "The sec- retary ")—and he should therefore call upon Mr. Prescott to withdraw his expression, as he would not allow either him or anyone else to say that he was making anything out of the society. Mr. Prescott said he was sorry that Mr. Glover had taken the expression to himself, as it was not meast for him, but for Mr. Adams (the secretary), Mr. Frost said he was one of the managers, and he had drawn the payment mentioned in the balance sheet. He thought it was a most barefaced insult on the part of Mr. Prescott to u'se the expressions he had done with respect te the managers. Colonel McCorquodale : I have done all I can and have called Mr. Prescott's attention to the matter with the view of getting him to say that he did not mean to hurt anyone's feelings. Mr. Davies said he agreed with the Chairman that these vague and unfair remarks should not be made. He tho‘Nht it was an unfortunate expression, and he must ask Mr. Frost and others not to take any notice of it. The Chairman afterwards put the motion to the meetings The voting was pretty close, but the accounts were passed by a narrow majority.
• ELECTION OF OFFICERS. The next business was the election. of officers;ond the

appointment of managers created a lively "scene." When ths voting was taking place there were several cries of "Now lads another £6O man," alluding to the reduction of the secretary's salary. These interruptions called forth severe censure from the chairman. The following were ultimately elected managers, those re-elected being denoted by an asterisk :—Messrs. *B. B. Glover (chairman), *James Bridge, *E. Fairclough, *F. A. •Frost, *Thomas Howard, *Joseph Jackson, *Thomas Mitchell, *James Liptrott, *Wm. Mitchell, *Thomas Ritchie, J. Goff, and A. Funblett. Messrs. F. A. Frost and E. Fairclongb were re-appointed stewards, and Mr. J. Pennington was re-elected surveyor. Messrs. W. Appleby (Manchester), and James Lawton (Gol- borne) were anpointed auditors. On the motion of Mr. B. J. Glover, seconded by Mr. Prescott a vote of thanks was passed to the chairman, and the meeting concluded.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1885.
GENERE, NEWS.
LIBERAL MEETING AT PENKETH.

OuR HEREDITARY LEGIsLATORS.—The Committee of the People's League to Abolish the Heriditary Legislative Chamber have issued a number of leaflets, on which are pointed out the various important measures which have been rejected by the House of Lords during the present century. , A catechism as to what a peer is, whence he gets his title, and his claim to the honour, gives much information in a simple form. The People's League appeals to the electors to make the abolition of the Hereditary Chamber a test question with Parliamentary candidates. CRICKET PLAYING ON SUNDAY.—On the Abbey Meadows, Leicester, on Sunday, several thousand persons assembled to witness the resumption of the game of cricket com- menced the previous Sunday to test the legality of playing on Sunday. Great pressure had been exercised to induce the Secularists not to persevere in their efforts, and they have been officially informed that the right to Use the ground is undisputed. At the request of the authori- ties, however, the resumption of the game was adjourned for a fortnight, owing to the public excitement which pre- vailed on the question. There was no disturbance. IRISH NeTipNALIsTS AND LORD SPENCER. Mr. T. O'Sullivan, MT , speaking at a meeting at the National League, on Tuesday, said a more bitter and determined enemy of Ireland than Lord Spencer never left it. His office expired with the expiration of the Crimes Act, which was not wanted to repress crime but as a political engine. The prospects of gaining Irish rights and liberties were never brighter.—Mr. Harrington, M.P , invited Lord Spencer to do something for the families of the innocent men whom he had sent to the grave. He had tempted Lord Spencer to prosecute him that he might show Myles Joyce's innocence. THE BRADLAIIGH QUESTION.—Mr. Bradlaugh has written a letter to the Speaker of the House of Commons withdraw- ing and cancelling the letter he addressed to him prior to the reassembling of the Parliament for the second session of 1884, in which he undertook to make no attempt to take his seat in the House until judgment had been given in the the proceediems then about to be taken by the Crown with reference to his self-administration of the oath. This letter the Speaker did not submit to the House of Commons. Mr. Bradlaugh further intimates his intention, as soon as the new Cabinet has been formed and the re-election of minis- ters has taken place, to present himself once more for the purpose of taking his seat. CHESHIRE BAPTISTS. —Tbe annual business meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptist Churches was held on Wedneslay, at Liverpool. After the transaction of some formal business, the Moderator (Mr. J. W. Scholefield) delivered his annual address. The annual report, which was read by the Secretary (the Rev. R. Lewis, showed that there are 111 churches connected with the association, and that during the year there has been a 1 net increase of 548 in the number of members connected with the churches. There are 3,321 Sunday school teachers, and 34,674 scholars. A petition to the House of Commons in favour of the closing of public-houses on Sun- days was adopted, In the evening the public association mission meeting was held. METHODIST NEW CONNEEION CONFERENCE.—The busi- ness sessions of this conference were opened on Monday morning, at Salem Chapel, Manchester, when there was a large gathering of the ministers and representatives ef the Connexion. The President (Rev. T. D. Crothers, Staly- bridge) proceeded to constitute the Conference. Cases of dispute having been settled, a formal resolution was passed welcoming the Rev. J. Innocent on his return from China as a missionary, and making him a fall member of the Conference. Mr. Innocent received a splendid ovaticn, and briefly replied under great emotion. A vacancy having oc- curred in the guardian representation, occasioned by the death of the Rev. Dr. Cooke, quite a number of names were submitted in nomination for the honour. The Rev. T. D. Crothers, the retiring president, was declared duly elected by ballot. The Conference elected as president the Rev. Alex. MiCurdy. Mr. Addyman was elected Confer- ence secretary. The Rev. D. Heath was appointed journal secretary. A number of committees were afterwards ap- pointed. Tree DRINKING CUSTOMS OF EUROPE.—A remarkable I reaper on the "Drink Traffic in Germany," prepared by Dr. I Baer, the head physician at the Plotzensee Prison, has been , reprinted by the English Foreign Office for the collection of publications on "subjects of commercial and general interest." Dr. Baer has been at pains to get at the con- sumption of intoxicating liquors in all the chief European States, and the result of his inquiries is that Denmark heads the list of spirit-drinking nations, consuming not less than 180 litres per head of the population. Russia comes next with 16.0 litres, then Sweden with 11.2, North Germany with 104. Belgium with 975, Holland with 967, Switzer- land with 7.5, Great Britain with 6, Austria with 40, France with 31 and Norway with 34. Belgium is the greatest , beer-drinking country. consuming 160 litres per head ; and Great Britain follows with 147 litres, North Germany standing at 88.5, and France at 23. France consumes 74 litres per head of wine, Switzerland 100, and Great Britain 2.5. An Englis'a gallon, we may remind our readers, con- tains rather more than 41 litres. THE COBDEN CLUB DINNER.—The annual dinner of the Cobden Club was held on Saturday evening at the Ship Hotel, Greenwich, whither the members proceeded by steamer from Westminster. Sir Charles Dilke proceeded. Mr. Chamberlain, Lord Harlington, and many other Liberal members of Parliament attended. In proposing the memory of Cobden, Sir C. Dilke remarked that there had been in re- cent years a considerale advance towards the adoption of Cobden's principles in this country and abroad. First, there was the reference to arbitration of a great international dis- pute between this country and another Power. A war, which would have involved one-third of the human race had thereby been averted, and averted by honourable means. —Mr Chamberlain, referring to Sir Charles Dhke's part in the commercial negotiations with France, said it was a fallacy to call those negotiations frutitless, since they had resulted in obtaining for us the most favoured nation clause. He had seen the extraordinary statement that Lord Salisbury would not assume office but he received it with incredulous indignation. But if the Conservative party understood the responsibilities of office they must continue on the same lines of the policy which they had so Often condemned. LAUNCH or AN IRONCLAD BY MRS. Gums-roma—On Mon- day afternoon the Benbow, one of the largest of the Admiral class of ironclads, was launched from the Orchard Yard of the Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company at Blackwell, the ceremony of naming the vessel being per- formed by Mrs. Gladstone. The Benbow is armour-plated iron faced with steel of a total thickness of 18in , and is 33011. in length. 681 t. Gin. hi breadth, and 371 t. Thin, in depth. Her armament will consist of two 110 ton guns, twelve small quick firing guns, ten Gin. breechloaders, 14 machine galls, and torpedoes.—Responding on behalf of Mrs. Gladstone to the toast of be' health, which proposed by leer. A well attended meeting of Liberals was held at Penketh on Wednesday evening, in support of the candidature of Colonel McCerquodele for the Newton Division, and to ' listen to an address by the Rev. D. S. Prosser, of Walkden, on the subject Why should working-men be Liberals i" Mr. Parker occupied the °hair, and amongst those present were Messrs... Hall and T. Howard (Eerlesiown), F. Dignum, E. Randall, T. Guy, Greenhalgh, Walters, Meinley, Seed, Atherton, A. J. White, Bestwick, J. Thomson, J. Davies, W. Lengshaw, J. C. Routledge, H. Hughes, Sec. Toe CRiIRMAN, in his opening remarks, said that they as Liberals of the Newton Division of South-West Lanca- shire proposed supporting Colonel MeCorquodale because be bad pledged himself to support Mr. Gladstone and the great principles to which Mr. ladstone had ever been attached—(beer, hear)—the principles which the Liberal party held dear, those of Liberty, Reform, and the brother- hood and equality of man. (Applause.) He should not like them to honour their chief only in his personality, but because he had through life so consiatentle advocated those principles. (Applause.) The LECTURER said that the political sky was at present overcast, but the blue would by-and-bye appear. Several tillage had happened since a Belie& of meetings, of which that was on were arranged. It brit by them been intended i to serve two purposes—one to pass, if they could, votes of ernfidence in her Majesty's Government, and the other to aid the candidature of Colonel McCorquedale at the next f general election. The Liberal party had realised a reverse, 1 whilst the series of meetings Was in progress, and now the t Liberal Government had resigned and were only conducting ' the necessary affairs of the country until their successors ' can relieve them of their datiee and responsibilities. It was probable that Conservatives here, as elsewhere, were realis- , log a pleasant surprise in finding themselves once more the party in office, although, unfortunately for them, they could not congratulate themselves on being the party in power. In a few days a Conservative Ministry would be established in office, but they would go into office with the knowledge that their opponents had a majority in the House of Commons. He thought that the more sober and thoughtful of them would be prepared also to admit that the Liberal party had a majority in the coun• try. (Applause.) Great blame had attached to the Minis- try for resigning upon the adverse vote of the House of Commons, but it was most unreasonable for the Conserva- tives to blame their opponents. He held that when what was really a vote of censure was carried by the responsible Opposition, it was the duty of the Liberal Government, if they were defeated to resign, and unless the Conservative party were prepared to accept office they had no right as a ' party to lend themselves at all to the vote, and support it when it was presented to the House. It was something strange to see the House of Commons first of all unani- mously pass a vote for the expenditure of eleven millions of money and than to find the responsible Opposition refusing , to grant the Government the power necessary to raise such sum To his mind far the more honourable course would , have been for the Opposition to have challenged the vote; , not having accepted the resolution for the spending of eleven millions, to have refused the Government the power ,to raise the money. Ha did not think thd Liberal party had need complain of what bad happened. It was a serious thing for all patriotic Englishman to consider, that the Coneervatives came into office by the support of Mr. Par- nell and his irreconcilable followers. The Liberal party had no reason to complain of being defeated by a resolution in , connection with which it was boldly and openly stated that a tax should te put upon tea rather than upon spirits and beer. He did not think anything was likely to make the Liberal party more popular, especially with the new elector. ate, than the fact that they refused to increase the duty upon tea, and preferred to tax an article that could bear the increase 1 which would not have fallen upon the consumer as much as I upon the wholesale and retail vendor, The Liberal party 11 was in this matter strengthened rather than weakened. ' (Hear, bear.) Again, it was no small benefit to them that the leaders of the party would for a time be untrammelled by the cares and responsibilities of office. We should have their presence amongst us, and they would be able to render I much personal assistance to Liberal principles, that it would not otherwise have been in their power to do. It would also enable their great chief—(applause)—to take his position at the bead of the army, and Mr. Gladstone, they hoped, would be one of the foremost in the fight upon which they soon would enter. That they had reason to hope that would be so was to be gathered from the news that Mr. Gladstone had declined to accept a peerage. (Ap- plause.) They were most grateful to him that be had de- termined thus to stand by his own name and to live and die I the most popular and powerful Cammoner in the British I Empire. (Applause.) Before it was known that a Conser- vative Government would come into office, both political parties were solicitous et securing the sympathy of the Two Millions just admitted to the franchise. It was easy to understand this solicitude for the working-men, in a broad and general sense, really had the future destinies of the country under their control. The interest taken by the Conservative party was borne of the fact that the working- men would soon have power, but the Liberal party had taken an interest in the working classes for years, and had for long championed their cause. The result had been the admission of the working clauses to the franchise. It would be said that no one party had a right to monopolise the credit of passing the Franchise and Redistribution Bills. In connection with the Redistribution there had certainly been compromise and agreement,- but that would I not have been entered into by the Conservatives unless they had seen that the admission of the masses was unavoidable, and therefore they made a virtue of necessity. Mr. Prosser then spoke at length on the various beneficient measures passed by Liberal Govern- ments, and urged strong arguments in favour of Liberal principles—principles which they believed to be just and right, and which therefore must prevail. Mr. HALL proposed the first resolution, which read as follows a—" That this meeting considers Colonel McCorquo- dale, J.P., a fit and proper person to represent this Division in the New Parliament, and, pledges itself to use all legiti- mate means to secure his return at the next election." Be spoke in terms of praise of the candidate. Mr. GREENHALO3I seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously. Mr. WALTERS proposed " That this meeting heartily ap- I proves of the conduct of Mr. Gladstone and his Government in resigning their official positions in consequence of the adverse vote on the Budget proposals, and pledges a con- tinued and increased support to Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party." He thought that the resolution would corn- .mend itself to every Liberal. (Applause ) He applauded Mr. Gladstone for not taking a sleepy position in another House at the present juncture of affairs, and thought that the Liberals had acted wisely throughout. Mr. F. Diabrom, who thought that the Government had taken the only course open to them under the circum- stances, seconded the resolution, which was carried with &Kamm. Votes of thanks concluded the meeting.

COPPER-COLORED.—I have been afflicted with a troublesome skin disc tse, covering almost completely the upper p.rt of my body, causing my skin to assume a copper-oolored hue. It could be rubbad off like dandruff, and at times causing intol- erable itching, and the most intense suffering. I have us,-d blood purifiers, pills and other advertised remedies, but expe- rienced no relief until I procured the OUTICURA REMEDIES, which, although used carelessly and irregularly, cured me, alias log that terrible itching, and restoring my skin to its natural color. lam willing to make affidavit to the truth of this statement. B. G. BUXTON, Milan, Michigan, 117.8. A- .

ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, Judge. SINGULAR ACCIDENT SOCIETY CASE.—Mrs. Ann Reid, residing at Eccleston, for whom Mr. lt. W. H. Thomas ap- peared, sued the St. Helens Foundry Accident Society for the recovery of £5, an amount alleged to be due under the rules of the society.—Mr. Thomas stated that the plaintiff was the widow of the late Joseph Reid, who was a member of the Accident Society established at Messrs. Daglish's Foundry. At his death the sum of £5 was doe, and the plaintiff now sought that amount. Several other claimants had come forward and demanded the money from the trea- surer, and the workmen declined to pay the money until they had a judgment from his honour. The plaintiff had taken out letters of administration for the estate, and asked for judgment.—Mrs. Reid said her husband died ow the 3rd February in the Liverpool Infirmary.—Mr. Thomas then re- marked that the only question was as to who was entitled to the money.—Mr. Willgoose, cashier at Messrs. Daglish's Foundry, said they did not dispute that £5 was due, but they wished to know to whom they had to pay the money. There were two other claimants.—His Honour observed that he thought the society would be quite safe in paying the plaintiff, and he would made an order for payment. A REVELATION.—Thomas Howarth, a furiaaceman, at present working at Weston, near Widnes, was sued for the recovery of 19s, alleged to be due to Thomas Probvn, a grocer, in Beaumont-street, Widnes.—Mrs. Probyn stated that the defendant formerly lodged at her house, and he and a woman with whom he was living were supplied with groceries. The amount claimed was owing on the account. —The defendant said he was living with a married woman at Mrs. Probya's. She was not his wife, but armee then her husband had died, and he (defendant) had married her. His wife's sister-in law had got the goods unknown to him.—His Honour ultimately gave a verdict for the plain- tiff for the amount claimed.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

IRANSFER.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday the license of the Mill field Inn, Appletm, was transferred from George Roulding to Thomas Thornley Lee. DEATH OF MRS. SAMPSON.—On Sunday afternoon, Mrs Sampson, widow of the late L. W. Sampson, vicar of Pres- cot, died at the Crescent, where she had resided since the death of her husband, three years ago, at the age of 78. She was interred on Thursday at noon in a vault of the ceme- tery adjoining the church. The Rev. F. Lee, senior curate, conducted the service with the assistance of the Rev. R. P. Crockett, vicar of Eccleston.

ZION CHAPEL—Oa Sunday two sermons were preached in the above place of worship by Mr. A. Roscoe, of Bolton, vice-president of the Primitive Methodist Connexion, after- noon and evening. The annual collections were made at the close of each service in aid of the trust fund, which realised £2 15s 10a. The schools on behalf of which funds are needed are in a favourable condition with 180 children on the books. The afternoon service was but moderately attended, but in the evening there was a fair congregation. A RUNAWAY HORSE.—At noon, on Tuesday, a horse, drawing a heavily-laden cart of earthenware, belonging to Samuel Twist of St. Helens, took fright in the High-street, Prescot, and, getting beyond the control of the driver, gal- loped down the steep thoroughfare, Derby-street, at a tre- mendous pace, scattering its load right and left, the har- ness flying in pieces. One or two vehicles had a narrow escape of collision. When near the bottom of the brcw the horse fell, and when extricated was found to be badly in- jured.

A FATHER AND MOTHER'S SUPPORT —At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday Charles Critchley, employed as a porter at Liverpool by the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Co., was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute towards the support of his aged father and mother, both of whom are chargeable to the Prescot Union. It was stated that the defendant, who did not appear, was a married man with three children and he was in receipt of 249 per week as , wages. The Bench made an order for Is per week. CONSERVATIVE ORGANISATION.—A meeting was called for the purpose of adopting rules and the election of a com- mittee of an electoral association for the Prescot district of the Ormskirk division of the county. It was held in the club, Daly-street, and was fairly attended. Mr. J. D. Banks, Sen., vice-president, occupied the chair in the ab- sence of Mr. W. L.. Evans. The following were elected : Dr. E. F. Hall, Messrs. P. G. Twist, J. Case, sen., P. Tay- lor, G. Eaton, E. Range, R. Gore, T. Browebill, W. Pres- cott, L. Gardner, H. Cross, H. Whitfield, J. Stockley, G. Wilson, E. Baylis, E. Rimmer, T. Evans, J. W. MacMillan, R. Mercer, and J. Hall. The further proceedings were of a business character in connection with registration. A PRESOOT COLLIER IN DIFFICULTIES.-011 Tuesday, at the 'Southport County Court, Mr. T. E. Williams, solicitor, I applied to the judge, Mr. J. F. Collier, for an administra- tion order under section 122 of the Bankruptcy Act, 1883, on behalf of a James Martland, formerly a collier living at Prescot, and who also bad there a hardware shop. About eight years age he met with an accident in the mine, and since that time he had been in very delicate health. He came to reside in Southport, and W3S now employed by the Corporation at 17s per week. Martland was in debt to the extent of £44 12s 54. most of which was incurred at Pres- cot, and he offered Is in the pound, to be paid at 3s per month.—Elis Honour said the offer was very little indeed. There was however, 2s in the pound for fees, and the order would be for 2s ed in the pound, payable at 31 per month.

A CARELESS MOTHER.—Before Messrs. T. Pilkington and C. Barnes, at the Present Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Mary Rigby, a widow, formerly residing in Brown's Square, off Eccleston-street, Prescot, was brought up for deserting her family of four children whereby they became chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr. Thomas Parkinson, relieving officer, stated that on the 21st May from information he received he visited the prisoner's house and found four children, whose ages were ten, nine, four, and three years. They were entirely destitute and nearly naked. There was no furniture in the house and no lsread for them. The

children informed him that their mother had been away for a month. Ile got a cab and took them to the workhouse. He believed the woman had been leading an immoral life. The Bench considered .the case a very bad one, and committed

the prisoner to prison for one month. THE SCHOOL BOLHD held its monthly meeting at the Clerk's Office on Monday evening, when there were present —Messrs. H. Fogg (in the chair), J. T. Hall, T. P. Hewitt, J. B. Sanders, W. Goldswortb, and H. Cross (clerk.)—Mr. Goldsworth reported that the coat of levelling and cindering the ground in front of the schools would be about £7, and it was ordered that the work be carried out during the holi- days. A question arose as to painting the outside and whitewashing the inside of the schools, and it was ultima- tely resolved that it be left to Mr. J. T. Hall and Mr. Golds- worth to obtain tenders and order the work to be done dur- ing the holidays. A letter was read from Mr. Doke, of War- rington-road, Prescot, applying for the transfer of his daughter—a pupil teacher in the infant school—to the girls' school. The Board consented to the transfer. Miss Guy (pupil teacher in the girls' school) having obtained an ap- pointment at Southprt gave notice that she wished to leave at once, and she kindly asked the Board for a testi. . _ .

monial. The request was cheerfully complied with. BOARD OF GtIARDIANS.--The fortnightly meeting was held on Thursday week at the Whiston Workhouse. Mr. Leatherbarrow presided. A letter was read from the Local Government Board asking what decision the Guardiass had arrived at regarding a water supply to the Workhouse.— The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) was instructed to reply that th 9 Guardians had not yet arrived at a decision.—Another com- munication was read from the Local Government Board,

- stating that they would shortly issue an order for an elec- tion of a Guardian in Eccleston township to fill the vacancy caused by the death of the late Mr. John Fidler.—A Guar- dian asked if the Rainhill vacancy was about to be filled up, to which the Clerk replied that there was no mention of it in the communication.—The Rev. Thomas Chambers: The Local GoYernment Board is disorganised at the present day. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Henry Sumner, architect, of Liverpoel, applied for the payment of £l5O for professional services rendered. The letter was referred to the Finance Commit- tee.—The Clerk said a tradesman had offered to supply the Workhouse with goad fresh fish. The fish dinners, however, bad been discontinued, so that they would not entertain it. In reply to a question, the Clerk said the reason of the dis- continuance was that there was a loss of 30s or 40s per day, and the inmates were dissatisfied with it.—The Rev. T. Chambers: But fish is supposed to be beneficial to the intellect on account of the phosphorus it con- taine.—The Clerk: But that is not much reunited for in- mates of the Workhouse. (Laughter.)—Mr.Longton called attktion to the case of an Irishman who was found ill in a barn on Pemberton's farm premises, Sutton, en Saturday week, and who while being removed to the Workhouse on the following Monday diea in the cab. He (Mr. Longton) understood that the relieving officer could not be found, hence the delay in his removal. He asked if some explana- tion could be given.—The Clerk said as a matter of fact there was no blame attachable to the Union officials. When the man was found, Mr. Pemberton sent for Dr. Casey in his private capacity, and not as Union medical officer, and offered to pay him for his services. Dr. Casey attended the man until Mr. Pemberton said he must be removed. At this stage he became a pauper, and Dr. Casey sent word to the workhouse that the man must be removed at all risks. The cab was sent, and the poor fellow died in it. Strictly speaking the body of the man ought not to have been brought to the workhouse, but ought to have been left in the borough of St. Helens. An inquest was held, but no blame was then attacberi to the Union officers, and he (the clerk) respectfully submitted that as such legal in- quiry had been held there was no need for the guardians to re-open the inquiry.—Mr. Longton said he understood the relieving officer was sought for nearly three days, but could not be found, and he thought they might ask him where he was.—The guardians held that there was no necessity to go into the matter, as the inquest was closed, and Mr. Long- ton said he was satisfied with the explanation so far as it went.

CHURCH CLERGY IN NONCoNIAJAMIST PULPITS.—CoNn- seI's opinion has been obtained on the question as to whether a clergyman is legally entitled to preach in a Nonconformist place of worship. We hear that an opinion has been given to the effect that a clergyman may legally 2ccupy a Non- conformist pulpit in his own parish. It is believed that he has no such right in any other parish. THE VISIT OF THE PRINCH OF WALES TO LANCASHIRE.— On all hands preparations are actively proceeding for the reception of the Prince of Wales at Preston and Ormskirk. A fine awning is to be constructed a' Ormskirk railway station. Committees are canvassing for subscriptions, and efforts are being made to get over two thousand pounds. At Ormskirk it is expected that rive hundred pounds will be raised.

EARL ES TOWN. FAILURE AT EARLESTOWN.—Ga Wednesday, at the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, before Mr. Registrar Bell- ringer, Mr. Thomas Cooper, watchmaker and joweher, carrying on business in Market-street, Earlestown, pre- sented a petition in his own behalf, and was adjudicated a bankrupt. A receiving order was made, and the 29th inst. was fixed for the public examination of the debtor. THE CONSUALPTION OF GAS AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.—From a statement prepared by Mr. R, Brierley, clerk and surveyor to the Newton Improvement Commis- sioners, it appears that the total amount of gas made at the Commissioners' gasworks during the year ending the 25th March last was 24,719,200 cubic feet. The gas consumed by meters during the same period was estimated at 20,226,900 cubic feet; estimated consumption by Public lamps and works, 2,505,000 cubic feet; while "leakages and unaccountable gas" was put down at 1,987,300 cubic feet.

SWING BOAT ACIDENT AT EARLESTOWN. —During race week a number of swing boats, shows, and other " at- tractions " for visitors were erected on the Earlestown mar- ket ground, and on Thursday night a serious accident hap- pened in connection with one of the swings. A lad residing at Parr was swinging in one of the boats when he accideut- ally fell out, and alighted on his back. The lad sustained severe injuries and was rendered insensible. He was subse- quently conveyed to the Welcome Coffee Palace, Market- place, where he remained unconscious until his removal home in a cab. THE GAMBLING AT NEWTON RACES.—Last week we reported that a number of persons were apprehended ups fined for,gambling at Newton Races on Thursday. On the following day (Friday) when the Great Newton Cup was run for even more gamblers and rogues were taken into custody by the police. A second special court was held at the Police Station, Earlestown, on Friday night, before Col. George McCorquodale. Ten persons, hailing from Man- chester, Liverpool, Leeds, and Wolverhampton were charged with gambling with dice," turn tables," &c., while one was also charged with attempting to Pink the pocket of a female. Fines varying from lOs to 20s and costs were imposed.

---- EartmEsTow.er GOSPEL Mostpw.—The friends and members of the Earlestown Gospel Mission had a very en- joyable Pic-nic to. Helsby, near Frodsham, on Saturday afternoon. They were accompanied as far as Frodsham by a party of friends connected with the Baptist Chapel. Earlestown. The anniversary services in connection with the Gospel Mission were held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle•street, on Sunday. Sermons were preached morning and evening by Mr. A. B. Godden, of Liverpool, and the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn (Wesleyan Minister) preached in the afternoon. There were fairly large attendances. Specially selected hymns were sung on each occasion, Mr. H. J. Dar- man accompanying on the harmonium. The collections were in aid of the school funds. NEWTON RACES AND TICKETLESS TRAVELLERS. —At the Manchester County Police Court, on Monday, Henry Thompson, of Leeds, was charged with endeavouring to de- fraud the London and North-Western Railway Company by travelling with the return half ef an out of date ticket on the 12th instant from Earlestown to Leeds. The pri- soner, who pleaded guilty, was fined 403 and costs or a month's imprisonment.—Three other men were also charged with travelling in the same train without tickets, one of whom had secreted himself under the seat. The men had all been taken into custody at Patricroft, where the trim was stopped and the tickets collected. The three mew were each fined 408 and costs, or in default a month's imprison- ment.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST a JOCKEY AT NEWTON RACES.—The sporting correspondent of a Liverpool con- temporary writes :—" The running at Newton proved com- pletely inexplicable, horses beaten out of sight one day win- ning the next. In one instance, I believe, accusAtions were openly made against a well-known jockey, and it is not im- probable that the matter will be heard of again" Another correspondent says As for the running at Newton, the Jockey Club would be doing a great service were they to order an inquiry into the performances of one or two animals there. That at least one downright robbery was perpetrated almost goes without saying. If the blame cm only be fixed on the right individuals an example ought to be made of them."

A VIOLENT F.naletLE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions 1 on Saturday, Ellen Dean, a married woman, was summoned 1 for using threatening language to Mary Ann Wilson on the I Bth inst. The complainant stated that she lived in Crow- i lane, and on the date nained the defendant used abusive , language to her and threatened to do her injury. She was , bound over to keep thEi peace for six months,—The defen- dant was further summoned for assaulting Mary Simister, at Earlestown, on the Bth inst. 'The complainant deposed that the defendant committed an unprovoked assault upon her, and also smashed her umbrella. She produced her urn- , brella in court, and remarking that "this is it," she. shot it up, with its torn cover and smashed ribs. She held it over her head while speaking to the court, and the chairman ulti- mately observed, " you can put it down, now."—The defen- dant denied the assault,obut the Bench bound her over to keep the peace for a further period of six months, making twelve months in all. . MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE OF A YOUNG WOMAN.— A young woman, residing near the Baptist Chapel, Market- street, E irlestown, disappeared somewhat mysteriously on Sunday night. The young woman or girl (for she was only 17 years of age) has not been possessed of a very bright in- tellect, and that fact gave rise to unpleasant suspicious and fears regarding her welfare. As Usual, she left home for the purpose of attending the evening service in the place of worship mentioned, but as she failed to return home at the accustomed hour fears and alarm were excited among her parents and friends. Inquiries were instituted as to her whereabouts without avail, and until an early hour on the Monday morning the roads in the district were searched. Information was also conveyed to the police offices at Earlestown, Newton, Haydock, &., but nothing further was ascertained until the afternoon of Monday, when a telegram was received from the Warrington police authorities stating that the girl had been discovered walking in the fields be- tween Winwick and Warrington. It is supposed that she had been for a walk on leaving chapel and on getting out- side the town missed her way. KEEPING a DOo wrerrour B.,Lremenn.—At the New- ton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. George Mc- Corquodale, EL Houghton and C. Piikiragton, Daniel Mather, manager and secretary of the Havdock Park Coursing Grounds, was summoned for keeping a dog without a license.--Mr. Hall, of Wigan, supervis)r of excise, prosecu- ted. He stated that he appeared for the Commissianers of Inland Revenue, in support of the summons for keeping A dog without a license, the penalty for which was £5. In December last the officer of Inland Revenue, stationed at Wigan, sent to the defendant a form of declaration in order that he might renew his establishment dog licence. The licence should have been renewed in the month of Januarys but it was not renewed until the following March. In the month of February the officer, finding the dog licence had not been renewed, sent a printed form to the defendant, call- ing•his attention to the fact. On the 13:h of that month the officer visited the defendant's premises and raw a dog for which no licence had been taken out. The licences were not renewed until some days afterwards. The defen- dant said that he was called from home by a telegram on the day he received the notice and he forgot to take out the licence until a few days later. He had had no intention of defrauding the Inland Revenue. Overwork, business at Haydock, and other matters had called him frequently away, and it was carelessness on his part. He had taken out dog licences for 25 years, and he had never had anything of that sort before.—The Chairman : The Bench have considered this case, and, as remarked by one of the magistrates, this is not the case of a poor man or an uneducated man, and if we were to show any preference here we should be acting unfairly to those poor people who come up and through negligence omit to take out their licences. Therefore we must fine you 5s and costs. THE " EARLESTOWN SWEEP" IN COURT. —At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, before Colonel George McCorquodale, Mr. It. Houghton, and Mr. C. Pilkington, another application for an ejectment order in respect to the dwelling-house, 3, Princess-street, Earleetown, occupied by John Carlin, a sweep, was made by Mr. Henry Linden Riley, solicitor, on behalf of James Woods, rent agent, Queen-street, Earlestown. Mr. Riley stated that on the 25th April he made an application against John Carlin, known as the Earleatown sweep, for an order of ejectment from his house, and by consent of the magistrates he was allowed 30 daya within which the warrant could he execu- ted. Too foolishly they bad allowed that 30 days to elapse on promises that he would go, and now when it had expired and they could not issue the warrant he bad put them to the necessity of applying again. He (Mr. Riley) would 1 I therefore have to again go through the formalities of prov- ing the notices, and then their Worships were bound to ' enact the section of Small Tenements Act which enabled ' them to give orders of ejectment within 21 or 30 days , The Chairman : Then it arises from your own negligence or rather I should say your leniency? Mr. Riley : Yes, I sir.—James Woods, of 30. Queen-street, agent for John Wil- son Stelfox, proved having served a notice to quit upon the L defendant on the 30th March last —The Bench made an ' order of ejectment within 30 days.—Mr. Riley was rising I to address the court on an application for , costs when Carlin entered the court-room and addressinz ) the Bench, said he was a tenant under John Wilson Stel- I fox and lied occupied the house 3 Princes street, about 13 , years. He had a wife and six children to keep and was 1 a master sweep by profession. He was a steady man and ' got a honest living and his wife and family were looking ) up to him. He had always paid his rent and kept the ' house door open without anyone helping him and he L had gone on pretty well up to January this year when ?. he had occasion to summon a neighbour named Millward ) for assaulting him. Millward was not fined but was • ordered to pay the costs. On the Monday morning t following, Mr. Woods gave him a notice to leave. He asked him why the notice was given and Mr. Woods replied "why you have had Millward at Newton and . now you must go when there has been this bother." . He had been after a house far and near, and had exhausted ; every effort to secure one up to the present. He had got a promise ot one, but it was not ready yet. The only object . of Mr. Woods in making the applicati-n was "sheer spite." 1 —The Clerk said the magistrates had only one curse to take, and that was make an order.—Mr. Riley again applied for the costs, but the Chairman remarked that it iva,4 , through their negligence, and he did not see that the deEnd- -1 ant should pay.
