div.head: -OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: -OUR LONDON LETTER.
Trees

LONDON, THURSDA.T. The transformation scene so recently and so suddenly accomplished will be completed to-mor- row, should Parliament meet with the Conserva- tives to the right of the Speaker and the Liberals to the left. The curious unanimity of sat- isfaction with which this arrangement has from the first been regarded, continues in unabated force. Conservatives are glad because, at a time when every- thing looked black they have the chance of a taste of the joys of office. The Liberals are pleased be- cause the Government have been delivered from a hopeless impasse, and no particular harm beyond the addition of some permanent charges to the Consoli- dated Fund can accrue from the Conservatives tem- porarily removing to the Treasury Bench. If it were for a more or less indefinite time it would be another thing. If the Conservatives had at their disposal the full range of a session, things would look serious. But they come in for a clearly de- fined period that cannot in any circumstances last beyond five months. The chief business of the session is accomplished. What remains to be done is, with two exceptions, of a formal character. One is the arrangement of the Budget, the other the renewal of the .Coercion Bill. But the Conservatives may be counted upon to deal with these matters in a way that will give them the least possible trouble. As to the Budget they will pass over till next year the deficit arising out of the abandonment of the increased spirit duty, doing this with the greater satisfaction since they know it will then fall to the lot of a Liberal Chan- cellor of the Exchequer to provide the money. As to coercion they will let it slide. They were pre- pared to denounce the Liberal Government if they had not renewed the Coercion Act; but for them- selves they will leave it alone, a course which is perhaps more easy of adoption than moral in principle. The pleasure of the Conservatives on finding themselves safe and dry-footed in office is added to by the experiences they have gone through during the week. None of the new Ministers save one can think without a shudder of what happened on Mon- day night. Lord Salisbury had been home a day from Balmoral, and was still fretting and fuming against the petty tactics which embarrassed him by the official announcement in the Court Circular that he had accepted office. He had not taken, as indeed he could not take, any such step. Pressed by her Majesty to supply the vacancy created by the un- hesitating acceptance of Mr. Gladstone's resigna- tion, Lord Salisbury had undertaken to consult his friends and colleagues on the subject of forming an Administration. The Court newsman, meddling with high politics, sought to close the door against Mr. Gladstone's return by declaring that everything. was settled, whereas, as was shown on Monday mght, everything was in a particularly unsettled state. Lord Randolph Churchill had taken an, early opportunity of communicating his views to Lord Salisbury. First and foremost Sir Stafford North cote must go; secondly, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach must be the figure-head behind which Lord Ran- dolph would lead the party in the House of Com- mons; thirdly, there must be a general clearing out of the old fogies, and the introduction of what Lord Randolph calls "new blood ;" lastly, but this as a matter of course, Randolph and his merry men must all have 6opd places. It is little wonder that Lord Salisbury positively declined to treat on these terms." Lord Randolph received his answer on Mon- day morning and played his trump card on Monday night. 'Mr. Gladstone, in fulfilment of a pledge to Lord Salisbury, proposed, to deal onoMonda ynight with the Lords' amendments to the Seats Bill. Sir S. Northcote approved the arrangement; where- upon Lord Randolph Churchill, interposing, pro- tested, finally dividing the House and carrying with , him Sir M. Hicks-Beach and thirty-four other mote Or less considerable personages. The next morning the white flag was hung out over No. 20, Arlington- street. Lord Salisbury capit'alated, and with some appearance of comprenthe with respect .to Sir Richard Cross, Lord Randolph had all his stipule- ng conceded. If Mr. Gladstone was not in the early part of this week more popular than at any period ofhis life the highest stage was reached upon the announcement that he had declined a. peerage. In Liberal circles, where politics are closely studied, there is more both in the offer and the refusal than meets the eye. It is no secret that Mr. Gladstone is not a persona grata in:Court circles. If he had never done anything else, he overthrew Lord Beaconsfield in 1880. Mr. Glad- stone has himself, with perhaps unconscious irony, described in the House of Commons the alacrity with which his resignation was accepted, and the promp- titude with which steps were taken to fill up his place, lest an outburst of popular feeling should compel him to resume it. Even now he is politically scotched, not killed. He might in November re- appear on the scene like a giant refreshed, sweep aside Lord Salisbury as he did Lord Beaconsfield, and make an indefinite end of Toryism. If he could be got to accept a peerage things would look more hopeful. He would, per- haps insensibly, have loosed his hold upon the affec- tions of the people. A peer, even though his red mantle obscured the familiar form of Mr. Gladstone, could not direct another Midlothian campaign. Per- haps the ease and dignity of the Upper Chamber would cure him of all longing for political warfare. Mr. Gladstone's refusal is held to indicate apprecia- tion of these considerations, and an intention of once more coming to the front and leading the people to a great victory at the polls. When Sir Robert Walpole found Pultency a dangerous adver- sary, he induced the King to make him a peer. "I remember," says Horace Walpole in his Memoirs, "my father's action when he returned from court and told me what he had done. I have turned the key of the closet on him, making the motion with his hand." Mr. Gladstone has declined to have the key of the closet turned on him. However this be, and I merely mention it as the talk in political circles, there remains the great fact that Mr. Glad stone has declined a coronet, and all the millions of commoners throughout England, including the Two Millions just enfranchised, are the prouder and the gladder. hear from a private friend of Prince Krapotkine that his health has seriously suffered from his con- finement at Clairveaux. His prison house was once a Benedictine Monastry, and the site was chosen with less care than was usually bestowed upon this matter by the Nfonks of old. It is in a narrow valley which the sun rarely visits, and through which in winter time pitiless winds sweep. The place is also very damp. The unfortunate prince has suffeted from all kinds of troubles. Ile has had rheumatism, scurvy, and has developed a tendency to dropsy. Amongst minor ills that have befallen him he has lost every tooth in his head since he was incarcerated in this bleak spot. The only sun- shine that has visited him has been the presence of his wife, a young, beautiful, and highly accom- plished girl, who has renounced all the pomps and vanities of this wicked world, and has during her husband's imprisonment been living as close to the walls of his jail as was possible. Krapotkine has many friends in England, amongst his most , intimate being a well-known M.P. for a northern constituency. But I believe that in his letters he has never referred to his own. ailments. Mr. Galers drama "A True Story," first brought out, I believe, at Leicester, has found a suitable home at Drury-lane, and a worthy manager in the Eentleman familiarly known as Augustus Drury o Lanus. plenty of The melodrama is of the good old style, glory and gunpowder, with fights in Seven Dials and battles round beleaguered Paris. For some tastes it is perhaps a little warm for the weather. But that it suits its audience is testified to by repeated applause. To judge by the booksellers' windows, there is a revival just now in the publication of cheap edi- tions. After the rapid fall of the paper-backed " sixpennies," ugly in shape and awkward to carry, which followed very quickly upon their equally rapid rise, there was a temporary hill, as if pub- lishers wished to recover their breath after making so deep a plunge for popularity. Now, like the gentleman in comic opera, they "bob up serenely," and give us cheap books in a better style. They are, learning that the purchasing public is not enamourea of paper covers, and does not particularly admire paper s boards. A neat cloth binding is demanded by hoe who wish to keep their books, and the new and* cheaper issues of Dickens, and Lytton, and Lever are accordingly cloth-bound. In the art season drawing to a close the chief fea- ture has been the sudden and general popularity of etchings. The old line engraving is almost a thing of the past, but etchings of all schools are to be met with in all directions. Whistler's influence is Very visible, an influence both for good and evil, lie has a school of followers, of whom Joseph Penneh is certainly the most notable. In the Etchers' Exhibi- tion, at the Egyptian Hall, Whisilerism, by which I mean the recognition of the artistic fact that the strongest effects and the subtlest effects may be obtained by. a very f,nv lines, is rampant. But it is interesting in this collection to watch the career of mien who, acknowledging no master, are gradually

and tentatively feeling their strength and ascertain- ing their power. I would cite T. C. Farrer's "Pine Trees •' as illustrating this independence of English art. The dark trees in the foreground fill the left side of the flat, and their overhanging branches frame a tract of distance over which the young moon is just beginning to set. No subject could more happily illustrate the strength that can be produced by deep biting, which has been so boldly carried out that the ink seems to bear out from the paper, like the fretted bark of the tree itself. A singular experiment is about to be tried—a great culinary triumph or fiasco. It is not exactly the old question of the vegetarian dinner. It is something much better, and yet meat is to be jea- lously eschewed. The Roman Catholics dine very pleasantly on Fridays. It is a diner maigre which all the same can be made very palateable and very satisfying. Soups, fish, poached eggs, Greek and Italian wines, and then all the vegetable kingdom and superlative coffee—a man might dine worse. Now, this entirely new experiment hopes to supply such a dinner in incomparable style: A great cook, a chef of untarnished reputation, will be engaged and the guests will be fit and not necessarily few. The dinner will be neither cheap nor nasty. Per- haps it may lead to the establishment of a diner maigre for the benefit of Roman Catholicg all through Lent. The scheme is only now being got up; the middle or end of August will be the date. We shall hear plenty about it by-and-bye.

div.head: Xetters to the edttor.
div.p: Xetters to the edttor.

LO ,AL OPTION AND THE NEXT ELECTION. Sir,—There is great rejoicing in the ranks of liquordom at the sudden collapse of the Gladstone Ministry. The members of the " grogocracy " are gleefully boasting of what seems a renewal of their power, which since the advent of the Liberals to office in 1830, had been seriously on the wane. The carrying of the stupid amendment of Sir Michael Beach, that tea, and not intoxicating liquor, should bear the additional taxation necessary to raise the requi- site revenue, and which led to the downfall of the "G.0.M.," gives a colouring of truth to the boast of " Bout- face " that the publican and the brewer are still a political power in the country. The temperance pirty is not likely to under-rate the power of the enemy it has been seeking for the last fifty years to overthrew. The lesson of this mel- ancholy event, to the temperance elector, is that his claims must be urged with greater energy. For there is no dis- guising the fact that it was in deference to the publican and brewing interests in several constituencies that so many members of Parliat.nent were " indisposed " to be in attmdance when their presence was required to keep their party in office. Mr. Herbert Gladstone has told the temperance party they must lift up their voice above that of the liquor party if they are to be heard by say Government. Tne Times has said that the reason the publicans were more successful than the temperance men was they were better at electioneering. The time has therefore arrived when, setting aside every consideration of sect or party, all true citizees should combine with a view to procuring such temperance legislation as shall set at rest, at once and for ever, the vexed question of licensing. Toe leading workers in the cause of temperance legislation are directing their energies more particularly to the pass- ing of an efficient measure of Local Option. The terms of the resolution (which Sir Wilfrid Lawson has three times carried in this Parliament) were taken from one of the recommendations adopted by the Convocation lof the Province of , Canterbury in its Report on In- temperance and its Remedies in 1869, and are as follows 1" That inasmuch as the ancient wed avowed object of licen- sing the sale of intoxicating liquor is to supply a supposed I public want, without detriment to the pubic welfare, this I House is of opinion that a legal power of restraining the I issue or renewal of licenses should be placed in the hands of the persons most deeply interested and affected—namely, the inhabitants themselves—who are•entitled to protection from the injurious consequences of the present system by ',511119 • Cf.4ciT3IEPOLIFO of local option." The eel of thiti resolution is the proPsal to place the power of restraining the issue or renewal of licences in the hands of the inhabitants themselves, in various locaities, not by means of a county board or any other authority. Local Optioniets are tired of those circumlocutary offices where the science of " How not to do it" is carried to per- fection. What can be easier than to allow the vote of a district to be final, without increasing the duties of the proposed county boards? This direct vote is what the supporters of Sir W. Lawson claim, and while they will , accept gladly any scheme that will tend towards the ree. I pressioa of Intemperance they will never cease to agitate uetil this just measure is conceded. A " four line whip " has been sent to the supporters of the cause in Runcorn for the purpose of holding a conference on Lecal Option as it relates to the coming election in the Northwich Division, and to seek to get the candidates to support their views by their votes in Parliament. With not a few, this question is one of "life and death" at the polls. If the Liberal party is wise it will seek to unite the temperance voters with them in a solid vote for Mr. Brunner, for it is not likely that Mr. Verdin will risk the loss of the beer interest by conceding anything to the temperance party. The late defeat of the Liberal party resulted from the abstentions on the part of Liberals ; a few abstentions oa the day of election may wreck the hopes of the Liberal party in the Nortbwich Division in November next.—Yours, &c., Runcorn, June 18th, 1885. ANTI-PUB.

GORDON VERSUS BRADLAUGH. Sir,—Shakespeare, in one of his most imaginative moods, makes that lively sprite, Puck, boast that he could "put a girdle round about the earth in forty minutes." 'lhat was a very notable feat even for a "lob of spirit," but your correspondent, Captain Cuttle," almost equals it in his way. He does not put a girdle round about the globe in forty minutes, but he deals in a way satisfactory to himself with almost every subject, religious and secular, that the human mind can cope with in the space of a letter that can los read in less than half forty minutes. The dangers of hero-worship, the wickedness of jingoism, the chastity of Mr. Bradlaugh, the delinquencies of the clergy, the virtues of the Radical party, peace at any price, the new constitu- e,,cies, and the composition of Parliament, are some of the subjects he descints upon, and when he stops he, like another Alexander. appears only to stop for the want of new conquests to make. Now I should like to know what all this has to do with the clear issue, "Gordon teNUS Bradlaugh." "Captain Cuttle," I hope, does net think that In subscribing " Defender" as my signature I was taking a brief as a sort of Defender-General of the shortcomings of humanity and human institutions ,all the world over. All I Intended to do was to attempt ta expose the hollowness of charges made by a professional lecturer who found it con- venient in the way of business to malign a noble character. These charges, as I pointed out, were in eftect that Gordon was mercenary and inhumane. "Captain Cattle " says Mr. Bradlaugh held in his band chapter and verse for all he said, but that is impossible. It is upon record that Gordon left China as poor as he entered it, that he refused large sums of money for his services in the Soudan, and that when living at 'Gravesend he often possessed less coin of the realm than the beggar who asked him for alms, and this although be might, had he so minded, been as wealthy as ens of the old Anglo-Indian cabobs. How can a charge of mercen- ariness be supported by either Mr. Bradldugh or anybody else In face of facts like these? And then with regard to the charge of inhumanity, how is that to be driven home again a man whose very name calls up the idea of practical devoted philanthropy? "Captain Cottle" does nothing to prove the truth of Mr. Bradlauch's assertions; he merely repeats some of them in a vaguer and more intangible form, whilst discretly ignoring others. He seems to feel the necessity of chan4iog his points of attack, because instead of pursuing the old charges he begins to, make new ones. Gordon, we are now told, always took the side of "might against rigkt." Vell, all that can be said about that is that it is a matter of opinion, and that "Cap- tain Cutt'e " and a few others are on one side and the rest of the world on the other. Gordon is denounced for permitting slavery in the Soudan," Captain Cottle" being 110 hard pressed for material with which to blacken the re- . natation of a fellow man that it is made a matter of re- proach he did not do the Impossible. Gordoo never at- tempted the abolition of slavery, for, as he said, when you have got the ink which has soaked into blotting- paper out of it then slavery will cease in these lands." His aim was the suppression of slave-raiding and the closing of slave markets. The dire .difficulties which "Captain Cottle" meets with in trying to give even the semblance of reality to the grave charges he would like to prove is strikingly manifested when he falls back upon the old platitudes about Gordon's demand that nbehr Pasha might be sent to the Soudan. I should have thought so experienced a contro- versialist would have studiously avoided any mention of an incident in relation to which events have so signally justi- fied the prescience of General Gordon. Gordon, having ar- rived at Khartoum, at once grasped the situation, and found that, as the Mandi was not to be " smashed" by English • or Turkish troops, Le had but a choice of evils. By the appointment of Zebehr the Mandi's power for ' mischief might be counteracted or destroyed, and the country saved ' from chaotic disorder ; without that appointment there was likely to be nothin./ but confusion and anarchy, and a pos- sible invasion of Egypt. To appoint Z.behr or to leave the country in the bands of an aggressive fanatic was Gordon's choice of evils ; he chose the lesser, and "Captain Cattle," who looks at the actions of a man whom other men delight to honour with a " jaundlced eye," blames him for not choosing the greater. Had Zebehr been appointed as Gordon wished, the slave trade would probably have been tolerated but comparative order might have been main- t tined in the Soudan ; now we have the slave trade with the horrors of civil war super-added. and in addition to all there hangs over Egypt, like a Damocles' sword, the con- tinual threat of an invasion, the det astating nature of which would recall t.c.e days of Genghis Khan and Tamerlane. Before closing this already too-long letter, I should juet like to allude to the passage in my last letter which has made "Captain Cattle " use unparliam,ntary language. The reference to free-love doctrines, of which Mr. Brad- laugh is said to be enamomed, was only the expression of j an opinion which is current among many people who have not vet agreed to the apotheesis of that gentleman. For I my own part I have never pri d into or felt any curiosity about Mr. Bradlaugh's private life. He may live the life of an anchorite for anything I know ; and, indeed, may be a modern Simeon Stylites with moral fibre so much tougher 1 than that of his ancient prototype that he does not find it

necessary to get on the top of a pillar to be out Of tempta- tion's way. All I will say is that, judging Mr. Bradlaugh as we judge other men, the popular opinion referred to has more plausibility than many popular opinions. DEFENDER.

TORIES AND "THE TRADE." Sir,—Nothing tests the value of a man's patriotism so much as asking him to pay his quota of the expense. The publican has been weighed in the balance, and is found wanting. No doubt Whatever can exist in the mind of any- one, that as a class publicans are entirely given over to one great object in life, that of money making. Whoever or whatever sinks or swims, "the trade" must be supported in its dastardly attempts to over-ride all national and patriotic

requirements. These remarks are forced from me in consequence of the recent action taken by publicans is their crusade against Mr. Childers' proposed method of raising the £11,000,000, so unanimously voted by the House of Commons. No sooner did the Chancellor of the Exchequer touch the fringe of this huge social wen, but at once a wild cry rent the air, against all taxation that touched the vested interests of "the trade." As a combination devoid of all political, principle, and exis:ing for the sole purpose of thwarting all , legislation that tends towards keeping the people abreast of the spirit of the age, it at once called all its forces to the front, and, after such deliberation as it was capable of, de- cided that not upon the war-loving and patriotic publican should fall the burden of increased taxation, but upon his patrons should the tax be levied. 'Having 2e per gallon to pay on spirits, they at once charged at the rate of 58 71-d per gallon, to make themselves safe ; and to guard against all possibility of less they, in the most patriotic fashion, decided to take this course, before even the Budget becomes law. Immediately following this most laudable sten, a system of agitation is planned and attempted to be carried out, but here the publican reckoned without his master. The work- ing men refused at every meeting to be quelled• by the mercenaries of "the trade,' and in spite of free taps drove 1" vested interests" out of the field ; this happened several , times in London, and it may be taken as an indication of the mind and spirit of the whole people. Writing as a moderator, determined to have a glass of beer. I am yet determined 80 far as in me lies to keep the publican in his place, and to frustrate his knavish political tricks. Vending, as he does, an article that adds nothing to the wealth of the country, but in consequence of its lia- bility to abuse, rather tends towards pauperising the people, the publican must understand that he, like his beer and spirits, must be kept under the strictest surveillance the people's representatives can possibly devise. 'lime was when Radicals charged that an unholy alliance , existed between Beer and Bible; this charge can no longer Ibe maintained. The Church in its wisdom sees the neces- sity for at once disassociating itself from so pernicious an alliance, and through its leading organ rates the Conserva- tives roundly for being led away by the wild cry of taxing the poor man's beer. The London Guardian says it was "A fair and reasonable way of raising the money, and the bill to give effect to it ought not to have been rejected for no better reason than because other t ixes on consumption might have been preferable to those actually chosen." The Church of England Temperance Society has through its committee passed the following resolution :—"'ibis com- mittee desires to express its regret that in dealing with a purely fiscal measure misconceptions appear to have arisen in the House of Commone, evidenced in the discussion last night, as to the relation of temperance reformers to politi- cal parties. This committee, representing allpartiss. recog- j Rises the fact that the proposed increase of taxation en spirits and beer has excited opposition, partly because no increase has been proposed in the wine duties, partly he- cause of the mistaken assumption that alcoholic drinks are at present taxed at higher rates than non-alcoholic; while the revenue returns show that the average price of tea in band is about is per lb., from which a duty of 6d is exacted —i.e., an ad valorem rating 50 per cent.; whereas on beer, worth as it comes from the brewer from 10d to is per gal- lon, the rating is only 20 per cent.; and this committee deprecates any action which is likely to turn an economic proposal hat° a political party question." Leaving the publicans to "stew in their own juice," we may well ask what is to los the result of the action of weak•kneed Liberals and publicans' selfishness ? What are We to expect from Tory rule? Such portion of their pro- gramme as we already know is of so startling a character that if once put in operation I fancy the Tory working- man will at once vanish. Fancy, Sir M. H. Beach taxing the greatest luxury the working-man and his wife has, tea! Imagine the great benefits commerce and the people have derived from cheap sugar, and the Tories being allowed to harrass their business ; Lowther allowed to tax bread ; and Chaplin to vent his spleen on imported beef, and all for what ? Why, to pay for a spirited foreign policy, against which Radicals have all along protested, and in support of which Tories to a man voted. Mr. Gladstone, in his speech on Monday June Bth, exposed ths real reason of Tory op- position to the Budget. and Mr. Chaplin has with great candour since avowed it. Mr. Gladstone said, "The death duties in reality constitute the ground and basis of these proceedings. The death duties invade the sanctuary of landed property." This then is the secret of the Thy op- position to the Budget, and it behoves working-men to make themselves thoroughly acquainted with the meaning of the term "death duties." Doing this they will find it but an honest attempt to make the heir to landed estate pay in taxes to the State, a similar sum comparatively to what the poor nal pays on inheriting a small sum of money. Who- ever the working-man may be, that cheers Sir M. 11. Beach on his successful piece of selfishness, that man must like Dogberry be written down "an ass." No doubt the Tories hope that the general run of English- men are not as yet much iaaproved, or much more enligh- tened in politics than they were years ago. Hoping this, they will look forward to gaining the Treasury Benches, where they will have full opportunity for bringing forward some of their pet projects. Tea that is taxed 50 per cent. must have another 25 per cent. added to it. Beer that is only taxed 20 per cent, raust remain al it istout of deference' to the powerful influence wielded by the owners of bung I and tap. We must have at once an inquiry into the pre- sent depressed state of trade; a costly commission must be appointed, and no doubt we shall have the report as soon as trade revives, say, sometime at the beginning of next cen- tury. Our relations with the Continental despots must be made of a more friendly character, and by imitating the German Chancellor. our rulers must give us new lessons in Imperialism. Afghanistan must be conquered, Russia must be compared to a bankrupt swindler, or else an abject apol- ogy given, and to wind up all, the famous Beaconsfield manifesto should be publicly burnt as a tribute to the peaceful and happy state of Ireland. June 15th, 1885.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JUNE 20. 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JUNE 20. 1885.
LA TEST NEWS.
The latest news from Cairo is that Kassala is still holding out. _ _ .
, A Central New@ telegram states that Ragheb Pacba, who *as premier at the time of the bombardment of Alexandria, is dead. . .
A telegram from Durban conveys the unwelcome intelli- gence that the Zulus are hunting the missionaries out of Zululand. .

On Friday 450 navvies arrived at Woolwich on board the transport Twerton from the Sondan. Thirty deaths oc- curred during their two weeks' stay at Suakim. Information just received in Liverpool from Ligos, West Coast of Africa, reports that a fire occurred there in the native quarter of the town. Over a hundred native houses were consumed. _

Afire occurred on Friday morning at the residence of Mr. Goddard, pianoforte maker, Gloucester. The inmates had a narrow escape, Mr. Goddard, two young ladies, and the servant being badly injured. About one o'clock on Thursday morning North-western Argyleshire was visited by an earthquak., the shock of which was distinctly felt at Ballachullish, and in many houses in the slate quarry district of Glencoe.

div.head: SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL BILL.
At the meeting of the Select Committee of the House of Commons on Friday, evidence was given on the advantages of the canal to the cotton trade.—The Chairman, address-

lug the counsel for the promoters, said the commercial evi- dence might be divided into two branches; first, that as to the saving that was alleged to be made by the canal; and, secondly, the advtatages to the trade of the saving. In a matter of this tremendous importance the committee could not take upon themselves to say that they would not hear the evidence, but after the evidence given and the agree- I ment of all parties that a saving in transit of Gs per ton meant an additional one per cent interest upon the capital of the cotton trade, the committee desired to submit to the promoters whether it would be worth while to give any further evidence to prove the advantage of such a saving or a corresponding saving in other trades by the canal, and whether they would not be securing the interests of their clients if they limited the future commercial evidence to such additional evidence, that there would be this saving as they might think necessary.—Mr. Pope interposing, ob- served that there might be this saving of one per cent over a limited area served by the canal, but it would not amount to one per cent on the whole of the capital of the cotton trade.—Mr. Pember intimated that he would endeavour to conform with the suggestion of the committee as far as he • thought consistent with the interests of his clients. On Friday afternoon the .weekly meeting of the Provi- . . .

sional Committee was held in the -Board room 704 Market- street, Manchester, Mr. Alderman Husband (in the absence of the chairman, Mr. Adamson, in London) pre- siding. Reports as to the progress of the inquiry before the Select Committee of the House of Com- mons were submitted from which it appeared that a large number of witnesses had now been examined, and that the Committee had repeatedly suggested tbat the evidence 80 far as regards the commercial part of the case should be abridged. It was felt that everything should be. done to save unneces- sary expense on both sides, consistently with a fair and prop.r presentation of the case, and no doubt an effort will be made to reach that portion of the evidence relating to the estuary of the Mersey as speedily as practicable. A resolu- tion was submitted passed by the Manchester and Salford I Butchers' Guardian Association in support of the bill.

div.head: ANOTHER RUSSO-AFGHAN DIFFICULTY.
div.p: ANOTHER RUSSO-AFGHAN DIFFICULTY.

ST. PETERSBURG. FRIDAY.—The Novosti publishes intel- ligence stating that Abdurrahman has concentrated nearly all his troops in Afghan Turkestan under his own personal command. The journal adds that the men forming one of the detachments of the Afghan force are armed with 3,000 breech-loaders lately presented to the Ameer by the Indian Government. They are also using the latter's gift of 15 field guns. The Novosti expresses the opinion that this de- tachment threatens the communications between sevetal of the advanced Russian outposts in the Trans-Caspian terri- tory, and would constitute a dange r.

div.head: PENDLEBURY COLLIERY EXPLOSION.
div.p: THE PENDLEBURY COLLIERY EXPLOSION.
APPALLING LOSS OF LIFE.

PIT Beam, FRIDAY, 11.45.—The work of exploration at Clifton Hall Colliery has been going on uninterruptedly all morning. About two o'clock Mr. Barker, manager of the Pendleton Colliery, and Mr. John Crook, manager of the Agecroft pit, went down, each accompanied by a party. Mr. Barker took the No. 1 west side district, and Mr. Crook the No. 1 east side. Both gentlemen returned to the surface about 5-20. Mr. Barker reported that he had been to the far end of the Jig Brow, where he found two dead bodies. One of these he brought up with him, and it was subse- quently identified as that of a man named James Williams. Mr. Crook's report was to the effect that he bad seen 17 dead bodies in the No. 1 east side, and two others at the top of the lower side place. Since then explorers have been steadily engaged in both districts. Something like an approximation can now be obtained of the full extent of the disaster, so far, at least, as hu- man life is concerned. Since the explorations com- menced on Thursday morning 48 dead bodies have been brought to the bank. ( This number includes those found at Agecroft). In addition to the 48 found killed, four others subsequently died from their injuries, making a total of 52. There are believed to be still 86 bodies in the workings, so that the gross total of killed is 138. The 26 dead brought up between ten o'clock last night and the present time have not all been identified yet. So unique is a disaster of this description in the district that some defects as regards general organisation might be looked for and ex- cused. It is satisfactory to be able to state, however, that not a single hitch has occurred, and the arrangements made have been perfect of their kind. Inspectors Burke and Kelly, in charge of the county police contingent, deserve credit for the order which has been maintained. LATEST DETAILS.—MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN.

PENDLEBURY. 4-30 P.M.—Up till the present time be- tween 60 and 70 bodies have been brought to the surface. It is thought that about a hundred have still to be got out. Some twelve or fourteen of them have been found, and will be brought up immediately. The remainder cannot be reached at present, being embedded in the debris. No doubt is now entertained that all the men still below are dead. The work of exploration will be stopped at six o'clock on account of the water that is flowing down the Up-Cast shaft. It is thought desirable to ascertain the pre- cise nature of the flooding, in order that, if it be found possible, fires may be lit and the ventilation thoroughly restored. This forenoon the following telegram from Mr. Ellis Lever, of Bowdon' Cheshire, was received by the Rev. Dr. Dawes, rector of St. Augustine's Church, Pendlebary Sir Henry Ponsonby telegraphed to me from Windsor Castle last night, expressing deep regret, and he is asking for full particulars of disaster through Home Office." A further telegram from the Queen is expected this after- noon. _ _

The following telegrams have passed between the Lord Mayor of London and the Mayor of Manchester :—" From the Lord Mayor of London to the Mayor of Manchester— Grieved to hear of the sad colliery accident. Shall be very hd ppy to open a relief fund if necessary. Wire latest par- ticulars." From the Mayor of Manchester to the Lord Mayor of London—Thanks for your telegram. I have just returned from the scene of the explosion. Upwards of 160 are known to be dead. Some of those taken out alive have died thia morning. Your Lordship's assistance will be highly valued."

THE INQUEST. On Friday morning Mr. F. Price, district coroner, was officially in-formed of the terrible calamity which, has oc- curred at Messrs. A. Knowles and Sons pits at Clifton Hall, Pendlebury, and has decided to formally open the inquest on the bodies of the victims at the Mechanic's Institution, at ten o'clocs on Saturday.
THE POLITICAL CRISIS.
THE FORMATION OF THE NEW MINISTRY.

The Standard save :—We are enabled to make an announcement which will be received with general satisfac- tion. Sir Stafford Northcote will not, as was anticipated, become Lard President of the Council, but will be First Lord of the Treasury. The arrangement, however, for which there Is a precedeht, still leaves the Premiership in the hands of Lord Salisbury. In addition to the list of ap- pointments we announced on Thursday, we understand that Mr. A. J. Balfour will be the President of the Local Go- vernment Board, but without a seat in the Cabinet; and that Mr. Stanhope will become Vice-President of the Coun- cil. The Chief Secretaryship for Ireland has not yet been filled up. So far the following appointments may be re- garded as settled:—

- Prime Minister and Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Marquis of Salisbury. Lord Chancellor, Sir Hardinire G,ffard. First Lord of Treasury, Sir Stafford Northcote, who will be raised to the Peerage.
Chancellor of the Exchequer and Leader of the House of Commons, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach. Secretary of State for the Home Department, Sir R. Assheton Cross.
Secretary of State for the Colonial Department, Colonel Frederick A . Stanley.
Secretary of State for the War Department, Mr. W. H, Smith.
Secretary of State for India, Lord Randolph Churchill. First Lord of the Admiralty, Lord George Hamilton.
Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland-, the Earl of Carnarvon. Postmaster-General, Lord John Manners.
Attorney-General, Ir. Edward Clarke, Q.C. Solicitor-Gt.neral, Mr. Gorst, Q.C. Lord Chaucellor of Ireland, Mr. E. Gibson, Q.C.
P.esident of the Local Government Board, Mr. Arthur Balfour.

Attorney-General for Ireland, Mr. Hugh Hulmes, Q.C. Solicitor-General for Ireland, Mr. John Monroe, QC. Vice-President of the Council, Mr. E. Stanhope. It is understood that places in the Cabinet will be found for the Duke of Richmond, and Viscount Cranbroek. Amongst the rumours current was that Lord Lytton and Sir Henry Drummond Wolff will be appointed to important embassies. The name of Mr. Webster, Q.C., was also men- tioned in connection with one of the law nffices of the Crown. We believe, however, that in none of these matters has any definite arrangement been arrived at. The rumour that Mr D. Plunket had been offered the Under-Secretary- ship of Foreign Affairs is without foundation. LORD SALISBURY'S DIFFICULTIES.
The ni-e-mbele-oiiii:-Ciladsto-n-eilitniiiii-r-allon met in

Downing-street on Thursilay,afternoon, and at the close ef their deliberations Mr. Gladstone proceeded to Windsor. It was asserted in some of the clubs on Thursday night that this meeting and subsequent visit to the Queen were in con- nection with the efforts of Lord Salisbury to obtain from the retiring Government a more comprehensive promise of as- sistance than they are prepared to concede. It is under. toed that the TAberal statesmen:were unable to give to the Conservative leaders more than a general assurance that so far is their influence ette ded they would not encourage any obstruction or factious opposition to their successors in carrying on the necessary business of the remainder of the session. On Thursday the Conservative leaders held a short formal mewing at Lord Salisbury's residence in Arlington- street, after which Sir S. Northcote proceeded to Windsor to have an audience of Her Majesty. The right hon. gentle- man reached the Castle a quarter of an hour after Mr. Glad- stone had left. On Thursday night it was known that the Queen had conferred the dignity of an earldom upon Sir Stafford, and that he had selected the tktle of Earl of Iddes- leigh and Viscount St. Cyres. The Central News, telegraphing last night, says the political excitement has been greater than at any time dur- ing the past week. Enquiries made early in the day in in spired quarters left no doubt that something in the nature of a hitch had occurred, but the Central News is enab'ed to state that in the highest Conservative quarters there is still a confident belief that Lord Salisbury will succeed not only in forming a Cabinet—a work which has been already prac- tically completed—but in obtaining such assurances from the members of Mr. Gladstone's Cabinet as will enable the , Conservative Ministry to carry on the Queen's Government until it be possible to obtain the opinion of the new constituencies upon the real points at issue between the two parties. The Central News is informed upon reliable authority that no negotia- tions properly, so called, have taken place between the party leaders, but Lord Salisbury, with thrlaoproval of his political friends, suggested the desirability of endeavouring to come to an understanding with the Liberal leaders in re- gard to the transaction of such business and the enactment of such measures as may be fairly uonsider.d to be indis- pensably necessary for the winding up of the expiring ses- sion. Lord Salisbury resumed his consultations with the

leaders of the Conservative party yesterday morning from half-past eleven to half-past twelve. His most important visitor during the afternoon was undoubtedly the Duke of Northumberland, whose unexpected visit to his old col-

league caused the greatest excitement at the political clubs, as his grace from the very first strongly opposed the policy of taking office in the present peculiar circumstances. . Considerable sensation has been caused by the action of

the Conservative peers in once more postponing the consi- deration of the Redistribution 8,11, as it is thought, not- withstanding Lord Salisbury's disclaimer, to indicate an intention to take a general election on the existing register. Lord Randolph Churchill and Sir Henry Drummond Wolff attended Ascot Races yesterday. As they proceeded by way of Windsor, it was at once rumoured that they had been summoned by her Majesty in connection with the Ministerial crisis. Both gentlemen, however, drove straight from the railway station to Ascot.

LAST NIGI-IT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at fear o'clock. ANOTIIER ADJOURNMENT.— Ile Marquis of SALISBURY asked Earl Granville to consent to a further adjournment until Tuesday, on the ground that the comtnunications which bad been going on had not yet reached a condition to enable either side of the House to make a statement. He was quite aware of the importance of getting the Redistri- bution Bill passed to enable local authorities to make the necessary arrangements for registration, but a serious con- stitutional question had arisen. It appeared that the Re- distribution Bill, when passed, absolutely took away, from now till November next, the power of dissolution. Earl Granville, not consenting to the proposal, Lord Salisbury, on the motion to consider the Commons' reasons for dis- agreeing to some of the Lords' amendments, moved the ad- journment of their consideration until Tuesday, because the bill as it stool deprived the Sovereign of the power of dissolution, which should not happen unless responsible Government were in power.—Earl KIMBERLEY could not understand the motive of the adjoarnment, unless it was In contemplation to dissolve Parliament before the new register was completed.—The Marquis of SALISBURY had no such intention; he only asked for an adjournment of four days.—On a division the adjeurnment was carried by 124 to 56. The Princess Beatrice's Annuity Bill was read a third time and passed, and the House adjourned until Tuesday. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. There was a very full attendance on both sides of the House at prayers The Lord Advocate and Mr. G. Russell were the only occupants of, the Government bench, • that of the Opposition being untenanted. Sir M. H. Beach and Sir W. Hart Dyke were the first to take their seats on the Opposition bench, and they were followed by Lord G. Hamilton and Sir D. R. Cross. Sir Stafford Northcote arrived shortly before half-past four, and was received with loud cheers. Then members began to crowd into the House. The Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir W. Harcourt, and Sir C. Dilke were amongst the first arrivals on the Govern- ment buch. TORY. OPPOSITION TO BUSSIA.—At half-past four, Mr. Gladstone arrived, and was received with loud cheers.—Mr. LABOUCHERE gave notice that on an early day he should ask, whoever might be leader of the House, whether any communication had been received from the Russian Gov-rn- rnent as to the public statements made by the member for Woodstock and Lord Salisbury, and, if no communication had been made, whether any apology would be made to the Russian Government for the said statements. TEE BRADLAUGH QUESTION.—The SPEAKER informed the House that he had received a letter from Mr. Bradlaugh recalling his promise not to attempt to take his seat in that House.—The letter was read by the clerk at the table.—Sir S. NORTRCOTE asked Mr. Glads Lone what course he intended to adopt regarding the letter.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply, said no case had yet occurred for his submitting a motion on the letter. THE POLITICAL CRISIS.—THE TORIES IN A FIX. Mr. GLADSTONE said he had received an intimation from Lord Salisbury, and he intended to move that the House adjourn until Tuesday, He (Mr. Gladstone) therefore moved that this House at its rising adjourn until Tuesday. LABOUCHERE asked if any communications had taken place between Mr. Gladstone and Lord Salisbury as to certain assurances. A great many members on that side objected to assurances being given. There would be no fac- tious opposition, and good measures would receive cordial support (Cheers and laughter.) He wanted to know if these adjournments were to be kept ue until Lord Salis- bury got the assurances he required.—Mr. GLADSTONE said he had said on the last occasion that no assurances had been given, but Mr. Llbouchere had given assurances himself. (Laughter.)—He had, however, now to state that communications had taken place between himself and Lord Salisbury, but he could assure the House that the result of those communi- cations, whatever it might be, would be made publit pro- perty. There would be no secrecy whitever. Lord Salis- bury fully joined in that being so. Under such circum- stances the House might rest assured that whatever took place regarding or resulting from those communications would be made absolutely public. (Loud cheering.)—The motion for adjournment was agreed to, and the House rose at five o'clock.

The French Government has decided to send reinforce- ments to the extent of a battalion of infantry to Mada- gascar. The Marriage of Princess Beatrice to Prince Henry of Battenberg has been definitely fixed to take place on the 24th July. AGRICULTURAL SHOW .kT BIRRENHEAD.—The annual show at the Wirral and Birkenhead Society was opened at Birkenhead on Wednesday. It has long held the dignified position of a three-days' show, and the premiums it offers are handsome enough to attract the best stock within a wide radius. Its particular district, of course, is the peninsula of Wirral, one side of wbich is washed by the busy waters of the Mersey. The show this year is smaller than usual. Last year the entries were 1493, and the present list is about 150 shrift of that number. The authorities say the falling off is due to the fact Oa it a large number of shows are being held about the same time. In the cattle classes the principal places were taken by Mr. George Cooke, Clayley Hall, CheAer, and Mr. John Bewley, Stanney, Chester. Other first prizes for cattie fell to Mr. Bewley. The whole class for dairy COWS Wail COollnended by the judges. As a whole the young bulls were inferior in quality to the animals in the older classes. In dealing with the horses the judges seemed to have no great trouble. Among the stallions the Eatl of Chester, belobging to Mr. J. Per. tin, Birkenhead, was put first. ' There was a fairly good , turnout of sheep. Leicester! and Bbrop.shires were the breeds shown. In dogs the show was rather richer than usual. This was no doubt attributable to the fact that this year for the first time the show is conducted under the Ken- nel Club rules. There was,*howeyer, no lack of the useful implements of all sorts, from a potato washer and peeler to traction engine. The members of the society lunched to- gether. with Mr. Macgregor Laird in the chair. Among those present were Lord t ombermere. Captain Cotton (Con- servative candidate for Wirral), Mr. James TOmkinSOn ( Liberal candidate for Wirral), Mr. W. Laird, and others. There was a large attendance at the show in the course of the afternoon. On Thursday _there was a larger attendence of visitors than on the second day of the show for a number of years past. It is also satisfactory to learn that the num- ber of persons who passed through tt e stiles on Wednesday &needed that of recent years on the first day. The pro- gramme on Thursday comprised a grand parade of prize horses at noon, within the space set apart for the leaping competition. The various animals were much admired, the roadsters and hunters especially being considered the best I classes of the kind ever shown in the yard.

JOSPK MAZZINI, a memoir by E. A. V., with two essays by Mazzini : (1) "Thoughts on Democracy;" (2) " The duties of man." No pecuniary profit is desired from this publication; but it is hoped that this eloquent memorial of a noblepatriot and a good man may awaken a true patriotic enthusiasm in the hearts of many young English readers.; and that the principles set forth may help to the forma- tion of wise and just political opinions. People's edition, with portrait, price 6d. To be obtained from Jour S. GREEN, bookseller, &c., 34, Bridge- street, Warrington.—Advt.

WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS. This annual festival, which commenced on Friday even- ing, was concluded en Saturday afternoon last. The, weather was again magnificient, and this circumstance, added to the faet that L. E. Myers, of the Manhattan (U.S.) Athletic Club; J. M. Cowie, of the London A.G. ; and W. Snook, of the Moseley Harriers, were present to compete in several events, brought people from all parts of the North of Eng- land. The railway companies ran special trains from Man- chester, Liverpool, Warrington, &c., and at least 7,000 spec- tators lined the enclosure, whilst the grand stand was well patronised by ladies and gentlemen of the neighbourhood. In witnessing the performance of the famous American athlete the Widnesians had a treat that has not bken equalled at any sports this season, and when for the third time he came in the winner, having defeated 22 opponents, with various long starts, in the hilf.mile handicap, they showed their appreciation by vociferously cheering him. His long easy stride and graceful style were much admired. J. M. Cowie won the scratch 100 yards very easily, but in the 120 yards handicap he had to accept a defeat in the fine) after winning his heat in grand style. Snook was scarcely up to his usual form, but he made short work of his oppo- nents in the one mile scratch race, but in the two miles' handicap he retired after he had atcomplished about half the distance. A very enjoyable contest was the three miles' bicycle race, which became a struggle between J. Clarke, of Ditton, and T. H. Pickering, of Sefton, and in an exciting finish Clarke managed to secure the verdict by about three yards. The performances of about 20 members of the Liverpool Gymnasium, und or the direction of Mr. Alexander, was a pleasant feature in the afternoon's programme. De- tails :

div.head: CLIFFORD DIX.
div.p: CLIFFORD DIX.
THE ESTATE OF THE LATE RICHARD
HARRISON, OF WARRINGTCN.
HORNER V. THE QUEEN.

This matter was before the Lord Chancellor, Lord Black- burn, and Lard Fitzgerald, in the House of Lords on Mon- day. It is an appeal from an order of the Court of Appeal whereby it was declared that the wife of Mr. Stagg. M.P. (Catherine Parker) bed proved that John Harrison No. 2 (the husband of Elizabeth Walmsley) was the legitimate son Of John Harrison No. 1, by Anne, his wife, formerly Anne Harrison, widow of John Harrison, and previously Anne Proctor. The case has reference to the estate of the late Richard Harrison, of Warrington, who died intestate in September, 1863, possessed of considerable real personal estate. This case has reference only to the possession of the real estate, and the point in dispute is ae to the mater- nity of John Harrison, an ancestor of the intestate, the simple point being whether he was the son of John Harri- son, formerly of Lea, near Preston, by his first wife, or by his second wife, Anne Harrison, formerly Anne Proctor. The parties to the dispute are Henry Horner, Blackburn, who claims from a sister of the grandmother of the intes- tate, and Mrs. Slagg. the wife of Mr. Slagg, M.P. for Man- chester. Mrs. Slagg claims through one of the three daughters of Anne Harrison by her first marriage, and the question is whether those three daughters were the half I sisters of John Harrison, the intestate's ancestor. At the time Richard Harrison died, in 1863, various claimants came forward to claim the property, but none of them could then establish s title, and since that time various persons have been trying to make good their title to the estates. In 1869 the Crown issued a commission of escheat, when it was found that the intestate died without any known I heir, and thereupon the Crown took Possession of the estate and have remained in possession ever since. The appel- lant, Mr. Horner, presented a petition to the Master of the ' Rolls, alleging that he was the heir-at-law of Richard Har- rison, and the Master of the Rolls' chief clerk so certified, but the Court of Appeal reversed the order, they holding in favour of Mrs. Slagg's contention that John Harrison was the legitimate son of the John Harrison by his marriage with Anne Harrison. foemerly Proctor.—Mr. Horace Davey, Q C., who opened the case for the appellant, s iid unless Mrs. Slagg could show that John Harrison, who married Elizabeth Walmsley, and was an ancestor of the intestate, was connected through his mother with j Elizabeth Harrison, she would fail altogether. If ! the John Harrison who married Elizabeth Walms- ley was merely a son of Ann Prector's second husband, then of course there was no relationship between Ann Proctor's children by her first husband and her ! son. His submission was that not only had Mrs. Stagg failed to prove that the John Harrison who married Eliza- beth Walmaley was the son of Ann Proctor, but that they I had got the most potent evidence that he was not. The Master. of the Rolls was of that opinion, and he dismissed ! Mrs. Stagg's claim.—The learned gentleman had not con- cluded when their lodships adjourned.

I ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE IN LIYERPOOL.—On Monday, Patrick Ward, 70 yeaas of age, living in Caton- street. Liverpool, attempted to murder his wife, aged 70, and then cut his own throat. Ward lives With his wife and two ' grown•up sons, and early in the morning the sons were aronsed by cries of murder proceeding from their parents' num. On going there they found theit mother bleeding from wounds on the.head and hands, and their father stand- ing with a pocket knife covered blood in his right hand. Having dressed their mother's wounds as well as they could, they went for a doctor. In the meantime' Ward had gone downstairs and cut his throat in a terrible manner. Ward was removed to the hospital, where be remains in a critical condition. Ward had been drinking for sone thus past.

TEMPORARILY MISLAID. "Now, my dear," said Mr. Spoopendyke, cheerfully, "be lively. It's twenty minutes past ten, and we mustn't be late at church. Most ready ?' "Yes, dear," beamed Mrs. Spoopendyke, "I'm all ready. Got everything ?" "I think so. Hymn-book, umbrella, and—where's the prayer-book? I have not got the prayer-book." " Where did you leave it?" asked Mrs. Spoopendyke, turn- ing over the volumes on the table hurriedly. ' If I knew where I left it, I'd strut right to that spot and get it," retorted Mr. Spoopendyke. " I left it with you. Where did you put it? Can't you remember what you do with things?" " I haven't seen it since last Sunday," returned Mrs. Spoopendyke, faintly. "I know," she continued, "perhaps it is at chnrch." " Perhaps it is." mimicked Mr. Spoopendyke," " perhaps it got up early, took a bath, and went ahead of us. Did you ever see a prayer-book prowl off to church all alone? Ever see a prayer-book h'st up it's skirts and strike out for the sancruary without an escort? S'pose a prayer-book knows the difference between a church and a ham sandwich? Where did you put it ?" "I mean, yen may have left it in the pew-rack. You know you did once," suggested Mrs. Spoopendyke.', "I didn't do anything of the sort. I brought it horns and gave it to you. Where do you keep it? What did YOu do with it? S'pose I'm going to awash aeon ad that service without knowing whether they are doing the Apostle's Creed or an Act of Congress? Spring around and find it, can't you? What are you looking for? Don't you know the difference between a prayer-book and the Wandering Jew? Find it, can't you ?" "Never mind it, dear," fluttered Mrs. Spoopendyke, " I know all the responaes and I'll help you along.' "Oh, yes, you know 'em all. What you don't know about religion wouldn't wad a gun. All you want is a bell and a board fence to be a theological seminary. Think you can find that prayer-book between nolor and the equinoctial ? " howled Mr. Spoopendyke. "Got any idea whether you sold the measly thing for china vases or stirred it into the wheat cokes? Have I been chewing divine grace all the morning? Where's that prayer7book ? Going to get that prayer-book before the Revelations come to pass?" and Mr. Spoopen- dyke plunged around the room, tumbling books about and breathing heavily. "I don't see the use of making such a fuss over a thing you don't really need," sobbed Mrs. Spoopendyke through her indignant tears. "Oh, you don't," raved Mr. Spoopendyke. "You don't see any use in putting things where they belong, either, do you? How d'ye s'pose I'm going to keep up with religion without a praver•book ? How d'ye s'pose I'm going to know when it's my turn to show what Christianity has done for me unless you find that dod-gasted book between now and the resurrection?" and Mr. Spoopendyke spun around on his heel like a top, and knocked over a Parian jar. "Wit a minute my dear," said Mrs. Spoopendyke, look- ing at him earnestly. Then she went behind him and fished Out the prayer-book. " Got it, didn't you," he growled. "Had it all the time, I s'pose. Where was it, any way ? " "In your coat-tail pocket, dear." and Mrs. Spoopendyke jabbed the powder puff in her eyes and stalked downstairs, leaving her liege to follow.—Brooklyn Eagle.
